19--- ## Behavioral Equivaleence
20-
21--- In an earlier chapter, we investigated the correctness of a very simple
22--- program transformation: the `optimize0plus` function. The programming
23--- language we were considering was the first version of the language of
24--- arithmetic expressions -- with no variables -- so in that setting it was
25--- very easy to define what it means for a program transformation to be
26--- correct: it should always yield a program that evaluates to the same number
27--- as the original.
28-
29--- To talk about the correctness of program transformations for the full Imp
30--- language -- in particular, assignment -- we need to consider the role of
31--- mutable state and develop a more sophisticated notion of correctness, which
32--- we'll call *behavioral equivalence*.
33-
34--- For example:
35-
36--- - `X + 2` is behaviorally equivalent to `1 + X + 1`
37--- - `X - X` is behaviorally equivalent to `0`
38--- - `(X - 1) + 1` is *not* behaviorally equivalent to `X`
39-
40--- ### Definitions
41-
42--- For `aexp`s and `bexp`s with variables, the definition we want is clear:
43--- Two `aexp`s or `bexp`s are "behaviorally equivalent" if they evaluate to
44--- the same result in every state.
45-
46-def Aexp.Equiv (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : Prop :=
47-  ∀ (st : State),
48-    a₁.eval st = a₂.eval st
49-
50-theorem Aexp.equiv_def {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} :
51-    a₁.Equiv a₂ ↔ ∀ (st : State), a₁.eval st = a₂.eval st := by rfl
52-
53-def Bexp.Equiv (b₁ b₂ : Bexp) : Prop :=
54-  ∀ (st : State),
55-    b₁.eval st = b₂.eval st
56-
57-theorem Bexp.equiv_def {b₁ b₂ : Bexp} :
58-    b₁.Equiv b₂ ↔ ∀ (st : State), b₁.eval st = b₂.eval st := by rfl
59-
60--- Here are some simple examples of equivalences of arithmetic and boolean
61--- expressions.
62-
63-example : Aexp.Equiv
64-    (aexp { X - X })
65-    (aexp { 0 }) := by
66-  rw [Aexp.equiv_def]
67-  intro st
68-  simp
69-
70-example : Bexp.Equiv
71-    (bexp { X - X = 0 })
72-    (bexp { true }) := by
73-  rw [Bexp.equiv_def]
74-  intro st
75-  simp
76-
77--- For commands, the situation is a little more subtle. We can't simply say
78--- "two commands are behaviorally equivalent if they evaluate to the same
79--- ending state whenever they are started in the same initial state," because
80--- some commands, when run in some starting states, don't terminate in any
81--- final state at all!
82-
83--- What we need instead is this: two commands are behaviorally equivalent if,
84--- for any given starting state, they either (1) both diverge or else (2) both
85--- terminate in the same final state. A compact way to express this is "if the
86--- first one terminates in a particular state then so does the second, and
87--- vice versa."
88-
89-def Com.Equiv (c₁ c₂ : Com) : Prop :=
90-    ∀ {st st' : State},
91-      (st =[ c₁ ]=> st') ↔ (st =[ c₂ ]=> st')
92-
93-theorem Com.equiv_def {c₁ c₂ : Com} : c₁.Equiv c₂ ↔
94-    ∀ {st st' : State}, (st =[ c₁ ]=> st') ↔ (st =[ c₂ ]=> st') := by rfl
95-
96--- ### Simple Examples
97-
98-namespace Com
99-
100--- For examples of command equivalence, let's start by looking at a trivial
101--- equivalence involving `skip`.
102-
103-theorem skip_left {c : Com} : (imp { skip; ~c }).Equiv c := by
104-  rw [equiv_def]
105-  intro st st''
106-  constructor
107-  · intro h
108-    inversion h with
109-    | seq st' h1 h2 =>
110-      inversion h1
111-      exact h2
112-  · intro h
113-    exact EvalR.seq EvalR.skip h
114-
115--- ### Exercise (2 stars): skip_right ⭐⭐
116-
117--- Prove that adding a `skip` *after* a command also results in an equivalent
118--- program.
119-
120-theorem skip_right {c : Com} : (imp { ~c; skip }).Equiv c := by
121-  rw [equiv_def]
122-  intro st st''
123-  constructor
124-  · intro h
125-    inversion h with
126-    | seq st' h1 h2 =>
127-      inversion h2
128-      exact h1
129-  · intro h
130-    exact EvalR.seq h EvalR.skip

132--- Similarly, here is a simple equivalence that optimises `if` commands.
133-
134-theorem if_true_simple {c₁ c₂ : Com} : (imp {if (true) {~c₁} else {~c₂}}).Equiv c₁ := by
135-  rw [equiv_def]
136-  intro st st'
137-  constructor
138-  · intro h
139-    inversion h with
140-    | ifTrue hb hc => exact hc
141-    | ifFalse hb hc => simp at hb
142-  · intro h
143-    apply EvalR.ifTrue _ h
144-    simp
145-
146--- Of course, no programmer would write a conditional whose condition is
147--- literally `true`. (At least, no human programmer -- compilers and macro
148--- preprocessors do this sort of thing internally all the time!) But they
149--- might write one whose condition is *equivalent* to true:
150-
151--- Note to developers (Sati @satiscugcat):
152---     The to_verso script seems to use `\[\]` blocks, but these seem to cause
153---     problems with the tilde. Currently skipping them and just using
154---     backticks.
155-
156--- *Theorem*: If `b` is equivalent to `true`, then `if (~b) {~c₁}
157--- else {~c₂}`
158--- is equivalent to `c₁`. *Proof*:
159-
160--- - (`->`) We must show, for all `st` and `st'`, that if
161---   `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'` then `st =[ c₁ ]=> st'`.
162-
163---   Proceed by cases on the rules that could possibly have been used to show
164---   `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'`, namely `Com.EvalR.ifTrue`
165---   and `Com.EvalR.ifFalse`.
166-
167---   - Suppose the final rule in the derivation of
168---     `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'` was `Com.EvalR.ifTrue`. We
169---     then have, by the premises of `Com.EvalR.ifTrue`, that `st =[ c₁ ]=> st'`.
170---     This is exactly what we set out to prove.
171-
172---   - On the other hand, suppose the final rule in the derivation of
173---     `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'` was `Com.EvalR.ifFalse`. We
174---     then know that `b.eval st = false` and `st =[ c₂ ]=> st'`.
175-
176---     Recall that `b` is equivalent to `true`, i.e., forall `st`,
177---     `b.eval st = (bexp {true}).eval st`. In particular, this means that
178---     `b.eval st = true`, since `(bexp {true}).eval st = true`. But this is a
179---     contradiction, since `Com.EvalR.ifFalse` requires that `b.eval st = false`.
180---     Thus, the final rule could not have been `Com.EvalR.ifFalse`.
181-
182--- - (`<-`) We must show, for all `st` and `st'`, that if `st =[ c₁ ]=> st'`
183---   then `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'`.
184-
185---   Since `b` is equivalent to `true`, we know that `b.eval st` =
186---   `(bexp {true}).eval st = true` = `true`. Together with the assumption that
187---   `st =[ c₁ ]=> st'`, we can apply `Com.EvalR.ifTrue` to derive
188---   `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'`.
189-
190--- Here is the formal version of this proof:
191-
192-theorem if_true {b : Bexp} {c₁ c₂ : Com} (hb : b.Equiv (bexp {true})) :
193-    (imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}}).Equiv c₁ := by
194-  rw [equiv_def]
195-  rw [Bexp.equiv_def] at hb
196-  intro st st'
197-  constructor
198-  · intro h
199-    inversion h with
200-    | ifTrue hb' hc =>
201-      exact hc
202-    | ifFalse hb' hc =>
203-      rw [hb] at hb'
204-      simp at hb'
205-  · intro h
206-    apply EvalR.ifTrue _ h
207-    rw [hb]
208-    simp

236-    (imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}}).Equiv
237-    (imp {if (¬ ~b) {~c₂} else {~c₁}}) := by

258--- For `while` loops, we can give a similar pair of theorems. A loop whose
259--- guard is equivalent to `false` is equivalent to `skip`, while a loop whose
260--- guard is equivalent to `true` is equivalent to `while (true) {skip;} end`
261--- (or any other non-terminating program).
262-
263--- The first of these facts is easy.
264-
265-theorem while_false_equiv {b : Bexp} {c : Com} (hb : b.Equiv (bexp {false})) :
266-    (imp {while (~b) {~c}}).Equiv
267-    (imp {skip}) := by
268-  rw [equiv_def]
269-  rw [Bexp.equiv_def] at hb
270-  intro st st''
271-  constructor
272-  · intro h
273-    inversion h with
274-    | whileFalse => exact EvalR.skip
275-    | whileTrue st' hb' hc hloop =>
276-      simp [hb] at hb'
277-  · intro h
278-    inversion h
279-    apply EvalR.whileFalse
280-    simp [hb]

282--- ### Exercise (2 stars): while_false_informal (Advanced, manually graded) ⭐⭐
283-
284--- Write an informal proof of `while_false_equiv`.
285-
286--- To prove the second fact, we need an auxiliary lemma stating that `while`
287--- loops whose guards are equivalent to `true` never terminate.
288-
289--- *Lemma*: If `b` is equivalent to `true`, then it cannot be the case that
290--- `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`.
291-
292--- *Proof*: Suppose that `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`. We show, by
293--- induction on a derivation of `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`, that this
294--- assumption leads to a contradiction. The only two cases to consider are
295--- `Com.EvalR.whileFalse` and `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`; the others are
296--- contradictory.
297-
298--- - Suppose `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` is proved using rule
299---   `Com.EvalR.whileFalse`. Then by assumption `b.eval st = false`. But this
300---   contradicts the assumption that `b` is equivalent to `true`.
301-
302--- - Suppose `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` is proved using rule
303---   `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`. We must have:
304-
305---   1. `b.eval st = true`, and
306-
307---   2. there is some `st₀` such that `st =[ c ] => st₀` and
308---      `st₀ =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`.
309-
310---   3. Also, we are given an induction hypothesis saying that
311---      `st₀ =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` leads to a contradiction,
312-
313---   We obtain a contradiction by 2 and 3.
314-
315-theorem while_true_nonterm {b : Bexp} {c : Com} {st st' : State} (hb : b.Equiv (bexp {true})) :
316-    ¬ st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st' := by
317-  intro contra
318-  generalize heq : (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) = com at contra
319-  induction contra with
320-  | @whileFalse b' s0 c0 hb' =>
321-    injection heq with hbeq hceq
322-    subst hbeq
323-    rw [Bexp.equiv_def] at hb
324-    simp [hb] at hb'
325-  | @whileTrue s0 s0' s0'' b' c0 hb' hc' hwhile ih1 ih2 =>
326-    exact ih2 heq
327-  | skip | asgn | seq | ifTrue | ifFalse =>
328-    contradiction -- heq says that different commands are equal
329-
330--- ### Exercise (2 stars): while_true_nonterm_informal (manually graded) ⭐⭐
331-
332--- Explain what the lemma `while_true_nonterm` means in English.

334--- ### Exercise (2 stars): while_true ⭐⭐
335-
336--- Prove the following theorem. *Hint*: You'll want to use
337--- `while_true_nonterm` here.
338-
339-theorem while_true {b : Bexp} {c : Com} (hb : b.Equiv (bexp {true})) :
340-    (imp {while (~b) {~c}}).Equiv
341-    (imp {while (true) {skip}}) := by
342-  rw [equiv_def]
343-  intro st st'
344-  constructor
345-  · intro h
346-    exfalso
347-    exact while_true_nonterm hb h
348-  · intro h
349-    exfalso
350-    apply while_true_nonterm _ h
351-    rw [Bexp.equiv_def]
352-    intro
353-    rfl

355--- A more interesting fact about `while` commands is that any number of copies
356--- of the body can be "unrolled" without changing meaning.
357-
358--- Loop unrolling is an important transformation in any real compiler, so its
359--- correctness is of more than just academic interest!
360-
361-theorem loop_unrolling {b : Bexp} {c : Com} :
362-    (imp {while (~b) {~c}}).Equiv
363-    (imp {
364-      if (~b) {~c} else {skip};
365-      while (~b) {~c}
366-    }) := by
367-  rw [equiv_def]
368-  intro st st'
369-  constructor
370-  · intro h
371-    inversion h with
372-    | whileFalse hb =>
373-      apply EvalR.seq (st' := st)
374-      · exact EvalR.ifFalse hb EvalR.skip
375-      · exact EvalR.whileFalse hb
376-    | whileTrue stmid hb hc hloop =>
377-      apply EvalR.seq _ hloop
378-      exact EvalR.ifTrue hb hc
379-  · intro h
380-    inversion h with
381-    | seq stmid h1 h2 =>
382-      inversion h1 with
383-      | ifTrue hb hc =>
384-        exact EvalR.whileTrue hb hc h2
385-      | ifFalse hb hc =>
386-        inversion hc
387-        exact h2

442--- ## Properties of Behavior Equivalence
443-
444--- We next consider some fundamental properties of program equivalence.
445-
446--- ### Behavioral Equivalence is an Equivalence
447-
448--- First, let's verify that the equivalences on `Aexp`s, `Bexp`s, and `Com`s
449--- really are *equivalences* -- ie, that they are reflexive, symmetric, and
450--- transitive. These proofs are all easy.
451-
452-end Com
453-
454-theorem Aexp.equiv_refl (a : Aexp) : a.Equiv a := by
455-  rw [equiv_def]
456-  intro st
457-  rfl
458-
459-theorem Aexp.equiv_symm {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} (h : a₁.Equiv a₂) : a₂.Equiv a₁ := by
460-  rw [equiv_def] at h ⊢
461-  intro st
462-  rw [h]
463-
464-theorem Aexp.equiv_trans {a₁ a₂ a₃ : Aexp} (h₁ : a₁.Equiv a₂) (h₂ : a₂.Equiv a₃) :
465-    a₁.Equiv a₃ := by
466-  rw [equiv_def] at h₁ h₂ ⊢
467-  intro st
468-  rw [h₁, h₂]
469-
470-theorem Bexp.equiv_refl {b : Bexp} : b.Equiv b := by
471-  rw [equiv_def]
472-  intro st
473-  rfl
474-
475-theorem Bexp.equiv_symm {b₁ b₂ : Bexp} (h : b₁.Equiv b₂) : b₂.Equiv b₁ := by
476-  rw [equiv_def]
477-  intro st
478-  rw [h]
479-
480-theorem Bexp.equiv_trans {b₁ b₂ b₃ : Bexp} (h₁ : b₁.Equiv b₂) (h₂ : b₂.Equiv b₃) :
481-    b₁.Equiv b₃ := by
482-  rw [equiv_def]
483-  intro st
484-  rw [h₁, h₂]
485-
486-theorem Com.equiv_refl {c : Com} : c.Equiv c := by
487-  rewrite [equiv_def]
488-  intro st st'
489-  rfl
490-
491-theorem Com.equiv_symm {c₁ c₂ : Com} (h : c₁.Equiv c₂) : c₂.Equiv c₁ := by
492-  rw [equiv_def] at h ⊢
493-  intro st st'
494-  rw [h]
495-
496-theorem Com.equiv_trans {c₁ c₂ c₃ : Com} (h₁ : c₁.Equiv c₂) (h₂ : c₂.Equiv c₃) :
497-    c₁.Equiv c₃ := by
498-  rw [equiv_def] at h₁ h₂ ⊢
499-  intro st st'

502--- ### Behavioral Equivalence is a Congruence
503-
504--- Less obviously, behavioral equivalence is also a *congruence*. That is, the
505--- equivalence of two subprograms implies the equivalence of the larger
506--- programs in which they are embedded:
507-
508--- aequiv a a' ------------------------- cequiv (x := a) (x := a')
509-
510--- cequiv c1 c1' cequiv c2 c2' -------------------------- cequiv (c1;c2)
511--- (c1';c2')
512-
513--- ... and so on for the other forms of commands.
514-
515--- (Note that we are using the inference rule notation here not as part of an
516--- inductive definition, but simply to write down some valid implications in a
517--- readable format. We prove these implications below.)
518-
519--- We will see a concrete example of why these congruence properties are
520--- important in the following section (in the proof of
521--- `fold_constants_com_sound`), but the main idea is that they allow us to
522--- replace a small part of a large program with an equivalent small part and
523--- know that the whole large programs are equivalent *without* doing an
524--- explicit proof about the parts that didn't change -- i.e., the "proof
525--- burden" of a small change to a large program is proportional to the size of
526--- the change, not the program!
527-
528-theorem Com.congruence.asgn {x : Ident} {a a' : Aexp} (ha : a.Equiv a') :
529-    (imp {x := ~a}).Equiv
530-    (imp {x := ~a'}) := by
531-  rw [equiv_def]
532-  intro st st'
533-  constructor <;>
534-  · intro h
535-    inversion h with
536-    | asgn n h =>
537-      subst h
538-      apply Com.EvalR.asgn
539-      rw [Aexp.equiv_def] at ha
540-      rw [ha]
541-
542--- The congruence property for loops is a little more interesting, since it
543--- requires induction.
544-
545--- *Theorem*: Equivalence is a congruence for `while` -- that is, if `b` is
546--- equivalent to `b'` and `c` is equivalent to `c'`, then `while (~b) {~c}` is
547--- equivalent to `while (~b') {~c'}`.
548-
549--- *Proof*: Suppose `b` is equivalent to `b'` and `c` is equivalent to `c'`.
550--- We must show, for every `st` and `st'`, that
551--- `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` iff `st = while (~b') {~c'}
552--- ]=> st'`. We
553--- consider the two directions separately.
554-
555--- - (`->`) We show that `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` implies
556---   `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`, by induction on a derivation of
557---   `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`. The only nontrivial cases are when the
558---   final rule in the derivation is `Com.EvalR.whileFalse` or
559---   `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`.
560-
561---   - `Com.EvalR.whileFalse`: In this case, the form of the rule gives us
562---     `beval st b = false` and `st = st'`. But then, since `b` and `b'` are
563---     equivalent, we have `beval st b' =false`, and `Com.EvalR.whileFalse`
564---     applies, giving us `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`, as required.
565-
566---   - `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`: The form of the rule now gives us
567---     `beval st b = true`, with `st =[ c ]=> st'0` and
568---     `st'0 =[ while {~b} {~c} ]=> st'` for some state `st'0`, with the induction
569---     hypothesis `st'0 =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`.
570-
571---     Since `c` and `c'` are equivalent, we know that `st =[ c']=> st'0`. And
572---     since `b` and `b'` are equivalent, we have `beval st b' = true`. Now
573---     `Com.EvalR.whileTrue` applies, giving us `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`,
574---     as required.
575-
576--- - (`<-`) Similar.

54-
55--- In an earlier chapter, we began applying the mathematical tools developed
56--- in the first part of the course to studying the theory of a small
57--- programming language, Imp.
58-
59--- - We defined a type of *abstract syntax trees* for Imp, together with an
60---   *evaluation relation* (a partial function on states) that specifies the
61---   *operational semantics* of programs.
62-
63---   The language we defined, though small, captures some of the key features of
64---   full-blown languages like C, C++, and Java, including the fundamental
65---   notion of mutable state and some common control structures.
66-
67--- - We proved a number of *metatheoretic properties* -- "meta" in the sense
68---   that they are properties of the language as a whole, rather than of
69---   particular programs in the language. These included:
70-
71---   - determinism of evaluation
72-
73---   - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the definitions (e.g.,
74---     functional and relational definitions of arithmetic expression evaluation)
75-
76---   - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
77-
78---   - correctness (in the sense of preserving meaning) of a number of useful
79---     program transformations
80-
81---   - behavioral equivalence of programs (in the Equiv chapter).
82-
83--- If we stopped here, we would already have something useful: a set of tools
84--- for defining and discussing programming languages and language features
85--- that are mathematically precise, flexible, and easy to work with, applied
86--- to a set of key properties. All of these properties are things that
87--- language designers, compiler writers, and users might care about knowing.
88--- Indeed, many of them are so fundamental to our understanding of the
89--- programming languages we deal with that we might not consciously recognize
90--- them as "theorems." But properties that seem intuitively obvious can
91--- sometimes be quite subtle (sometimes also subtly wrong!).
92-
93--- In another volume of this series (*Type Systems*), we expand upon the theme
94--- of metatheoretic properties of whole languages when we discuss *types* and
95--- *type soundness*. In this chapter, though, we turn to a different set of
96--- issues.
97-
98--- Our goal in this chapter is to develop the tools to work through some
99--- simple examples of *program verification* -- i.e., to use the precise
100--- definition of Imp to prove formally that particular programs satisfy
101--- particular specifications of their behavior.
102-
103--- We'll develop a reasoning system called *Floyd-Hoare Logic* -- often
104--- shortened to just *Hoare Logic* -- in which each of the syntactic
105--- constructs of Imp is equipped with a generic "proof rule" that can be used
106--- to reason compositionally about the correctness of programs involving this
107--- construct.
108-
109--- Hoare Logic originated in the 1960s, and it continues to be the subject of
110--- intensive research right up to the present day. It lies at the core of a
111--- multitude of tools that are being used in academia and industry to specify
112--- and verify real software systems.
113-
114--- Hoare Logic combines two beautiful ideas: a natural way of writing down
115--- *specifications* of programs, and a *structured proof technique* for
116--- proving that programs are correct with respect to such specifications --
117--- where by "structured" we mean that the structure of proofs directly mirrors
118--- the structure of the programs that they are about.
119-

121---     `HIDE: MRC'20: The terse version used to start with just an outline of
122---     what we've done and of this chapter, but it never mentioned Hoare logic!
123---     The text above seems like a better intro.
124---

126---
127---      What we've done so far:
128---
129---      - Formalized Imp
130---           - identifiers and states
131---           - abstract syntax trees
132---           - evaluation functions (for [aexp]s and [bexp]s)
133---           - evaluation relation (for commands)
134---
135---      - Proved some _metatheoretic_ properties
136---          - determinism of evaluation
137---          - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the
138---            definitions (e.g., functional and relational definitions of
139---            arithmetic expression evaluation)
140---          - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
141---          - meaning-preservation of some program transformations
142---          - behavioral equivalence of programs ([Equiv])
143---
144---      We've dealt with a few sorts of properties of Imp programs:
145---        - Termination
146---        - Nontermination
147---        - Equivalence
148---
149---      Topic:
150---        - A systematic method for reasoning about the _functional
151---          correctness_ of programs in Imp
152---
153---      Goals:
154---        - a natural notation for _program specifications_ and
155---        - a _compositional_ proof technique for program correctness
156---
157---      Plan:
158---        - specifications (assertions / Hoare triples)
159---        - proof rules
160---        - loop invariants
161---        - decorated programs
162---        - examples`

164--- ## Assertions
165-
166--- An *assertion* is a logical claim about the state of a program's memory --
167--- formally, a predicate of `State`s.
168-
169-open scoped Com MyGetElem
170-
171-abbrev Assertion := State → Prop
172-
173--- Note to developers:
174---     HIDE: MRC'20: pulled up these examples from the quiz/optional exercise
175---     so that there would be some modeling of the kinds of answers we expect.
176-
177--- For example,
178-
179--- - `fun st => st[X] = 3` holds for states `st` in which value of `X` is `3`,
180--- - `fun st => True` hold for all states, and
181--- - `fun st => False` holds for no states.
182-
183--- _Quiz:_
184-
185--- Paraphrase the following assertions in English (i.e., say which states
186--- satisfy them)
187-
188--- (A) `fun st => st[X] ≤ st[Y]`
189-
190--- (B) `fun st => st[X] = 3 ∨ st[X] ≤ st[Y]`
191-
192--- (C)
193--- `fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧ ¬ ((st[Z] + 1) * (st[Z] + 1) ≤ st[X])`

196-

198--- language).

201-def assertion1 : Assertion := fun st => st[X] ≤ st[Y]
202-def assertion2 : Assertion :=
203-  fun st => st[X] = 3 ∨ st[X] ≤ st[Y]
204-def assertion3 : Assertion :=
205-  fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧
206-            ¬ ((st[Z] + 1) * (st[Z] + 1) ≤ st[X])
207-def assertion4 : Assertion :=
208-  fun st => st[Z] = max st[X] st[Y]
209-
210--- 1. The value of X is less or equal than the value of Y.
211--- 2. The value of X is 3 or is less or equal than the value of Y.
212--- 3. The value of Z is the integer square root of X.
213--- 4. The value of Z is the greater of the values of X and Y

217--- ### Notations for Assertions
218-
219--- This way of writing assertions can be a little bit heavy, for two reasons:
220--- (1) every single assertion that we ever write is going to begin with
221--- `fun st => `; and (2) this state `st` is the only one that we ever use to
222--- look up variables in assertions (we will almost never need to talk about
223--- two different memory states at the same time). For discussing examples
224--- informally, we'll adopt some simplifying conventions: we'll drop the
225--- initial `fun st =>`, and we'll write just `X` to mean `st[X]`. Thus,
226--- instead of writing
227-
228---   fun st => st[X] = m
229-
230--- we'll write just
231-
232---   {{ X = m }}.
233-
234--- Here the "doubly curly" braces `{{` and `}}` delimit the scope of an
235--- assertion. We'll see more examples below.
236-
237--- This example also illustrates a convention that we'll use throughout the
238--- Hoare Logic chapters: in informal assertions, capital letters like `X`,
239--- `Y`, and `Z` are Imp variables, while lowercase letters like `x`, `y`, `m`,
240--- and `n` are ordinary Lean variables (of type `Nat`). This is why, when
241--- translating from informal to formal, we replace `X` with `st[X]` but leave
242--- `m` alone.
243-

273--- magic, using coercions and a custom grammar, much as we did with the
274--- `imp { … }` notation in Imp. This new notation automatically lifts `Aexp`s,
275--- numbers, and `Prop`s into `Assertion`s when they appear between the
276--- `{{ _ }}` brackets, or when Lean knows that the type of an expression is
277--- `Assertion`.

332-  match stx with
333-  | `(assn($st; $t:term)) =>
334-    let t ← elabTerm t none
335-    let ty ← Meta.inferType t
336-    -- if (← Meta.isDefEq ty (mkConst ``_root_.Ident)) then -- this incorrectly assigns metavariables
337-    if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Ident) then
338-      return mkApp6 (mkConst ``_root_.MyGetElem.getElem)
339-        (mkApp2 (mkConst ``TotalMap) (mkConst ``String) (mkConst ``Nat))
340-        (mkConst ``String)
341-        (mkConst ``Nat)
342-        (← Meta.synthInstance <| mkApp3 (mkConst ``_root_.MyGetElem)
343-          (mkApp2 (mkConst ``TotalMap) (mkConst ``String) (mkConst ``Nat))
344-          (mkConst ``String)
345-          (mkConst ``Nat))
346-        (← elabTerm st none) t
347-    if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Aexp) then -- Detect an embedded `Aexp` and turn it into `Aexp.eval st t`
348-      return (mkApp2 (mkConst ``Aexp.eval) (← elabTerm st none) t)
349-    else if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Bexp) then  -- Detect an embedded `Bexp` and turn it into `Bexp.eval st t`
350-      return (mkApp2 (mkConst ``Bexp.eval) (← elabTerm st none) t)
351-    else if ty.isMVar then -- This is a hack to guard against `Meta.isDefEq` assigning the type to be an `Assertion`
352-      return t
353-    else if (← Meta.isDefEq ty (mkConst ``_root_.Assertion)) then
354-      return mkApp t (← elabTerm st none)
355-    else
356-      return t
357-  | _ => throwUnsupportedSyntax

359--- `: Assertion` guards that the resulting type is `State → Prop`.
360-macro_rules
361-  | `({{ $t }}) => `((fun st : _root_.State => assn(st; $t) : Assertion))
362-
363-macro_rules
364-  | `(assn($st; ($P))) => ``((assn($st; $P)))
365-  | `(assn($st; $l = $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) = assn($st; $r))
366-  | `(assn($st; $l + $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) + assn($st; $r))
367-  | `(assn($st; $l - $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) - assn($st; $r))
368-  | `(assn($st; $l * $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) * assn($st; $r))
369-  | `(assn($st; $l ≤ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ≤ assn($st; $r))
370-  | `(assn($st; $l < $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) < assn($st; $r))
371-  | `(assn($st; $l ≥ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ≥ assn($st; $r))
372-  | `(assn($st; $l > $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) > assn($st; $r))
373-  | `(assn($st; $l ∧ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ∧ assn($st; $r))
374-  | `(assn($st; $l ∨ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ∨ assn($st; $r))
375-  | `(assn($st; $l → $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) → assn($st; $r))
376-  | `(assn($st; $l ↔ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ↔ assn($st; $r))
377-  | `(assn($st; ¬ $t)) => ``(¬ assn($st; $t))
378-  | `(assn($st; $f $args*)) => do
379-    let mut result := f
380-    for arg in args do
381-      result ← `($result assn($st; $arg))
382-    return result
383-end

429--- Function applications inside assertions automatically interpret their
430--- arguments in the current state. Thus, `{{ f e1 ... en }}` stands for
431--- `fun st => f (e1 st) ... (en st)`.
432-
433--- Occasionally it is simpler to write an assertion directly as a Lean
434--- function. Such a function can be placed inside the assertion notation
435--- without an escape marker.
436-
437--- For example, `{{ fun st => ∀ x, st[x] = 0 }}` indicates an assertion that
438--- every variable maps to `0` in the given state.

440--- ### Example Assertions
441-
442--- Here are some example assertions that take advantage of this new notation.
443-
444-namespace ExamplePrettyAssertions
445-
446-def assertion1 : Assertion := {{ X = 3 }}
447-def assertion2 : Assertion := {{ True }}
448-def assertion3 : Assertion := {{ False }}
449-def assertion4 : Assertion := {{ True ∨ False }}
450-def assertion5 : Assertion := {{ X ≤ Y }}
451-def assertion6 : Assertion := {{ X = 3 ∨ X ≤ Y }}
452-def assertion7 : Assertion := {{ Z = max X Y }}
453-def assertion8 : Assertion := {{ Z * Z ≤ X
454-                                 ∧ ¬ (((Nat.succ Z) * (Nat.succ Z)) ≤ X) }}
455-def assertion9 : Assertion := {{ Nat.add X Y > max Y X }}
456-variable {xs : List Nat}
457--- #check {{ xs = X }}
458-/--
459-info: def ExamplePrettyAssertions.assertion8 : Assertion :=
460-fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧ ¬st[Z].succ * st[Z].succ ≤ st[X]
461--/
462-#guard_msgs in
463-#print assertion8

465-end ExamplePrettyAssertions

467--- ### Printing Assertions
468-
469--- As in the Imp chapter, the assertion notation above is *input* only: Lean
470--- reads `{{ X ≤ 5 }}` but still prints the underlying function, as
471--- `#print assertion8` just showed. The delaborators below close the loop for
472--- plain assertions: a state lambda whose body Lean can rebuild is printed
473--- back in `{{ … }}` notation, and an assertion Lean cannot rebuild falls back
474--- to the raw `fun st => …` form, which is exactly this notation's escape
475--- syntax, so what you see is always valid input. Each time a new notation
476--- involving assertions appears below (implication, Hoare triples,
477--- substitution), a small delaborator defined next to it will extend this
478--- printing to cover it. As before, there is no need to understand the
479--- details.
480-
481--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing assertions back
482-
483-namespace Assertion.Delab
484-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
485-
486-/-- Rebuild the surface form of an assertion body, undoing the state
487-threading the `assn` elaborator performs: `st[X]` prints as `X`,
488-`Aexp.eval st a` as `a`, `Bexp.eval st b = true` as `b`, an applied
489-assertion `P st` as `P`, and a subterm that does not mention the state
490-prints as itself. -/
491-partial def delabBody (stId : FVarId) : DelabM Term := do
492-  let e ← getExpr
493-  if !e.containsFVar stId then
494-    delab
495-  else
496-    match_expr e with
497-    | MyGetElem.getElem _ _ _ _ st _ =>
498-      guard (st == .fvar stId)
499-      withNaryArg 5 delab
500-    | Aexp.eval st _ =>
501-      guard (st == .fvar stId)
502-      withAppArg delab
503-    | HAdd.hAdd _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
504-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) + $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
505-    | HSub.hSub _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
506-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) - $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
507-    | HMul.hMul _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
508-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) * $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
509-    | Eq _ l r =>
510-      -- `Bexp.eval st b = true` is the threaded form of a bare boolean `b`
511-      if r.isConstOf ``Bool.true && l.isAppOfArity ``Bexp.eval 2
512-          && l.appFn!.appArg! == .fvar stId then
513-        withNaryArg 1 <| withAppArg delab
514-      else
515-        `($(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)) = $(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)))
516-    | Ne _ _ _ =>
517-      `($(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)) ≠ $(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)))
518-    | LE.le _ _ _ _ =>
519-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) ≤ $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
520-    | LT.lt _ _ _ _ =>
521-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) < $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
522-    | GE.ge _ _ _ _ =>
523-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) ≥ $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
524-    | GT.gt _ _ _ _ =>

581--- ### Assertion Implication
582-
583--- Given two assertions `P` and `Q`, we say that `P` *implies* `Q`, written
584--- `P ->> Q`, if, whenever `P` holds in some state `st`, `Q` also holds.
585-
586-def AssertImplies (P Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
587-  ∀ st, P st → Q st
588-
589--- Note that the notation for *assertion implication* is analogous to the
590--- "usual" Lean implication `→`.
591-
592-notation:26 P:27 " ->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q
593-
594-theorem assertImplies_def {P Q : Assertion} : P ->> Q ↔ ∀ st, P st → Q st := by rfl
595-
596--- We'll also want the "iff" variant of implication between assertions:
597-
598-notation:26 P:27 " <<->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
599-
600-theorem assertIff_def {P Q : Assertion} : P <<->> Q ↔ AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
601-    := by rfl
602-
603--- The matching delaborators print implications and equivalences between
604--- assertions back in `->>` and `<<->>` notation.

614-  `($(← delabAssnArg 0) ->> $(← delabAssnArg 1))

616-/-- `<<->>` abbreviates a conjunction of two `AssertImplies`, so its
617-delaborator is keyed on `∧` and bails out unless the two conjuncts mirror
618-each other. -/
619-@[delab app.And]
620-def delabAssertIff : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
621-  let e ← getExpr
622-  guard <| e.isAppOfArity ``And 2
623-  let l := e.appFn!.appArg!
624-  let r := e.appArg!
625-  guard <| l.isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2 && r.isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2
626-  guard <| l.appFn!.appArg! == r.appArg! && l.appArg! == r.appFn!.appArg!
627-  `($(← withNaryArg 0 <| delabAssnArg 0) <<->> $(← withNaryArg 0 <| delabAssnArg 1))

633--- ## Hoare Triples, Informally
634-
635--- A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing a
636--- command. A commond notation for Hoare triples, and the one we use in this
637--- book, is
638-
639---   {{P}} c {{Q}}
640-
641--- meaning:
642-
643--- - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
644--- - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
645--- - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
646-
647--- Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is the
648--- *postcondition*.
649-
650--- For example,
651-
652--- - The Hoare triple
653-
654---   {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
655-
656--- states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which `X = 0` to
657--- a state in which `X = 1`.
658-
659--- - On the other hand,
660-
661---   ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
662-
663--- is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
664--- `{{X = m}} X :=
665--- X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`. Note
666--- that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean* variable `m`,
667--- which is bound outside the Hoare triple.
668-
669--- _Quiz:_
670-
671--- Paraphrase the following in English.
672-
673---   1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}
674-
675---   2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
676-
677---   3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
678-
679---   4) {{True}} c {{False}}
680-
681---   5) ∀ m,
682---        {{X = m}}
683---        c
684---        {{Y = real_fact m}}
685-
686---   6) ∀ m,
687---        {{X = m}}
688---        c
689---        {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}
690-
691--- _Quiz:_
692-
693--- Is the following Hoare triple *valid* -- i.e., is the claimed relation
694--- between `P`, `c`, and `Q` true?
695-
696---   {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}
697-
698--- (A) Yes
699-
700--- (B) No
701-
702--- _Quiz:_
703-
704--- What about this one?
705-
706---   {{X = 2}} X := X + 1 {{X = 3}}
707-
708--- (A) Yes
709-
710--- (B) No
711-

713-
714--- What about this one?
715-
716---   {{True}} X := 5; Y := 0 {{X = 5}}
717-
718--- (A) Yes
719-

721-

724--- What about this one?

727-
728--- (A) Yes

738--- (A) Yes
739-

741-

748--- (A) Yes
749-

815--- ## Hoare Triples, Formally
816-
817--- We formalize valid Hoare triples in Lean as follows:
818-
819-open scoped HasEval
820-
821-def ValidHoareTriple
822-    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
823-  ∀ {st st' : State},
824-    (st =[ c ]=> st') →
825-    P st →
826-    Q st'
827-
828--- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
829---     Somethings strange is going on in `theorem if_example`, using
830---     `apply hoare_consequence_pre` followed by `· exact hoare_asgn` works,
831---     but `refine hoare_consequence_pre hoare_asgn ?_` or
832---     `apply hoare_consequence_pre hoare_asgn` don't. The only solution I
833---     found was to mark `ValidHoareTriple` irreducible.
834---
835---     It has to do something with `apply` and `refine` looking inside the
836---     implication in `∀ {st st'}, ...`
837-
838--- Notation for Hoare triples. The command between the two assertions is
839--- parsed with the same grammar as the `imp { … }` notation, so a command that
840--- is a Lean variable (rather than concrete syntax) is spliced in with `~c`,
841--- just as in the `st =[ c ]=> st'` notation.
842-
843-class HasTriple (Com : Type) where
844-  Triple : Assertion → Com → Assertion → Prop
845-
846-namespace HasTriple
847-
848-/-- Hoare triple: `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` -/
849-scoped notation:lead "{{" P "}} " c:lead " {{" Q "}}" => Triple ({{ P }}) c ({{ Q }})
850-
851-/-- Hoare triple with `imp_com` command syntax -/
852-scoped syntax:lead (priority := high) "{{" term "}} " imp_com:lead " {{" term "}}" : term
853-scoped macro_rules
854-  | `({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }}) =>
855-      ``(HasTriple.Triple ({{ $P }}) (imp { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
856-end HasTriple
857-
858-instance : HasTriple Com where
859-  Triple := ValidHoareTriple
860-
861-open scoped HasTriple
862-
863-theorem validHoareTriple_def {P : Assertion} {c : Com} {Q : Assertion} :
864-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} ↔ ∀ {st st' : State},
865-      (st =[ c ]=> st') →
866-      P st →
867-      Q st' := by rfl
868-
869-attribute [irreducible] ValidHoareTriple
870-
871--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing triples back
872-
873--- The delaborator is agnostic to the command type: it prints the command with
874--- whatever printer is registered for its constructors and splices the result
875--- into the triple, so a language-extension chapter only has to register a
876--- printer for its own `Com`.
877-
878-namespace Assertion.Delab
879-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
880-@[delab app.HasTriple.Triple]
881-def delabTriple : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
882-  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``HasTriple.Triple 5
883-  let P ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssn
884-  let c ← withNaryArg 3 delab
885-  let Q ← withNaryArg 4 delabAssn
886-  match c with
887-  | `(imp { $c:imp_com }) => ``({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }})
888-  | c => ``({{ $P }} ~$c {{ $Q }})
889-
890-end Assertion.Delab

897--- ### Exercise (1 star): hoare_post_true ⭐
898-
899--- Prove that if `Q` holds in every state, then any triple with `Q` as its
900--- postcondition is valid.
901-
902-theorem hoare_post_true {P Q : Assertion} {c : Com} (h : ∀ st, Q st) :
903-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
904-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
905-  intro st st' hc hpre
906-  exact h st'

908--- ### Exercise (1 star): hoare_pre_false (Optional) ⭐
909-
910--- Prove that if `P` holds in no state, then any triple with `P` as its
911--- precondition is valid.
912-
913-theorem hoare_pre_false {P Q : Assertion} {c : Com} (h : ∀ st, ¬ (P st)) :
914-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
915-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
916-  intro st st' hc hpre
917-  specialize h st
918-  contradiction

920--- ## Proof Rules
921-
922--- The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for proving
923--- the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the structure of a
924--- program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of the program itself.
925--- To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce a rule for reasoning
926--- about each of the different syntactic forms of commands in Imp -- one for
927--- assignment, one for sequencing, one for conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple
928--- of "structural" rules for gluing things together. We will then be able to
929--- prove programs correct using these proof rules, without ever unfolding the
930--- definition of `ValidHoareTriple`.
931-
932--- ### Skip
933-
934--- Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
935-
936---   --------------------  (hoare_skip)
937---   {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
938-
939-theorem hoare_skip {P : Assertion} :
940-    {{ P }} skip {{ P }} := by
941-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
942-  intro st st' h hpre
943-  inversion h
944-  exact hpre
945-
946--- ### Sequencing
947-
948--- If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q` holds,
949--- and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R` holds, then
950--- doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P` holds to one
951--- where `R` holds:
952-
953---    {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
954---    {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
955---   ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
956---   {{ P }} c1; c2 {{ R }}
957-
958-theorem hoare_seq {P Q R : Assertion} {c1 c2 : Com}
959-    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
960-    {{ P }} ~c1; ~c2 {{ R }} := by
961-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
962-  intro st st' h hpre
963-  inversion h with
964-  | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>
965-    rw [validHoareTriple_def] at h1 h2
966-    exact h1 hc2 (h2 hc1 hpre)
967-
968--- Note that, in the formal rule `hoare_seq`, the premises are given in
969--- backwards order (`c2` before `c1`). This matches the natural flow of
970--- information in many of the situations where we'll use the rule, since the
971--- natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end of the
972--- program (with the final postcondition) and push postconditions backwards
973--- through commands until we reach the beginning.
974-
975--- ### Assignment
976-
977--- The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic proof
978--- rules. Here's how it works.
979-
980--- Consider this incomplete Hoare triple:
981-
982---   {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
983-
984--- We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`. What
985--- could the precondition be?
986-
987--- One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then assigning it
988--- to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare triple:
989-
990---   {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
991-
992--- It may seem as though coming up with that precondition must have taken some
993--- clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done it: if we
994--- take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with `Y`---that is,
995--- replace the left-hand side of the assignment statement with the right-hand
996--- side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
997-
998--- That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
999-
1000---   {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
1001-
1002--- If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
1003--- again leads to a valid Hoare triple:
1004-
1005---   {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
1006-
1007--- Why does this technique work? The postcondition identifies some property
1008--- `P` that we want to hold of the variable `X` being assigned. In this case,
1009--- `P` is "equals `1`". To complete the triple and make it valid, we need to
1010--- identify a precondition that guarantees that property will hold of `X`.
1011--- Such a precondition must ensure that the same property holds of *whatever
1012--- is being assigned to* `X`. So, in the example, we need "equals `1`" to hold
1013--- of `X + Y`. That's exactly what the technique guarantees.
1014-
1015--- In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary assertion `Q`, and
1016--- the right-hand side of the assignment could be some arbitrary arithmetic
1017--- expression `a`:
1018-
1019---   {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
1020-
1021--- The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences of `X` in it
1022--- replaced by `a`.
1023-
1024--- Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing occurrences: Define
1025--- `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is substituted in place of `X`".
1026-
1027--- This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
1028-
1029---   {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
1030-
1031--- One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement `X := a` to
1032--- terminate in a state that satisfies assertion `Q`, then it suffices to
1033--- start in a state that also satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is substituted
1034--- for every occurrence of `X`.
1035-
1036--- To many people, this rule seems "backwards" at first, because it proceeds
1037--- from the postcondition to the precondition. Actually it makes good sense to
1038--- go in this direction: the postcondition is often what is more important,
1039--- because it characterizes what will be true after running the code.
1040-
1041--- Nonetheless, it's also possible to formulate a "forward" assignment rule.
1042--- We'll do that later in some exercises.
1043-
1044--- Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
1045-
1046---   {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}         (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
1047---     X := X + 1
1048---   {{ X ≤ 5 }}
1049-
1050---   {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }}              (that is, 3 = 3)
1051---     X := 3
1052---   {{ X = 3 }}
1053-
1054---   {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}.  (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
1055---     X := 3
1056---   {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
1057-
1058--- To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea of "substituting an
1059--- expression for an Imp variable in an assertion", which we refer to as
1060--- assertion substitution, or `Assertion.subst`.
1061-
1062--- Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`, and an arithmetic
1063--- expression `a`, we want to derive another proposition `P'` that is just the
1064--- same as `P` except that `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P` mentions `X`.
1065-
1066--- This operation is related to the idea of substituting Imp expressions for
1067--- Imp variables that we saw in *Equiv* (`subst_aexp` and friends). The
1068--- difference is that, here, `P` is an arbitrary Lean assertion, so we can't
1069--- directly "edit" its text.
1070-
1071--- However, we can achieve the same effect by evaluating `P` in an updated
1072--- state, defined as follows:
1073-
1074-def Assertion.subst (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) : Assertion :=
1075-  fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
1076-
1077--- Note to developers (One An @meluge, before next release):
1078---     Introduce a notation typeclass for this (e.g. HasSubst)
1079-
1080-namespace Assertion
1081-
1082-/-- Assertion substitution, written inside the braces: `{{ (P) [X ↦ a] }}`.
1083-The substituted assertion is re-read with the same notation, so Imp
1084-variables in it mean state lookups as usual; a named assertion is passed
1085-through directly. -/
1086-scoped syntax:max term:arg " [" ident " ↦ " imp_aexp "]" : term
1087-
1088-macro_rules
1089-  | `(assn($st; $P [$x ↦ $a:imp_aexp])) =>
1090-    match P with
1091-    | `($_:ident) => ``(Assertion.subst $x (aexp { $a }) $P $st)
1092-    | _ => ``(Assertion.subst $x (aexp { $a }) ({{ $P }}) $st)
1093-
1094-theorem subst_def {x : Ident} {a : Aexp} {P : Assertion} :
1095-    Assertion.subst x a P = fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st) := by rfl
1096-
1097-@[simp]
1098-theorem subst_apply {x : Ident} {a : Aexp} {P : Assertion} {st : State} :
1099-    Assertion.subst x a P st ↔ P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st) := by rfl
1100-
1101-end Assertion
1102-
1103--- This notation allows us to write this operation as:
1104-
1105---   P [ X ↦ a ]
1106-
1107-#check (fun st => Assertion.subst X (aexp { 2 * X }) ({{ X ≤ 10 }}) st)
1108-#check {{ (X ≤ 10) [X ↦ 2 * X] }}
1109-#check (∀ st, ({{ (X ≤ 10) [X ↦ 2 * X] }}) st)
1110-
1111--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing substitutions back
1112-
1113-namespace Assertion.Delab
1114-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
1115-
1116-/-- Print an `Assertion.subst` back in `P [x ↦ a]` notation.  Emits the
1117-bare inside-the-braces form: the generic application case of `delabBody`
1118-picks it up inside an assertion body, and the enclosing printer supplies
1119-the single pair of braces. -/
1120-@[delab app.Assertion.subst]
1121-def delabSub : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
1122-  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``Assertion.subst 3

1136--- That is, `P [X ↦ a]` stands for an assertion -- let's call it `P'` -- that
1137--- behaves just like `P` except that, wherever `P` looks up the variable `X`
1138--- in the current state, `P'` instead uses the value of the expression `a`.
1139-
1140--- To see how this works in more detail, let's calculate what happens with a
1141--- couple of examples. First, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3]` -- that is,
1142--- more formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
1143-
1144---   fun st =>
1145---     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1146---     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st 3 ; st),
1147-
1148--- which simplifies to
1149-
1150---   fun st =>
1151---     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1152---     (X →ₜ 3 ; st)
1153-
1154--- and further simplifies to
1155-
1156---   fun st =>
1157---     ((X →ₜ 3 ; st)[X]) ≤ 5
1158-
1159--- and finally to
1160-
1161---   fun st =>
1162---     3 ≤ 5.
1163-
1164--- That is, `P'` is the assertion that `3` is less than or equal to `5` (as
1165--- expected).
1166-
1167--- For a more interesting example, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦
1168--- X + 1]`.
1169--- Formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
1170-
1171---   fun st =>
1172---     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1173---     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st),
1174-
1175--- which simplifies to
1176-
1177---   fun st =>
1178---     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st)[X] ≤ 5
1179-
1180--- and further simplifies to
1181-
1182---   fun st =>
1183---     (Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 })) ≤ 5.
1184-
1185--- That is, `P'` is the assertion that `X + 1` is at most `5`.

1314--- If `a` itself mentions `X`, then the value of `a` may be different in the
1315--- final state because of this update. For example, if `a` is `X + 1`, then
1316--- setting `X` to `a` certainly does not achieve the postcondition
1317--- `X = X + 1`! The underlying problem is that the state in which the
1318--- postcondition will be checked is different than the state in which `a` was
1319--- evaluated when it was assigned to `X`.

1325--- "work forwards" rather than backwards.

1329---     X := a
1330---   {{fun st => P (X →ₜ m ; st) ∧ st[X] = Aexp.eval (X →ₜ m ; st) a }}

1334--- value of `X` to reconstruct the state `st'` before the assignment took

1386--- ### Consequence
1387-
1388--- Sometimes the preconditions and postconditions we get from the Hoare rules
1389--- won't quite be the ones we want in the particular situation at hand -- they
1390--- may be logically equivalent but have a different syntactic form that fails
1391--- to unify with the goal we are trying to prove, or they actually may be
1392--- logically weaker (for preconditions) or stronger (for postconditions) than
1393--- what we need.
1394-
1395--- For instance,
1396-
1397---   {{(X = 3) [X ↦ 3]}} X := 3 {{X = 3}},
1398-
1399--- follows directly from the assignment rule, but
1400-
1401---   {{True}} X := 3 {{X = 3}}
1402-
1403--- does not. This triple is valid, but it is not an instance of `hoare_asgn`
1404--- because `True` and `(X = 3) \[X ↦ 3`] are not syntactically equal
1405--- assertions.
1406-
1407--- However, they are logically *equivalent*, so if one triple is valid, then
1408--- the other must certainly be as well. We can capture this observation with
1409--- the following rule:
1410-
1411---      {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1412---        P <<->> P'
1413---   ---------------------
1414---      {{P}} c {{Q}}
1415-
1416--- Taking this line of thought a bit further, we can see that strengthening
1417--- the precondition or weakening the postcondition of a valid triple always
1418--- produces another valid triple. This observation is captured by two *Rules
1419--- of Consequence*.
1420-
1421---          {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1422---             P ->> P'
1423---   -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence_pre)
1424---          {{P}} c {{Q}}
1425-
1426---          {{P}} c {{Q'}}
1427---            Q' ->> Q
1428---   -----------------------------    (hoare_consequence_post)
1429---          {{P}} c {{Q}}
1430-
1431--- Here are the formal versions:
1432-
1433-theorem hoare_consequence_pre {P P' Q : Assertion} {c : Com}
1434-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1435-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1436-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
1437-  intro st st' heval hpre
1438-  apply hhoare heval
1439-  rw [assertImplies_def] at himp
1440-  exact himp _ hpre
1441-
1442-theorem hoare_consequence_post {P Q Q' : Assertion} {c : Com}
1443-    (hhoare : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
1444-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1445-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
1446-  intro st st' heval hpre
1447-  rw [assertImplies_def] at himp
1448-  apply himp
1449-  exact hhoare heval hpre
1450-

1455---     X := 1

1508-    (htriple : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (hpre : P ->> P') (hpost : Q' ->> Q) :

1511-  · exact hoare_consequence_post htriple hpost

1514--- ### Automation
1515-
1516--- Many of the proofs we have done so far with Hoare triples can be
1517--- streamlined using the automation techniques that we introduced in the
1518--- *Automation* chapter of *Logical Foundations*.
1519-
1520--- Recall that `simp` rewrites with any lemmas we pass it. The definitions
1521--- whose meaning we keep needing to expose in this chapter --
1522--- `ValidHoareTriple`, `AssertImplies`, and `Assertion.subst` -- each come
1523--- with a characterizing lemma (`validHoareTriple_def`, `assertImplies_def`,
1524--- `Assertion.subst_def`) restating the definition as an equation. Passing
1525--- these lemmas to `simp` replaces the defined notions by their meanings
1526--- wherever they appear. We'll do that explicitly below (and shortly package
1527--- the recipe up as a tactic of our own).

1530---     The Rocq source here registers
1531---     `Hint Unfold assert_implies assertion_sub
1532---     t_update : core` for `auto`.
1533---     That only widens `auto`'s search (unlike the `Arguments /.` commands,
1534---     it does not affect `simpl`), so its Lean counterpart is the
1535---     `assertion_auto` tactic's simp list below -- not global `@[simp]`
1536---     lemmas as for the notation wrappers, whose folded names carry no
1537---     meaning in goals the way `->>` and `Assertion.subst` do.

1698--- ### Sequencing + Assignment
1699-
1700--- Here's an example of a program involving both sequencing and assignment.
1701--- Note the use of `hoare_seq` in conjunction with `hoare_consequence_pre` and
1702--- `apply`'s metavariables.
1703-
1704-theorem hoare_asgn_example3 (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
1705-    {{a = n}}
1706-      X := ~a;
1707-      skip
1708-    {{X = n}} := by
1709-  apply hoare_seq
1710-  · -- right part of seq
1711-    exact hoare_skip
1712-  · -- left part of seq
1713-    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1714-    · exact hoare_asgn
1715-    · assertion_auto
1716-
1717--- Informally, a nice way of displaying a proof using the sequencing rule is
1718--- as a "decorated program" where the intermediate assertion `Q` is written
1719--- between `c1` and `c2`:
1720-
1721---            {{ a = n }}
1722---   X := a
1723---            {{ X = n }};    <--- decoration for Q
1724---   skip
1725---            {{ X = n }}
1726-
1727--- We'll come back to the idea of decorated programs in much more detail in
1728--- the next chapter.

1813--- ### Exercise (4 stars): invalid_triple (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1814-
1815--- Show that
1816-
1817---   {{ a = n }} X := 3; Y := a {{ Y = n }}
1818-
1819--- is not a valid Hoare triple for some choices of `a` and `n`.
1820-
1821--- Conceptual hint: Invent a particular `a` and `n` for which the triple in
1822--- invalid, then use those to complete the proof.
1823-
1824--- Technical hint: Hypothesis `h` below begins `∀ a n, ...`. You'll want to
1825--- instantiate that with the particular `a` and `n` you've invented. You can
1826--- do that with `have` and `apply`, but you may remember (from the
1827--- *Automation* chapter of Logical Foundations) that Lean offers an even
1828--- easier tactic: `specialize`. If you write
1829-
1830---   specialize h your_a your_n
1831-
1832--- the hypothesis will be instantiated on `your_a` and `your_n`.
1833-
1834--- Having chosen your `a` and `n`, proceed as follows:
1835-
1836--- - Use the (assumed) validity of the given hoare triple to derive a state
1837---   `st'` in which `Y` has some value `y1`
1838-
1839--- - Use the evaluation rules (`Com.EvalR.seq` and `Com.EvalR.asgn`) to show
1840---   that `Y` has a *different* value `y2` in the same final state `st'`
1841-
1842--- - Since `y1` and `y2` are both equal to `st'[Y]`, they are equal to each
1843---   other. But we chose them to be different, so this is a contradiction, which
1844---   finishes the proof.

1846-theorem invalid_triple : ¬ ∀ (a : Aexp) (n : Nat),
1847-    {{ a = n }}
1848-      X := 3; Y := ~a
1849-    {{ Y = n }} := by
1850-  intro h
1851-  simp only [validHoareTriple_def] at h
1852-  specialize h (aexp { X }) 2 (st := X →ₜ 2) (st' := Y →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 2) ?_
1853-  · apply Com.EvalR.seq
1854-    · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
1855-    · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
1856-  simp at h

1858--- ### Conditionals
1859-
1860--- What sort of rule do we want for reasoning about conditional commands?
1861-
1862--- Certainly, if the same assertion `Q` holds after executing either of the
1863--- branches, then it holds after the whole conditional. So we might be tempted
1864--- to write:
1865-
1866---           {{P}} c1 {{Q}}
1867---           {{P}} c2 {{Q}}
1868---   ---------------------------------
1869---   {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 {{Q}}
1870-
1871--- However, this is rather weak. For example, using this rule, we cannot show
1872-
1873---   {{ True }}
1874---     if X = 0
1875---       then Y := 2
1876---       else Y := X + 1
1877---     end
1878---   {{ X ≤ Y }}
1879-
1880--- since the rule doesn't tell us enough about the state in which the
1881--- assignments take place in the "then" and "else" branches.
1882-
1883--- Fortunately, we can say something more precise. In the "then" branch, we
1884--- know that the boolean expression `b` evaluates to `true`, and in the "else"
1885--- branch, we know it evaluates to `false`. Making this information available
1886--- in the premises of the rule gives us more information to work with when
1887--- reasoning about the behavior of `c1` and `c2` (i.e., the reasons why they
1888--- establish the postcondition `Q`).
1889-
1890---   {{P ∧   b}} c1 {{Q}}
1891---   {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
1892---   ------------------------------------  (hoare_if)
1893---   {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
1894-
1895--- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
1896---     I have removed `bassertion` as it's an unnecessary abstraction and only
1897---     adds overhead for the reader.
1898---
1899---     The following theorem is now unnecessary.
1900-
1901-theorem bexp_eval_false (b : Bexp) (st : State) (h : b.eval st = false) :
1902-    ¬ ({{ b }}) st := by
1903-  dsimp
1904-  simp [h]
1905-
1906--- Here, we first reduce the expression to `¬Bexp.eval st b = true` with
1907--- `dsimp`, which is trivial after we instruct `simp` to rewrite `b.eval st`
1908--- to `false`.
1909-
1910--- Note to developers (One An @meluge):
1911---     The Rocq proof is the single tactic `congruence`. Using simp seems to
1912---     work but should we build our own `congruence` tactic?
1913-
1914--- Now we can formalize the Hoare proof rule for conditionals and prove it
1915--- correct.
1916-
1917--- The statement of the rule reads: given `htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{Q}}` and
1918--- `hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬b }} ~c2 {{Q}}`, we can conclude
1919--- `{{P}} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{Q}}`.
1920-
1921-theorem hoare_if {P Q : Assertion} {b : Bexp} {c1 c2 : Com}
1922-    (htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) (hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬ b }} ~c2 {{ Q }}) :
1923-    {{ P }} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{ Q }} := by
1924-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at htrue hfalse ⊢
1925-  intro st st' hE hpre
1926-  inversion hE with
1927-  | ifTrue hb hc1 =>
1928-    exact htrue hc1 ⟨hpre, hb⟩
1929-  | ifFalse hb hc =>
1930-    rw [← Bool.not_eq_true] at hb
1931-    exact hfalse hc ⟨hpre, hb⟩
1932-

1941-        Y := 2
1942-      } else {
1943-        Y := X + 1
1944-      }

1946-  apply hoare_if
1947-  · -- Then
1948-    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1949-    · exact hoare_asgn
1950-    · assertion_auto
1951-  · -- Else
1952-    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1953-    · exact hoare_asgn
1954-    · assertion_auto

1960-      if (X = 0) {

1963-        Y := X + 1
1964-      }
1965-    {{X ≤ Y}} := by
1966-  apply hoare_if <;> apply hoare_consequence_pre hoare_asgn (by assertion_auto)

1984--- #### Exercise: One-sided conditionals
1985-
1986--- Note to developers:
1987---     HIDE: Question from 2012, Midterm 2. One-sided conditionals.
1988-
1989--- In this exercise we consider extending Imp with "one-sided conditionals" of
1990--- the form `if1 (b) { c }`. Here `b` is a boolean expression, and `c` is a
1991--- command. If `b` evaluates to `true`, then command `c` is evaluated. If `b`
1992--- evaluates to `false`, then `if1 (b) { c }` does nothing.
1993-
1994--- We recommend that you complete this exercise before attempting the ones
1995--- that follow, as it should help solidify your understanding of the material.
1996-
1997--- The first step is to extend the syntax of commands and introduce the usual
1998--- notations. (We've done this for you, in a separate namespace to prevent
1999--- polluting the global name space. The `scoped` notations below are active
2000--- only inside `namespace If1`.)
2001-
2002-namespace If1
2003-
2004-inductive Com : Type where
2005-  | skip : Com
2006-  | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
2007-  | seq : Com → Com → Com
2008-  | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
2009-  | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
2010-  | if1 : Bexp → Com → Com
2011-
2012-/-- One-sided conditional -/
2013-scoped syntax "if1 " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : imp_com
2014-
2015-open Lean in
2016-scoped macro_rules
2017-  | `(imp { $x:ident }) =>
2018-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
2019-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
2020-  | `(imp { $c1; $c2 }) =>
2021-    `(Com.seq (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
2022-  | `(imp { $x:ident := $a }) =>
2023-    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
2024-  | `(imp { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
2025-    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
2026-  | `(imp { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
2027-    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
2028-  | `(imp { if1 ($b) {$c} }) =>
2029-    `(Com.if1 (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
2030-  | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
2031-    pure c
2032-
2033--- The delaborators are re-instantiated the same way: the Imp printer is
2034--- parameterized over the namespace of the command constructors, so the
2035--- extended printer is that printer at `If1.Com` plus one case for `if1`.
2036-
2037--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing the extended commands back
2038-
2039-namespace Delab
2040-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
2041-
2042-/-- Rebuild `imp_com` syntax from an `If1.Com` term. -/
2043-partial def delabComInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com) :=
2044-  delabComInnerFor ``Com do
2045-    let e ← getExpr
2046-    guard <| e.isAppOfArity ``Com.if1 2
2047-    let b ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
2048-    let c ← withAppArg If1.Delab.delabComInner
2049-    `(imp_com| if1 ($b) {$c})
2050-
2051-@[delab app.If1.Com.skip, delab app.If1.Com.asgn, delab app.If1.Com.seq,
2052-  delab app.If1.Com.cond, delab app.If1.Com.whileDo, delab app.If1.Com.if1]
2053-partial def delabCom : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
2054-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
2055-    | Com.skip => true
2056-    | Com.asgn _ _ => true
2057-    | Com.seq _ _ => true
2058-    | Com.cond _ _ _ => true
2059-    | Com.whileDo _ _ => true
2060-    | Com.if1 _ _ => true
2061-    | _ => false
2062-  match ← delabComInner with
2063-  | `(imp_com| ~$e) => pure e
2064-  | e => `(term| imp { $e })
2065-
2066-end Delab

2076-  | skip {st : State} :
2077-      EvalR (imp {skip}) st st
2078-  | asgn {st : State} (a : Aexp) {n : Nat} (x : Ident) (h : a.eval st = n) :
2079-      EvalR (imp {x := ~a}) st (x →ₜ n ; st)
2080-  | seq {c1 c2 : Com} (st st' st'' : State)
2081-      (h1 : EvalR c1 st st') (h2 : EvalR c2 st' st'') :
2082-      EvalR (imp {~c1; ~c2}) st st''
2083-  | ifTrue {st st' : State} (b : Bexp) {c1 c2 : Com} (hb : b.eval st = true)

2086-  | ifFalse {st st' : State} (b : Bexp) {c1 c2 : Com} (hb : b.eval st = false)
2087-      (hc : EvalR c2 st st') :

2089-  | whileFalse {b : Bexp} (st : State) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false) :

2091-  | whileTrue {st st' st'' : State} {b : Bexp} {c : Com}
2092-      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st st')
2093-      (hloop : EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c} }) st' st'') :

2095-  | if1True {st st' : State} {b : Bexp} {c : Com} (hb : b.eval st = true)

2127--- Now we have to repeat the definition and notation of Hoare triples, so that

2130-def ValidHoareTriple
2131-    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
2132-  ∀ {st st' : State},
2133-    (st =[ c ]=> st') →
2134-    P st →
2135-    Q st'
2136-
2137-instance : HasTriple Com where
2138-  Triple := ValidHoareTriple

2143-      P st →
2144-      Q st' := by rfl

2148--- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_if1 (manually graded) ⭐⭐
2149-
2150--- Invent a Hoare logic proof rule for `if1`. State and prove a theorem named
2151--- `hoare_if1` that shows the validity of your rule. Use `hoare_if` as a
2152--- guide. Try to invent a rule that is *complete*, meaning it can be used to
2153--- prove the correctness of as many one-sided conditionals as possible. Also
2154--- try to keep your rule *compositional*, meaning that any Imp command that
2155--- appears in a premise should syntactically be a part of the command in the
2156--- conclusion.
2157-
2158--- Hint: if you encounter difficulty getting Lean to parse part of your rule
2159--- as an assertion, try wrapping it in the `{{ … }}` brackets or adding a type
2160--- ascription. For example, if you want `e` to be parsed as an assertion,
2161--- write it as `(e : Assertion)`.
2162-
2163-theorem hoare_if1 (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (P Q : Assertion)
2164-    (htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c {{ Q }})
2165-    (hfalse : ({{ P ∧ ¬ b }}) ->> Q) :
2166-    {{ P }} if1 (~b) { ~c } {{ Q }} := by
2167-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at htrue ⊢
2168-  intro st st' heval hpre
2169-  inversion heval with
2170-  | if1True hb hc =>
2171-    exact htrue hc ⟨hpre, hb⟩
2172-  | if1False hb =>
2173-    apply hfalse
2174-    simp [hpre, hb]
2175-
2176--- For example (`hoare_if1_good`) your rule should be strong enough to show
2177--- the following Hoare triple is valid:
2178-
2179---   {{ X + Y = Z }}
2180---   if1 (Y ≠ 0) {
2181---     X := X + Y;
2182---   }
2183---   {{ X = Z }}
2184-
2185--- Before the next exercise, we need to restate the Hoare rules of consequence
2186--- (for preconditions) and assignment for the new `Com` type.
2187-
2188-theorem hoare_consequence_pre {P P' Q : Assertion} {c : Com}
2189-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
2190-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
2191-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
2192-  intro st st' heval hpre
2193-  exact hhoare heval (himp st hpre)
2194-
2195-theorem hoare_asgn {Q : Assertion} {x : Ident} {a : Aexp} :
2196-    {{Q [x ↦ ~a]}} x := ~a {{ Q }} := by
2197-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
2198-  intro st st' heval hQ
2199-  rw [Assertion.subst_apply] at hQ
2200-  inversion heval with
2201-  | asgn n h =>
2202-    subst h
2203-    exact hQ

2236--- ### While Loops
2237-
2238--- The Hoare rule for `while` loops is based on the idea of a *command
2239--- invariant* (or just *invariant*): an assertion whose truth is guaranteed
2240--- after executing a command, assuming it is true before.
2241-
2242--- That is, an assertion `P` is a command invariant of `c` if
2243-
2244---   {{P}} c {{P}}
2245-
2246--- holds. Note that the command invariant might temporarily become false in
2247--- the middle of executing `c`, but by the end of `c` it must be restored.
2248-
2249--- As a first attempt at a `while` rule, we could try:
2250-
2251---          {{P}} c {{P}}
2252---   ---------------------------
2253---   {{P}} while b do c end {{P}}
2254-
2255--- This rule is valid: if `P` is a command invariant of `c`, as the premise
2256--- requires, then, no matter how many times the loop body executes, `P` is
2257--- going to be true when the loop finally finishes.
2258-
2259--- But the rule also omits two crucial pieces of information. First, the loop
2260--- terminates when `b` becomes false. So we can strengthen the postcondition
2261--- in the conclusion:
2262-
2263---           {{P}} c {{P}}
2264---   ---------------------------------
2265---   {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
2266-
2267--- Second, the loop body will be executed only if `b` is true. So we can also
2268--- strengthen the precondition in the premise:
2269-
2270---         {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2271---   --------------------------------- (hoare_while)
2272---   {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
2273-
2274--- That is the Hoare `while` rule. Note how it combines aspects of `skip` and
2275--- conditionals:
2276-
2277--- - If the loop body executes zero times, the rule is like `skip` in that the
2278---   precondition survives to become (part of) the postcondition.
2279-
2280--- - Like a conditional, we can assume guard `b` holds on entry to the
2281---   subcommand.
2282-
2283--- Note to developers:
2284---     HIDE: The big comment will not display nicely. But I guess it's
2285---     folded...

2288---     We need to explain the `generalize` tactic.

2290-theorem hoare_while {P : Assertion} {b : Bexp} {c : Com}
2291-    (hhoare : {{P ∧ b}} ~c {{ P }}) :
2292-    {{ P }} while (~b) { ~c } {{P ∧ ¬ b}} := by
2293-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
2294-  intro st st' heval hpre
2295-  /- We proceed by induction on `heval`, because, in the "keep
2296-  looping" case, its hypotheses talk about the whole loop instead
2297-  of just `c`. We begin by generalizing over an
2298-  arbitrary command, together with an equation remembering that the
2299-  command is the original loop. The cases for commands other than
2300-  `while` are dismissed because their equations are contradictory. -/
2301-  generalize heq : (imp { while (~b) { ~c } }) = cmd at heval
2302-  induction heval with
2303-  | @whileFalse b0 s0 c0 hb =>
2304-    injection heq with hbeq hceq
2305-    simp_all
2306-  | @whileTrue s0 s0' s0'' b0 c0 hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
2307-    injection heq with hbeq hceq
2308-    subst hbeq hceq
2309-    exact ih2 (hhoare hc ⟨hpre, hb⟩) rfl
2310-  | skip | asgn | seq | ifTrue | ifFalse =>
2311-    contradiction

2330--- We call `P` a *loop invariant* of `while b do c end` if
2331-
2332---   {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2333-
2334--- is a valid Hoare triple.
2335-
2336--- This means that `P` will be true at the end of the loop body whenever the
2337--- loop body executes. If `P` contradicts `b`, this holds trivially since the
2338--- precondition is false.
2339-
2340--- For instance, `X = 0` is a loop invariant of
2341-
2342---   while X = 2 do X := 1 end
2343-
2344--- since the program will never enter the loop.

2493--- If the loop never terminates, any postcondition will work.

2495-theorem always_loop_hoare (Q : Assertion) :
2496-    {{True}} while (true) { skip } {{ Q }} := by
2497-  apply hoare_consequence_post
2498-  · apply hoare_while
2499-    apply hoare_post_true
2500-    intro st
2501-    exact True.intro
2502-  · intro st ⟨_, hguard⟩
2503-    simp at hguard
2504-
2505--- Of course, this result is not surprising if we remember that the definition
2506--- of `ValidHoareTriple` asserts that the postcondition must hold *only* when
2507--- the command terminates. If the command doesn't terminate, we can prove
2508--- anything we like about the post-condition.
2509-
2510--- Hoare rules that specify what happens *if* commands terminate, without
2511--- proving that they do, are said to describe a logic of *partial*
2512--- correctness. It is also possible to give Hoare rules for *total*
2513--- correctness, which additionally specifies that commands must terminate.
2514--- Total correctness is out of the scope of this textbook.

2529--- In this exercise, we'll add a new command to our language of commands:
2530--- `repeat { c } until (b)`. You will write the evaluation rule for `repeat`
2531--- and add a new Hoare rule to the language for programs involving it.
2532-
2533-namespace RepeatExercise
2534-
2535-inductive Com : Type where
2536-  | skip : Com
2537-  | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
2538-  | seq : Com → Com → Com
2539-  | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
2540-  | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
2541-  | repeatUntil : Com → Bexp → Com
2542-
2543--- `repeat` behaves like `while`, except that the loop guard is checked
2544--- *after* each execution of the body, with the loop repeating as long as the
2545--- guard stays *false*. Because of this, the body will always execute at least
2546--- once.

2548-/-- Repeat loop -/
2549-syntax "repeat" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") " until " "(" imp_bexp ")" : imp_com

2552-scoped macro_rules
2553-  | `(imp { $x:ident }) =>
2554-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
2555-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
2556-  | `(imp { $c1; $c2 }) =>
2557-    `(Com.seq (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
2558-  | `(imp { $x:ident := $a }) =>
2559-    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
2560-  | `(imp { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
2561-    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
2562-  | `(imp { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
2563-    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
2564-  | `(imp { repeat {$c} until ($b) }) =>
2565-    `(Com.repeatUntil (imp {$c}) (bexp {$b}))
2566-  | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
2567-    pure c

2665-theorem hoare_repeat {P Q : Assertion} {b : Bexp} {c : Com}
2666-    (h1 : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }}) (h2 : {{ Q ∧ ¬ b }} ~c {{ Q }}) :
2667-    {{ P }} repeat { ~c } until (~b) {{ Q ∧ b }} := by

2671-  induction heval generalizing P with

2673-    injection heq with hceq hbeq
2674-    subst hceq hbeq
2675-    exact ⟨h1 hc hpre, hb⟩
2676-  | @repeatLoop s0 s0' s0'' b0 c0 hc hb hloop ih1 ih2 =>
2677-    injection heq with hceq hbeq
2678-    subst hceq hbeq
2679-    apply ih2 h2 _ rfl
2680-    constructor
2681-    · exact h1 hc hpre
2682-    · simp [hb]
2683-  | skip | asgn | seq | ifTrue | ifFalse | whileFalse | whileTrue =>
2684-    contradiction

2782-    intro cmd s s' hev
2783-    induction hev with
2784-    | @repeatEnd s0 s0' b0 c0 hc hb =>
2785-        intro heq hp
2786-        injection heq with e1 e2
2787-        subst e1 e2
2788-        rw [validHoareTriple_def] at h

2793-        subst e1 e2
