2715--- ## Weakest Preconditions (Optional)
2716-
2717--- Note to developers:
2718---     HIDE: BCP 21: We talked about moving this stuff to the HoareAsLogic
2719---     chapter to lighten this chapter, but it fits awkwardly there, so I'm
2720---     leaving it here. It's optional anyway. We might consider assigning one
2721---     of the exercises as advanced-only though.
2722-
2723--- Some preconditions are more interesting than others. For example, the Hoare
2724--- triple
2725-
2726---   {{ False }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
2727-
2728--- is *not* very interesting: although it is perfectly valid, it tells us
2729--- nothing useful. Since the precondition isn't satisfied by any state, it
2730--- doesn't describe any situations where we can use the command `X := Y + 1`
2731--- to achieve the postcondition `X <= 5`.
2732-
2733--- By contrast,
2734-
2735---   {{ Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0 }}  X := Y + 1 {{ X <= 5 }}
2736-
2737--- has a useful precondition: it tells us that, if we can somehow create a
2738--- situation in which we know that `Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0`, then running this
2739--- command will produce a state satisfying the postcondition. However, this
2740--- precondition is not as useful as it could be, because the `Z = 0` clause in
2741--- the precondition actually has nothing to do with the postcondition
2742--- `X <= 5`.
2743-
2744--- The *most* useful precondition for this command is this one:
2745-
2746---   {{ Y <= 4 }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
2747-
2748--- The assertion `Y <= 4` is called the *weakest precondition* of `X := Y + 1`
2749--- with respect to the postcondition `X <= 5`.
2750-
2751--- Assertion `Y <= 4` is a *weakest precondition* of command `X := Y + 1` with
2752--- respect to postcondition `X <= 5`. Think of *weakest* here as meaning
2753--- "easiest to satisfy": a weakest precondition is one that as many states as
2754--- possible can satisfy.
2755-
2756--- `P` is a weakest precondition of command `c` for postcondition `Q` if
2757-
2758--- - `P` is a precondition, that is, `{{P}} c {{Q}}`; and
2759-
2760--- - `P` is at least as weak as all other preconditions, that is, if
2761---   `{{P'}} c {{Q}}` then `P' ->> P`.
2762-
2763--- Note that weakest preconditions need not be unique. For example, `Y <= 4`
2764--- was a weakest precondition above, but so are the logically equivalent
2765--- assertions `Y < 5`, `Y <= 2 * 2`, etc. It is easy to show that any two
2766--- weakest preconditions `P` and `P'` of a command `c` with respect to
2767--- postcondition `Q` are logically equivalent; that is, `P <<->> P'`.
2768-
2769-def IsWp (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
2770-  ValidHoareTriple P c Q ∧
2771-  ∀ P' : Assertion, ValidHoareTriple P' c Q → P' ->> P
2772-
2773--- ### Exercise (1 star): wp (Optional) ⭐
2774-
2775--- What are weakest preconditions of the following commands for the following
2776--- postconditions?
2777-
2778---   1) {{ ? }}  skip  {{ X = 5 }}
2779-
2780---   2) {{ ? }}  X := Y + Z {{ X = 5 }}
2781-
2782---   3) {{ ? }}  X := Y  {{ X = Y }}
2783-
2784---   4) {{ ? }}
2785---    if X = 0 then Y := Z + 1 else Y := W + 2 end
2786---    {{ Y = 5 }}
2787-
2788---   5) {{ ? }}
2789---    X := 5
2790---    {{ X = 0 }}
2791-
2792---   6) {{ ? }}
2793---    while true do X := 0 end
2794---    {{ X = 0 }}
2795-
2796---   1) X = 5
2797---   2) Y + Z = 5
2798---   3) True
2799---   4) (X = 0 /\ Z = 4) \/ (X <> 0 /\ W = 3)
2800---   5) False
2801---   6) True
2802-
2803--- ### Exercise (3 stars): is_wp (Advanced, Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
2804-
2805--- Prove formally, using the definition of `ValidHoareTriple`, that `Y <= 4`
2806--- is indeed a weakest precondition of `X := Y + 1` with respect to
2807--- postcondition `X <= 5`.
2808-
2809-theorem is_wp_example :
2810-    IsWp ({{ Y ≤ 4 }}) (imp {X := Y + 1})
2811-      ({{ X ≤ 5 }}) := by
2812-  sorry
2813-
2814--- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_weakest (Advanced, Optional) ⭐⭐
2815-
2816--- Show that the precondition in the rule `hoare_asgn` is in fact the weakest
2817--- precondition.
2818-
2819-theorem hoare_asgn_weakest
2820-    (Q : Assertion) (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) :
2821-    IsWp ({{ Q [x ↦ ~a] }}) (imp {x := ~a}) Q := by
2822-  sorry
2823-
2824--- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_havoc_weakest (Advanced, Optional) ⭐⭐
2825-
2826--- Show that your `havoc_pre` function from the `himp_hoare` exercise in the
2827--- Hoare chapter returns a weakest precondition.
2828-
2829-namespace Himp2
2830-
2831-theorem hoare_havoc_weakest (P Q : Assertion) (x : Ident)
2832-    (h : Himp.ValidHoareTriple P (Himp.Com.havoc x) Q) :
2833-    P ->> Himp.havoc_pre x Q := by
2834-  sorry

8--- # Imp: Simple Imperative Programs
9-
10--- Note to developers (before next release):
11---     Needs some WORKINCLASSes and some quizzes

14---     C-style arrays (i.e., indirect read/write). This sets up some really

16---     etc.).

19---     save a mismatch in the `dec_minimum` exercise in Hoare2?
20---
21---     At some point we could consider moving material from the old HoareLists
22---     to this chapter (and into later files, as appropriate). We haven't done
23---     it yet because it's a shame to complicate the nice simple presentation
24---     here when it's used as the basis for applications like Xavier's static
25---     analysis lectures. Also, we now have a whole volume on real separation
26---     logic...
27---
28---     MWH (port note): The Rocq chapter's "Rocq Automation" tour has been
29---     retooled here for Lean. The tactic combinators `try` and `repeat` (and
30---     the custom-tactic `macro`) are introduced in this chapter; `<;>` and
31---     `simp` were already introduced in Logical Foundations (`<;>` in
32---     `Induction`) so we use them freely and the `<;>` section below is a
33---     recap. For linear arithmetic we use `lia`; NOTE that LF currently
34---     introduces `omega`, not `lia`, so this needs to be reconciled
35---     volume-wide (either introduce `lia` in LF, or keep `omega`).
36-
37--- In this chapter, we take a more serious look at how to use Lean as a tool
38--- to study other things. Our case study is a *simple imperative programming
39--- language* called Imp, embodying a tiny core fragment of conventional
40--- mainstream languages such as C and Java.
41-
42--- Here is a familiar mathematical function written in Imp.
43-
44---   Z := X;
45---   Y := 1;
46---   while (Z ≠ 0) {
47---     Y := Y * Z;
48---     Z := Z - 1;
49---   }
50-
51--- We concentrate here on defining the *syntax* and *semantics* of Imp; later
52--- in this volume we develop a theory of *program equivalence* and introduce
53--- *Hoare Logic*, a popular logic for reasoning about imperative programs.
54-
55--- We build Imp in three layers. The first — a core language of *arithmetic
56--- and boolean expressions* — is developed in its own chapter, *Slang*; read
57--- that one first. There you meet the abstract syntax of arithmetic
58--- expressions (`Aexp`) and boolean expressions (`Bexp`), their evaluation
59--- both as a recursive *function* and as an inductive *relation* (proved
60--- equivalent), and a small `optimize0plus` program transformation together
61--- with its correctness proof. Those expressions are *variable-free*.
62-
63--- This chapter picks up from there. First we extend the expressions with
64--- *variables*; then we add a language of *commands* — assignment,
65--- conditionals, sequencing, and loops.
66-
67--- ## Expressions With Variables
68-
69--- Let's return to defining Imp. The next thing we need to do is to enrich our
70--- arithmetic and boolean expressions with variables. To keep things simple,
71--- we'll assume that all variables are global and that they only hold numbers.
72-
73--- ### States
74-
75--- Since we'll want to look variables up to find out their current values,
76--- we'll use total maps from the `Maps` chapter. A *machine state* (or just
77--- *state*) represents the current values of all variables at some point in
78--- the execution of a program.
79-
80--- For simplicity, we assume that the state is defined for *all* variables,
81--- even though any given program is only able to mention a finite number of
82--- them. Because each variable stores a natural number, we represent the state
83--- as a total map from strings (variable names) to `Nat`, and will use `0` as
84--- the default value in the store.
85-
86--- We give the type of variable identifiers a name, `Ident`. For now it is
87--- just `String`; naming it makes the intent clearer.
88-
89-open scoped MyGetElem
90-
91-abbrev Ident := String
92-abbrev State := TotalMap Ident Nat
93-
94--- ### Syntax
95-
96--- We can add variables to the arithmetic expressions we had before simply by
97--- including one more constructor. (This is a fresh `Aexp`, replacing the
98--- variable-free one from the *Slang* chapter.)
99-
100--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
101---     That should be a live chapter link.
102-
103-inductive Aexp where
104-  | num (n : Nat)
105-  | id (x : Ident)                -- NEW
106-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
107-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
108-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
109-
110--- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018):
111---     Rather than define identifiers as Ident, a more general approach is to
112---     use a **type variable** with `DecidableEq` (as the `Maps` chapter
113---     does), threaded through `Aexp`/`Bexp`/`Com`/`State`. Stashed for a
114---     future decision; the parameterized version would look like:
115---
116---     `inductive Aexp (V : Type) where
117---       | num (n : Nat)
118---       | id (x : V)
119---       | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
120---       | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
121---       | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
122---     -- … then `Bexp V`, `Com V`, `abbrev State (V) [DecidableEq V] :=
123---     -- TotalMap V Nat`, and `[DecidableEq V]` wherever a lookup/update is
124---     -- performed.`
125-
126--- The `Bexp` definition is unchanged, except that it now refers to the new
127--- `Aexp`.
128-
129-inductive Bexp where
130-  | bool (b : Bool)
131-  | eq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
132-  | neq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
133-  | le (a1 a2 : Aexp)
134-  | gt (a1 a2 : Aexp)
135-  | not (b : Bexp)
136-  | and (b1 b2 : Bexp)
137-
138--- Defining a few variable names as shorthands will make examples easier to
139--- read.
140-
141-def W : Ident := "W"
142-def X : Ident := "X"
143-def Y : Ident := "Y"
144-def Z : Ident := "Z"
145-
146--- ### Notations
147-
148--- To make Imp programs easier to read and write, we introduce some notations.
149-
150--- You do not need to understand exactly what these declarations do. Briefly,
151--- though, here is how the two blocks below fit together:
152-
153--- - The `declare_syntax_cat` directive adds a new non-terminal to Lean's
154---   grammar, called `imp_aexp`. We'll add additional non-terminals further
155---   below.
156-
157--- - Each `syntax` directive defines a grammar production, of which there are
158---   eight in total. The first two define literals, `num` and `ident`, as
159---   `imp_aexp`s. The next several directives define productions for building
160---   larger expressions, with some annotations to define precedence, etc.
161-
162--- - Finally, `macro_rules` is used to translate each production of the
163---   `imp_aexp` nonterminal into a Lean expression.
164-
165--- Boolean expressions and, later, commands follow this same pattern exactly,
166--- so their declarations are collapsed where they appear: open one if you want
167--- to see the pattern repeated, and skip them otherwise.
168-
169-/-- Arithmetic expressions of Imp -/
170-declare_syntax_cat imp_aexp
171-/-- Numeric literal -/
172-syntax:max num : imp_aexp
173-/-- Variable reference -/
174-syntax:max ident : imp_aexp
175-/-- Addition -/
176-syntax:65 imp_aexp:65 " + " imp_aexp:66 : imp_aexp
177-/-- Subtraction -/
178-syntax:65 imp_aexp:65 " - " imp_aexp:66 : imp_aexp
179-/-- Multiplication -/
180-syntax:70 imp_aexp:70 " * " imp_aexp:71 : imp_aexp
181-/-- Parentheses for grouping -/
182-syntax "(" imp_aexp ")" : imp_aexp
183-/-- Escape to Lean -/
184-syntax:max "~" term:max : imp_aexp
185-
186-/-- Embed an Imp arithmetic expression into a Lean term -/
187-syntax:min "aexp " "{" imp_aexp "}" : term
188-
189-open Lean in
190-macro_rules
191-  | `(aexp { $n:num }) => `(Aexp.num $(quote n.getNat))
192-  | `(aexp { $x:ident }) => `(Aexp.id $x)
193-  | `(aexp { ~$e }) => pure e
194-  | `(aexp { $a + $b }) => `(Aexp.plus (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
195-  | `(aexp { $a - $b }) => `(Aexp.minus (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
196-  | `(aexp { $a * $b }) => `(Aexp.mult (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
197-  | `(aexp { ($a) }) => `(aexp {$a})
198-
199--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: boolean expressions
200-
201-/-- Boolean expressions of Imp -/
202-declare_syntax_cat imp_bexp
203-/-- Boolean literal (`true` or `false`) -/
204-syntax:max ident : imp_bexp
205-/-- Equality of arithmetic expressions -/
206-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " = " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
207-/-- Disequality of arithmetic expressions -/
208-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " ≠ " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
209-/-- Less than or equal -/
210-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " ≤ " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
211-/-- Greater than -/
212-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " > " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
213-/-- Boolean negation -/
214-syntax:70 "¬ " imp_bexp:70 : imp_bexp
215-/-- Boolean conjunction -/
216-syntax:35 imp_bexp:36 " ∧ " imp_bexp:35 : imp_bexp
217-/-- Parentheses for grouping -/
218-syntax "(" imp_bexp ")" : imp_bexp
219-/-- Escape to Lean -/
220-syntax:max "~" term:max : imp_bexp
221-
222-/-- Embed an Imp boolean expression into a Lean term -/
223-syntax:min "bexp " "{" imp_bexp "}" : term
224-
225--- END DETAILS
226-
227--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: boolean expressions, macro rules
228-
229-open Lean in
230-macro_rules
231-  | `(bexp { $x:ident }) =>
232-    match x.getId with
233-    | `true  => `(Bexp.bool true)
234-    | `false => `(Bexp.bool false)
235-    | _      => Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'true' or 'false', got '{x.getId}'"
236-  | `(bexp { ~$e }) => pure e
237-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp = $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.eq (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
238-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp ≠ $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.neq (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
239-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp ≤ $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.le (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
240-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp > $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.gt (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
241-  | `(bexp { ¬ $b:imp_bexp }) => `(Bexp.not (bexp {$b}))
242-  | `(bexp { $b1:imp_bexp ∧ $b2:imp_bexp }) => `(Bexp.and (bexp {$b1}) (bexp {$b2}))
243-  | `(bexp { ($b:imp_bexp) }) => `(bexp {$b})
244-
245--- END DETAILS
246-
247-#check aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }
248-#check bexp { true ∧ ¬(X ≤ 4) }
249-
250--- ### Delaborators
251-
252--- The notations above are *input* only: they teach Lean how to **read**
253--- `aexp
254--- { … }` and `bexp { … }`, but Lean still **prints** an expression
255--- using its raw constructors -- `example_aexp` shows up as
256--- `Aexp.plus (Aexp.num 3) …` rather than `aexp { 3 + X * 2 }`. A
257--- *delaborator* closes the loop. Where a `macro` turns surface syntax into a
258--- term (*elaboration*), a delaborator does the reverse: it turns an
259--- elaborated term back into surface syntax so that Lean's own output uses our
260--- concrete Imp notation.
261-
262--- Each delaborator walks a term of the given type and rebuilds the matching
263--- piece of `imp_aexp`/`imp_bexp` syntax; a subterm Lean doesn't recognize is
264--- printed with the `~` escape. The `@[delab …]` attribute registers the
265--- top-level function to fire whenever Lean is about to display a term headed
266--- by one of those constructors -- unless notation printing has been switched
267--- off with `set_option pp.notation false`, which lets us fall back to the raw
268--- constructors when debugging (see *Desugaring Notations* below). The
269--- companion *category parenthesizer* re-inserts the parentheses the grammar's
270--- precedences demand, so that, e.g., `(1 + 2) * 3` prints with its
271--- parentheses intact.
272-
273--- You do not need to understand the details, and the code is collapsed below
274--- for that reason. The result is that a `#check`, an `#eval`, or a proof goal
275--- mentioning an Imp expression is displayed in readable Imp syntax rather
276--- than as a pile of constructors.
277-
278--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing expressions back
279-
280-namespace Imp.Delab
281-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer
282-
283-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `imp_aexp` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
284-@[category_parenthesizer imp_aexp]
285-def imp_aexp.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
286-  maybeParenthesize `imp_aexp true wrapParens prec <|
287-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `imp_aexp prec
288-where
289-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
290-    let pstx ← `(($(⟨stx⟩)))
291-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
292-
293-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `imp_bexp` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
294-@[category_parenthesizer imp_bexp]
295-def imp_bexp.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
296-  maybeParenthesize `imp_bexp true wrapParens prec <|
297-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `imp_bexp prec
298-where
299-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
300-    let pstx ← `(($(⟨stx⟩)))
301-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
302-
303-/-- Tag freshly built syntax with the term info that Lean's pretty printer expects. -/
304-def annAsTerm {any} (stx : TSyntax any) : DelabM (TSyntax any) :=
305-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
306-
307-/-- Rebuild `imp_aexp` concrete syntax from an `Aexp` term. -/
308-partial def delabAexpInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_aexp) := do
309-  let e ← getExpr
310-  let stx ←
311-    match_expr e with
312-    | Aexp.num _ =>
313-      match (← withAppArg getExpr).nat? with
314-      | some v => pure ⟨Syntax.mkNumLit (toString v) |>.raw⟩
315-      | none   => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
316-    | Aexp.id _ =>
317-      -- A variable reference like aexp { X } elaborates to Aexp.id X where X is the
318-      -- declared Ident constant, so the delaborators print the constant's name as a
319-      -- bare identifier (and also handle the .id "X" string-literal form).
320-      match ← withAppArg getExpr with
321-      | .const nm _      => `(imp_aexp| $(mkIdent nm):ident)
322-      | .lit (.strVal s) => `(imp_aexp| $(mkIdent (.mkSimple s)):ident)
323-      | _                => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
324-    | Aexp.plus _ _ =>
325-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
326-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
327-      `(imp_aexp| $s1 + $s2)
328-    | Aexp.minus _ _ =>
329-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
330-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
331-      `(imp_aexp| $s1 - $s2)
332-    | Aexp.mult _ _ =>
333-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
334-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
335-      `(imp_aexp| $s1 * $s2)
336-    | _ => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← delab))
337-  annAsTerm stx
338-
339-/-- Rebuild `imp_bexp` concrete syntax from a `Bexp` term. -/
340-partial def delabBexpInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_bexp) := do
341-  let e ← getExpr
342-  let stx ←
343-    match_expr e with
344-    | Bexp.bool _ =>
345-      match ← withAppArg getExpr with
346-      | .const ``Bool.true _  => `(imp_bexp| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
347-      | .const ``Bool.false _ => `(imp_bexp| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
348-      | _                     => `(imp_bexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
349-    | Bexp.eq _ _ =>
350-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
351-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
352-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp = $s2:imp_aexp)
353-    | Bexp.neq _ _ =>
354-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
355-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
356-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp ≠ $s2:imp_aexp)
357-    | Bexp.le _ _ =>
358-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
359-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
360-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp ≤ $s2:imp_aexp)
361-    | Bexp.gt _ _ =>
362-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
363-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
364-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp > $s2:imp_aexp)
365-    | Bexp.not _ =>
366-      let s ← withAppArg delabBexpInner
367-      `(imp_bexp| ¬ $s)
368-    | Bexp.and _ _ =>
369-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
370-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabBexpInner
371-      `(imp_bexp| $s1 ∧ $s2)
372-    | _ => `(imp_bexp| ~$(← delab))
373-  annAsTerm stx
374-
375--- END DETAILS
376-
377--- The `whenPPOption getPPNotation` wrapper lets
378--- `set_option pp.notation false` switch this delaborator off, revealing the
379--- raw constructors (see the "Desugaring Notations" discussion, after the
380--- commands are introduced).
381-
382--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: registering the delaborators
383-
384-@[delab app.Aexp.num, delab app.Aexp.id, delab app.Aexp.plus,
385-  delab app.Aexp.minus, delab app.Aexp.mult]
386-partial def delabAexp : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
387-  -- This delaborator only understands `Aexp`'s constructors -- bail otherwise.
388-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
389-    | Aexp.num _ => true
390-    | Aexp.id _ => true
391-    | Aexp.plus _ _ => true
392-    | Aexp.minus _ _ => true
393-    | Aexp.mult _ _ => true
394-    | _ => false
395-  match ← delabAexpInner with
396-  | `(imp_aexp| ~$e) => pure e
397-  | e => `(term| aexp { $e })
398-
399-@[delab app.Bexp.bool, delab app.Bexp.eq, delab app.Bexp.neq, delab app.Bexp.le,
400-  delab app.Bexp.gt, delab app.Bexp.not, delab app.Bexp.and]
401-partial def delabBexp : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
402-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
403-    | Bexp.bool _ => true
404-    | Bexp.eq _ _ => true
405-    | Bexp.neq _ _ => true
406-    | Bexp.le _ _ => true
407-    | Bexp.gt _ _ => true
408-    | Bexp.not _ => true
409-    | Bexp.and _ _ => true
410-    | _ => false
411-  match ← delabBexpInner with
412-  | `(imp_bexp| ~$e) => pure e
413-  | e => `(term| bexp { $e })
414-
415-end Imp.Delab
416-
417--- END DETAILS
418-
419--- With these delaborators in place, Lean pretty-prints Imp expressions with
420--- the higher-level notations rather than their raw constructors.
421-
422--- The pretty-printed version of an expression might not exactly match its
423--- original form. For example, the parentheses around `X * 2` in
424--- `aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }` are not printed because they are redundant -- which
425--- the parenthesizer knows.
426-
427-/-- info: aexp {3 + X * 2} : Aexp -/
428-#guard_msgs in
429-#check aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }

435--- ### Evaluation
436-
437--- The arithmetic and boolean evaluators must now be extended to handle
438--- variables, taking a state `st` as an extra argument. A variable is looked
439--- up in the state with the map-indexing notation `st[x]` from the
440--- `Typeclasses` chapter. For the notation to work, we used
441--- `open scoped MyGetElem` earlier, which opens only the scoped items like
442--- notation from the module.
443-
444-def Aexp.eval (st : State) (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
445-  match a with
446-  | num   n     =>  n
447-  | id    x     =>  st[x]                    -- NEW
448-  | plus  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval st + a2.eval st
449-  | minus a1 a2 =>  a1.eval st - a2.eval st
450-  | mult  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval st * a2.eval st
451-
452-def Bexp.eval (st : State) (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
453-  match b with
454-  | bool b      =>  b
455-  | eq   a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st == a2.eval st
456-  | neq  a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st != a2.eval st
457-  | le   a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st ≤  a2.eval st
458-  | gt   a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st >  a2.eval st
459-  | not  b1     =>  !b1.eval st
460-  | and  b1 b2  =>  b1.eval st && b2.eval st
461-
462-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_num (st : State) (n : Nat) : (num n).eval st = n := rfl
463-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_id (st : State) (x : Ident) : (Aexp.id x).eval st = st[x] := rfl
464-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_plus (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
465-    (plus a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st + a2.eval st := rfl
466-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_minus (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
467-    (minus a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st - a2.eval st := rfl
468-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_mult (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
469-    (mult a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st * a2.eval st := rfl
470-
471-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_bool (st : State) (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval st = b := rfl
472-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_eq (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
473-    (eq a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st == a2.eval st) := rfl
474-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_neq (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
475-    (neq a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st != a2.eval st) := rfl
476-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_le (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
477-    (le a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st ≤ a2.eval st : Bool) := rfl
478-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_gt (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
479-    (gt a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st > a2.eval st : Bool) := rfl
480-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_not (st : State) (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval st = !b.eval st := rfl
481-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_and (st : State) (b1 b2 : Bexp) :
482-    (and b1 b2).eval st = (b1.eval st && b2.eval st) := rfl

498--- ## Commands
499-
500--- Now we are ready to define the syntax and behavior of Imp *commands* (or
501--- *statements*). Informally, commands `c` are described by the following BNF
502--- grammar:
503-
504--- c ::= skip
505---     | x := a
506---     | c ; c
507---     | if b then c else c end
508---     | while b do c end
509-
510--- Here is the formal definition of the abstract syntax of commands.
511-
512-inductive Com where
513-  | skip
514-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp)
515-  | seq (c1 c2 : Com)
516-  | cond (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
517-  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
518-
519--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: commands, macro rules
520-
521-/-- Imp commands -/
522-declare_syntax_cat imp_com
523-/-- The command that does nothing (`skip`) -/
524-syntax ident : imp_com
525-/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
526-syntax imp_com ";" ppDedent(ppLine imp_com) : imp_com
527-/-- Assignment -/
528-syntax ident " := " imp_aexp : imp_com
529-/-- Conditional -/
530-syntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : imp_com
531-/-- Loop -/
532-syntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : imp_com
533-/-- Escape to Lean -/
534-syntax:max "~" term:max : imp_com
535-
536-/-- Include an Imp command in Lean code -/
537-syntax:min "imp" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
538-
539-namespace Com
540-
541-open Lean in
542-scoped macro_rules
543-  | `(imp { $x:ident }) =>
544-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
545-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
546-  | `(imp { $c1 ; $c2 }) =>
547-    `(Com.seq (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
548-  | `(imp { $x:ident := $a }) =>
549-    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
550-  | `(imp { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
551-    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
552-  | `(imp { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
553-    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
554-  | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
555-    pure c
556-
557-end Com
558-
559-open scoped Com
560-
561--- END DETAILS
562-
563--- Just as we did for expressions, we add a delaborator so that Lean prints
564--- commands back in the `imp { … }` concrete syntax (see the Delaborators
565--- section above). It reuses the expression delaborators for the condition of
566--- an `if`/`while` and for the right-hand side of an assignment, and prints an
567--- unrecognized subcommand with the `~` escape.
568-
569--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing commands back
570-
571-namespace Imp.Delab
572-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr
573-
574-partial def delabComInnerFor (ns : Name) (extra : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com)) :
575-    DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com) := do
576-  let e ← getExpr
577-  let stx ←
578-    -- Using `(imp_com| skip)` would delaborate as `skip✝`. `mkIdent` fixes this.
579-    if e.isConstOf (ns ++ `skip) then
580-      `(imp_com| $(mkIdent `skip):ident)
581-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `asgn) 2 then
582-      match ← withAppFn <| withAppArg getExpr with
583-      | .lit (.strVal s) =>
584-        let a ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
585-        `(imp_com| $(mkIdent (.mkSimple s)):ident := $a)
586-      | _ =>
587-        let `($x:ident) ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delab | failure
588-        let a ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
589-        `(imp_com| $x:ident := $a)
590-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `seq) 2 then
591-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
592-      let s2 ← withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
593-      `(imp_com| $s1; $s2)
594-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `cond) 3 then
595-      let b  ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
596-      let c1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
597-      let c2 ← withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
598-      `(imp_com| if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2})
599-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `whileDo) 2 then
600-      let b ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
601-      let c ← withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
602-      `(imp_com| while ($b) {$c})
603-    else
604-      extra <|> `(imp_com| ~$(← delab))
605-  annAsTerm stx
606-
607-/-- Rebuild `imp_com` concrete syntax from a `Com` term. -/
608-partial def delabComInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com) :=
609-  delabComInnerFor ``Com failure
610-
611-@[delab app.Com.skip, delab app.Com.asgn, delab app.Com.seq,
612-  delab app.Com.cond, delab app.Com.whileDo]
613-partial def delabCom : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
614-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
615-    | Com.skip => true
616-    | Com.asgn _ _ => true
617-    | Com.seq _ _ => true
618-    | Com.cond _ _ _ => true
619-    | Com.whileDo _ _ => true
620-    | _ => false
621-  match ← delabComInner with
622-  | `(imp_com| ~$e) => pure e
623-  | e => `(term| imp { $e })
624-
625-end Imp.Delab
626-

629--- As an example, here is the factorial function again, written as a formal
630--- definition. When this command terminates, the variable `Y` will contain the
631--- factorial of the initial value of `X`. (Compare this to the concrete Imp
632--- program at the very start of the chapter.)
633-
634-def fact_in_lean : Com := imp {
635-  Z := X;
636-  Y := 1;
637-  while (Z ≠ 0) {
638-    Y := Y * Z;
639-    Z := Z - 1
640-  }
641-}
642-
643--- Because we registered a delaborator, we can inspect a defined program with
644--- `#print`, which pretty prints the stored definition using the same syntax:
645-
646-/--
647-info: def fact_in_lean : Com :=
648-imp {
649-  Z := X;
650-  Y := 1;
651-  while (Z ≠ 0) {
652-    Y := Y * Z;
653-    Z := Z - 1
654-  }
655-}
656--/
657-#guard_msgs in
658-#print fact_in_lean

660--- ### Desugaring Notations
661-
662--- The `imp { … }` notation, together with the delaborators, is purely a
663--- convenience for reading and writing programs. Occasionally, such as when
664--- debugging a definition or a stuck proof, the concrete syntax `hide`s the
665--- underlying structure we want to see. For those moments we can switch the
666--- Imp notation off in Lean's output with `set_option pp.notation false`,
667--- which our delaborators honor.
668-
669--- Note that unlike a `def`, `imp { … }` is a `macro` which is expanded during
670--- elaboration, **before** the resulting term is type-checked. So
671--- `fact_in_lean` is not a program hidden behind a layer of notation that a
672--- proof must first peel back; it simply **is** the underlying tree of `Com`,
673--- `Aexp`, and `Bexp` constructors. Consequently, when a proof goal mentions
674--- an Imp program, tactics such as `cases`, `injection`, and `simp` already
675--- act on those constructors directly -- there is nothing to "unfold". The
676--- delaborators affect only how that tree is **displayed**. Nevertheless,
677--- seeing the raw constructors is sometimes very helpful!
678-
679-/-- info: imp {
680-  X := X + 1
681-} : Com -/
682-#guard_msgs in
683-#check imp { X := X + 1 }
684-
685-/-- info: Com.asgn X ((Aexp.id X).plus (Aexp.num 1)) : Com -/
686-#guard_msgs in
687-set_option pp.notation false in
688-#check imp { X := X + 1 }

722--- ## Evaluating Commands
723-
724--- Next we need to define what it means to evaluate an Imp command. The fact
725--- that `while` loops don't necessarily terminate makes defining an evaluation
726--- function tricky.
727-
728--- ### Evaluation as a Function (Failed Attempt)
729-
730--- Here's an attempt at defining an evaluation function for commands (with a
731--- bogus `while` case).
732-
733-def Com.ceval_fun_no_while (st : State) (c : Com) : State :=
734-  match c with
735-  | imp {skip} => st
736-  | imp {x := ~a} => (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
737-  | imp {~c1; ~c2} =>
738-      let st' := ceval_fun_no_while st c1
739-      ceval_fun_no_while st' c2
740-  | imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2}} =>
741-      if b.eval st then ceval_fun_no_while st c1
742-      else ceval_fun_no_while st c2
743-  | imp {while (~_) {~_}} => st     -- bogus
744-
745--- In a more conventional functional language like OCaml or Haskell we could
746--- add the `while` case as follows:
747-
748--- | .whileDo b c =>
749---     if b.eval st then ceval_fun st (.seq c (.whileDo b c))
750---     else st
751-
752--- Lean doesn't accept such a definition ("fail to show termination") because
753--- the function we want to define is not guaranteed to terminate. Indeed, it
754--- *doesn't* always terminate: the full `ceval_fun` applied to the `loop`
755--- program above would run forever. Since Lean aims to be not just a
756--- programming language but also a consistent logic, any potentially
757--- non-terminating function must be rejected. Here is what would go wrong if
758--- Lean allowed non-terminating recursive functions:
759-
760--- def loop_false (n : Nat) : False := loop_false n
761-
762--- That is, propositions like `False` would become provable (`loop_false 0`
763--- would be a proof of `False`), a disaster for logical consistency.
764-
765--- Thus, because it doesn't terminate on all inputs, the full `ceval_fun`
766--- cannot be written in Lean -- at least not without additional tricks and
767--- workarounds.
768-
769--- Note to developers:
770---     Perhaps that discussion should be moved to -- or previewed in --
771---     Logic.v? MRC'20: It's already in ProofObjects (which not everyone
772---     sees).
773-
774--- ### Evaluation as a Relation
775-
776--- Here's a better way: define `ceval` as a *relation* rather than a
777--- *function* -- i.e., make its result a `Prop` rather than a `State`, similar
778--- to what we did for `Aexp.EvalR` above.
779-
780--- This is an important change. Besides freeing us from awkward workarounds,
781--- it gives us more flexibility in the definition. For example, if we add
782--- nondeterministic features like `any` to the language, we want the
783--- definition of evaluation to be nondeterministic -- i.e., not only will it
784--- not be total, it will not even be a function!
785-
786--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
787---     I kind of hate this notation. Is there something more standard in Lean?
788---     CSLib precedent maybe?
789-
790--- We'll use the notation `st =[ c ]=> st'` for the `Com.EvalR` relation:
791--- `st =[ c ]=> st'` means that executing program `c` in a starting state `st`
792--- results in an ending state `st'`. This can be pronounced "`c` takes state
793--- `st` to `st'`".
794-
795--- Operational Semantics
796-
797--- Note to developers (before next release):
798---     BCP 21: I wonder if `seq` would be easier to work with if st' and st''
799---     were swapped...
800-
801--- Here is an informal definition of evaluation, presented as inference rules
802--- for readability:
803-
804---                         -----------------                  (skip)
805---                         st =[ skip ]=> st
806-
807---                         a.eval st = n
808---                 --------------------------------           (asgn)
809---                 st =[ x := a ]=> (x →ₜ n ; st)
810-
811---                         st  =[ c1 ]=> st'
812---                         st' =[ c2 ]=> st''
813---                       ---------------------                (seq)
814---                       st =[ c1;c2 ]=> st''
815-
816---                        b.eval st = true
817---                         st =[ c1 ]=> st'
818---              --------------------------------------        (ifTrue)
819---              st =[ if b then c1 else c2 end ]=> st'
820-
821---                       b.eval st = false
822---                         st =[ c2 ]=> st'
823---              --------------------------------------        (ifFalse)
824---              st =[ if b then c1 else c2 end ]=> st'
825-
826---                       b.eval st = false
827---                  -----------------------------             (whileFalse)
828---                  st =[ while b do c end ]=> st
829-
830---                        b.eval st = true
831---                         st =[ c ]=> st'
832---                st' =[ while b do c end ]=> st''
833---                --------------------------------            (whileTrue)
834---                st  =[ while b do c end ]=> st''
835-
836--- Here is the formal definition. Make sure you understand how it corresponds
837--- to the inference rules.
838-
839--- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018):
840---     TODO Propose you use inline notation such as
841---     `Com.EvalR (imp {skip;}) st st`
842-
843-inductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → State → Prop where
844-  | skip {st : State} : EvalR (imp {skip}) st st
845-  | asgn {st : State} {a : Aexp} {n : Nat} {x : Ident} (h : a.eval st = n) :
846-      EvalR (imp {x := ~a}) st (x →ₜ n ; st)
847-  | seq {c1 c2 : Com} {st st' st'' : State} (h1 : EvalR c1 st st') (h2 : EvalR c2 st' st'') :
848-      EvalR (imp {~c1; ~c2}) st st''
849-  | ifTrue {st st' : State} {b : Bexp} {c1 c2 : Com} (hb : b.eval st = true)
850-      (hc : EvalR c1 st st') :
851-      EvalR (imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2}}) st st'
852-  | ifFalse {st st' : State} {b : Bexp} {c1 c2 : Com} (hb : b.eval st = false)
853-      (hc : EvalR c2 st st') :
854-      EvalR (imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2}}) st st'
855-  | whileFalse {b : Bexp} {st : State} {c : Com} (hb : b.eval st = false) :
856-      EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st st
857-  | whileTrue {st st' st'' : State} {b : Bexp} {c : Com} (hb : b.eval st = true)
858-      (hc : EvalR c st st') (hloop : Com.EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st' st'') :
859-      EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st st''

914--- result state, rather than letting Lean's computation mechanism do it for
915--- us.

967---     st =[ ~c1 ~c2 ]=> st' →
968---     st =[ c1 ]=> st →
969---     st =[ c2 ]=> st'
970-
971--- (A) Yes (B) No (C) Not sure
972-
973--- _Quiz:_
974-
975--- Is the following proposition provable?
976-
977---   ∀ (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (st st' : State),
978---     st =[ if (~b) { ~c } else { ~c } ]=> st' →
979---     st =[ c ]=> st'
980-
981--- (A) Yes (B) No (C) Not sure
982-
983--- _Quiz:_
984-
985--- Is the following proposition provable?
986-
987---   ∀ (b : Bexp),
988---     (∀ st, b.eval st = true) →
989---     ∀ (c : Com) (st : State),
990---     ¬ ∃ st', st =[ while (~b) { ~c } ]=> st'
991-
992--- (A) Yes (B) No (C) Not sure

994--- _Quiz:_
995-
996--- Is the following proposition provable?
997-
998---   ∀ (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (st : State),
999---     (¬ ∃ st', st =[ while (~b) { ~c } ]=> st') →
1000---     ∀ st'', b.eval st'' = true
1001-
1002--- (A) Yes (B) No (C) Not sure
1003-
1004--- ### Determinism of Evaluation
1005-
1006--- Changing from a computational to a relational definition of evaluation is a
1007--- good move because it frees us from the artificial requirement that
1008--- evaluation be a total function. But it raises a question: is the relational
1009--- definition really a partial *function*? Could the same command, from the
1010--- same state, evaluate to two different final states? In fact this cannot
1011--- happen: `ceval` *is* a partial function.
1012-
1013-theorem ceval_deterministic (c : Com) (st st1 st2 : State)
1014-    (e1 : st =[ c ]=> st1) (e2 : st =[ c ]=> st2) : st1 = st2 := by
1015-  induction e1 generalizing st2 with
1016-  | @skip st =>
1017-      inversion e2
1018-      rfl
1019-  | @asgn st a n x h =>
1020-      inversion e2 with
1021-      | asgn h' => subst h; subst h'; rfl
1022-  | @seq c1 c2 st st' st'' h1 h2 ih1 ih2 =>
1023-      inversion e2 with
1024-      | seq st2' h1' h2' =>
1025-          have hst : st' = st2' := ih1 _ h1'
1026-          subst hst
1027-          exact ih2 _ h2'
1028-  | @ifTrue st st' b c1 c2 hb hc ih =>
1029-      inversion e2 with
1030-      | ifTrue hb' hc' => exact ih _ hc'
1031-      | ifFalse hb' hc' => simp_all
1032-  | @ifFalse st st' b c1 c2 hb hc ih =>
1033-      inversion e2 with
1034-      | ifTrue hb' hc' => simp_all
1035-      | ifFalse hb' hc' => exact ih _ hc'
1036-  | @whileFalse b st c hb =>
1037-      inversion e2 with
1038-      | whileFalse hb' => rfl
1039-      | whileTrue hb' hc' hl' => simp_all
1040-  | @whileTrue st st' st'' b c hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
1041-      inversion e2 with
1042-      | whileFalse hb' => simp_all
1043-      | whileTrue st2' _ hc' hl' =>
1044-          have hst : st' = st2' := ih1 _ hc'
1045-          subst hst
1046-          exact ih2 _ hl'
1047-
1048--- ### Exercise (3 stars): pup_to_n (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
1049-
1050--- Write an Imp program that sums the numbers from `1` to `X` (inclusive) in
1051--- the variable `Y`. Your program should update the state as shown in
1052--- `pup_to_2_ceval`, which you can reverse-engineer to discover the program
1053--- you should write. The proof of that theorem will be somewhat lengthy.
1054-
1055-def pup_to_n : Com := (
1056-  imp {
1057-    Y := 0;
1058-    while (1 ≤ X) {
1059-      Y := Y + X;
1060-      X := X - 1
1061-    }
1062-  })
1063-
1064-theorem pup_to_2_ceval :
1065-    (X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) =[ pup_to_n ]=>
1066-      (X →ₜ 0 ; Y →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 1 ; Y →ₜ 2 ; Y →ₜ 0 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) := by
1067-  unfold pup_to_n
1068-  apply Com.EvalR.seq (st' := (Y →ₜ 0 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅))
1069-  · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
1070-  · apply Com.EvalR.whileTrue (st' := (X →ₜ 1 ; Y →ₜ 2 ; Y →ₜ 0 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅))
1071-    · rfl
1072-    · apply Com.EvalR.seq (st' := (Y →ₜ 2 ; Y →ₜ 0 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅)) <;>
1073-        (apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl)
1074-    · apply Com.EvalR.whileTrue
1075-        (st' := (X →ₜ 0 ; Y →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 1 ; Y →ₜ 2 ; Y →ₜ 0 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅))
1076-      · rfl
1077-      · apply Com.EvalR.seq (st' := (Y →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 1 ; Y →ₜ 2 ; Y →ₜ 0 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅)) <;>
1078-          (apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl)
1079-      · apply Com.EvalR.whileFalse; rfl
1080-
1081--- ## Reasoning About Imp Programs
1082-
1083--- We'll get into more systematic and powerful techniques for reasoning about
1084--- Imp programs in the next chapter, but we can already do a few things
1085--- (albeit in a somewhat low-level way) just by working with the bare
1086--- definitions. This section explores some examples.
1087-
1088-theorem plus2_spec (st : State) (n : Nat) (st' : State)
1089-    (hx : st[X] = n) (heval : st =[ plus2 ]=> st') :
1090-    st'[X] = n + 2 := by
1091-  -- Inverting `heval` forces one step of the `ceval` computation: since
1092-  -- `plus2` is an assignment, `st'` must be `st` extended at `X`.
1093-  unfold plus2 at heval
1094-  inversion heval with
1095-  | asgn m h =>
1096-      simp only [Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_id, Aexp.eval_num] at h
1097-      rw [TotalMap.update_eq]
1098-      lia
1099-
1100--- ### Exercise (3 stars): XtimesYinZ_spec (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
1101-
1102--- State and prove a specification of `XtimesYinZ`.
1103-
1104-/- Here is a specification in the style of `plus2_spec`: -/
1105-theorem XtimesYinZ_spec1 (st : State) (nx ny : Nat) (st' : State)
1106-    (hx : st[X] = nx) (hy : st[Y] = ny) (heval : st =[ XtimesYinZ ]=> st') :
1107-    st'[Z] = nx * ny := by
1108-  unfold XtimesYinZ at heval
1109-  inversion heval with
1110-  | asgn n h =>
1111-      simp only [Aexp.eval_mult, Aexp.eval_id] at h
1112-      subst hx hy
1113-      rw [TotalMap.update_eq]
1114-      exact h.symm
1115-
1116-/- Though perhaps a cleaner specification would be: -/
1117-theorem XtimesYinZ_spec (st : State) :
1118-    st =[ XtimesYinZ ]=> (Z →ₜ st[X] * st[Y] ; st) := by
1119-  unfold XtimesYinZ
1120-  apply Com.EvalR.asgn
1121-  rfl
1122-
1123-/- A less informative specification would be ... -/
1124-theorem XtimesYinZ_spec2 (st : State) : ∃ st', st =[ XtimesYinZ ]=> st' := by
1125-  exact ⟨(Z →ₜ st[X] * st[Y] ; st), by unfold XtimesYinZ; apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl⟩
1126-
1127--- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
1128---     We should use the `generalize` tactic here instead of `have key`. I've
1129---     changed some Hoare proofs from `have key` to `generalize` but the
1130---     tactic hasn't been explained yet.
1131-
1132--- ### Exercise (3 stars): loop_never_stops ⭐⭐⭐
1133-
1134--- Hint: proceed by induction on the assumed derivation showing that `loop`
1135--- terminates. Most of the cases are immediately contradictory and so can be
1136--- solved in one step (by `simp`/`discriminate` on the impossible command
1137--- equation).
1138-
1139-theorem loop_never_stops (st st' : State) : ¬ (st =[ loop ]=> st') := by
1140-  intro contra
1141-  -- Generalize over the command so the induction remembers what `loop` is.
1142-  have key : ∀ (c : Com) (s s' : State), (s =[ c ]=> s') → c = loop → False := by
1143-    intro c s s' hce
1144-    induction hce with
1145-    | @whileFalse b s0 c0 hb =>
1146-        intro heq; unfold loop at heq; injection heq with e1 _
1147-        subst e1; simp at hb
1148-    | @whileTrue s0 s0' s0'' b c0 hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
1149-        intro heq; exact ih2 heq
1150-    | @skip s0 => intro heq; simp [loop] at heq
1151-    | @asgn s0 a n x h => intro heq; simp [loop] at heq
1152-    | @seq c1 c2 s0 s0' s0'' h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => intro heq; simp [loop] at heq
1153-    | @ifTrue s0 s0' b c1 c2 hb hc ih => intro heq; simp [loop] at heq
1154-    | @ifFalse s0 s0' b c1 c2 hb hc ih => intro heq; simp [loop] at heq
1155-  exact key loop st st' contra rfl
1156-
1157--- ### Exercise (3 stars): no_whiles_eqv ⭐⭐⭐
1158-
1159--- The following function yields `true` just on programs with no while loops.
1160--- Using `inductive`, write a property `Com.NoWhilesR` that holds exactly when
1161--- `c` is while-free, then prove it equivalent to `Com.no_whiles`.
1162-
1163-def Com.no_whiles (c : Com) : Bool :=
1164-  match c with
1165-  | imp {skip} => true
1166-  | imp {_x := ~_a} => true
1167-  | imp {~c1; ~c2} => no_whiles c1 && no_whiles c2
1168-  | imp {if (~_) {~ct} else {~cf}} => no_whiles ct && no_whiles cf
1169-  | imp {while (~_) {~_}} => false
1170-
1171-inductive Com.NoWhilesR : Com → Prop where
1172-  | skip : Com.NoWhilesR (imp { skip })
1173-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) : Com.NoWhilesR (imp { x := ~a })
1174-  | seq (c1 c2 : Com) (h1 : Com.NoWhilesR c1) (h2 : Com.NoWhilesR c2) :
1175-      Com.NoWhilesR (imp { ~c1; ~c2 })
1176-  | cond (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (h1 : Com.NoWhilesR c1) (h2 : Com.NoWhilesR c2) :
1177-      Com.NoWhilesR (imp { if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } })
1178-
1179-theorem no_whiles_eqv (c : Com) : c.no_whiles = true ↔ Com.NoWhilesR c := by
1180-  constructor
1181-  · induction c with
1182-    | skip => intro _; exact .skip
1183-    | asgn x a => intro _; exact .asgn x a
1184-    | seq c1 c2 ih1 ih2 =>
1185-        intro h; simp only [Com.no_whiles, Bool.and_eq_true] at h
1186-        exact .seq _ _ (ih1 h.1) (ih2 h.2)
1187-    | cond b c1 c2 ih1 ih2 =>
1188-        intro h; simp only [Com.no_whiles, Bool.and_eq_true] at h
1189-        exact .cond _ _ _ (ih1 h.1) (ih2 h.2)
1190-    | whileDo b c ih => intro h; simp [Com.no_whiles] at h
1191-  · intro h
1192-    induction h with
1193-    | skip => rfl
1194-    | asgn x a => rfl
1195-    | seq c1 c2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp [Com.no_whiles, ih1, ih2]
1196-    | cond b c1 c2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp [Com.no_whiles, ih1, ih2]
1197-
1198--- ### Exercise (4 stars): no_whiles_terminating ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1199-
1200--- Imp programs that don't involve while loops always terminate. State and
1201--- prove a theorem `no_whiles_terminating` that says this. Use either
1202--- `Com.no_whiles` or `Com.NoWhilesR`, as you prefer.
1203-
1204-theorem no_whiles_terminating (c : Com) (st : State) (h : Com.NoWhilesR c) :
1205-    ∃ st', st =[ c ]=> st' := by
1206-  induction h generalizing st with
1207-  | @skip => exact ⟨st, .skip⟩
1208-  | @asgn x a => exact ⟨(x →ₜ a.eval st ; st), .asgn rfl⟩
1209-  | @seq c1 c2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 =>
1210-      obtain ⟨st', hc1⟩ := ih1 st
1211-      obtain ⟨st'', hc2⟩ := ih2 st'
1212-      exact ⟨st'', .seq hc1 hc2⟩
1213-  | @cond b c1 c2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 =>
1214-      cases hb : b.eval st with
1215-      | true =>
1216-          obtain ⟨st', hc1⟩ := ih1 st
1217-          exact ⟨st', .ifTrue hb hc1⟩
1218-      | false =>
1219-          obtain ⟨st', hc2⟩ := ih2 st
1220-          exact ⟨st', .ifFalse hb hc2⟩
1221-
1222--- And here is an alternative solution by induction on `c` (using
1223--- `Com.no_whiles` instead of `Com.NoWhilesR`):
1224-
1225-theorem no_whiles_terminating' (c : Com) (st1 : State)
1226-    (hb : c.no_whiles = true) : ∃ st2, st1 =[ c ]=> st2 := by
1227-  induction c generalizing st1 with
1228-  | @skip => exact ⟨st1, .skip⟩
1229-  | @asgn x a => exact ⟨(x →ₜ a.eval st1 ; st1), .asgn rfl⟩
1230-  | @seq c1 c2 ih1 ih2 =>
1231-      simp only [Com.no_whiles, Bool.and_eq_true] at hb
1232-      obtain ⟨st1', hc1⟩ := ih1 st1 hb.1
1233-      obtain ⟨st1'', hc2⟩ := ih2 st1' hb.2
1234-      exact ⟨st1'', .seq hc1 hc2⟩
1235-  | @cond b ct cf ih1 ih2 =>
1236-      simp only [Com.no_whiles, Bool.and_eq_true] at hb
1237-      cases hbev : b.eval st1 with
1238-      | true =>
1239-          obtain ⟨st2, h⟩ := ih1 st1 hb.1
1240-          exact ⟨st2, .ifTrue hbev h⟩
1241-      | false =>
1242-          obtain ⟨st2, h⟩ := ih2 st1 hb.2
1243-          exact ⟨st2, .ifFalse hbev h⟩
1244-  | @whileDo b c ih => simp [Com.no_whiles] at hb

HL/SFLCompat.lean

1-module
2-
3--- This will let the code actions spread to extracted projects
4-public import Batteries.CodeAction
5-public meta import Lean.Elab.BuiltinCommand
6-
7-namespace SLFCommand
8-
9-open Lean Elab Command
10-
11-meta section
12-
13--- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
14--- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
15--- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
16--- through spanshot tasks.
17-private def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
18-  match (← get).scopes with
19-  | [] => act
20-  | h :: t =>
21-    let mut orig : Option Bool := none
22-    try
23-      orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
24-      modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
25-      act
26-    finally
27-      if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
28-        let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
29-        modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
30-
31-private def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
32-  let savedState ← get
33-  try
34-    m
35-  finally
36-    let state ← get
37-    set { savedState with
38-      -- Preserve the info tree
39-      infoState := state.infoState
40-      messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }
41-
42-namespace IndentedCommands
43-
44-/-! # Block Commands Parser
45-  Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
46-  Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure`,
47-  we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
48-  because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure` itself.
49-  One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
50-  and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
51--/
52-
53-open Parser
54-
55-private def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
56-  eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
57-
58-/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
59-private def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
60-  takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
61-
62-/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
63-  If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
64-  requiring the indentation.
65--/
66-private def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
67-  takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
68-  (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
69-    (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
70-
71-private def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
72-  rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
73-
74-private def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
75-
76-@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
77-private def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
78-
79-@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
80-private def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
81-
82-private partial def runRawCmdsAux
83-    (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
84-  let state ← get
85-  let scope := state.scopes.head!
86-  let pctx :=  {
87-      env := state.env
88-      options := scope.opts
89-      currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
90-      openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
91-    }
92-  let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
93-  modify fun state => { state with messages }
94-  unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
95-    elabCommand cmd
96-    runLinters cmd
97-    unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
98-      runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
99-
100-/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
101-private def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
102-  let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
103-    | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
104-  let fileName ← getFileName
105-  let fileMap ← getFileMap
106-  -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
107-  -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
108-  -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
109-  let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
110-  if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
111-    let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
112-      (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
113-    runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
114-  else
115-    throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
116-
117-end IndentedCommands
118-
119-end
120-
121-public meta section
122-
123-open Parser IndentedCommands
124-
125-/--
126-Elaborates the enclosed commands and reports their diagnostics,
127-but discards their effects afterwards.
128-
129-Example:
130-```lean
131-sf_experiment
132-  def hidden : Nat := 1
133-  #check hidden
134--- `hidden` is not available here.
135-```
136--/
137-def experimentTk := leading_parser
138-  "sf_experiment"
139-
140-@[command_parser] def experimentCmd := leading_parser
141-  experimentTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
142-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
143-
144-/--
145-Succeeds only if the enclosed commands fail.
146-Diagnostics from the expected failure are suppressed.
147-
148-Example:
149-```lean
150-sf_expect_failure
151-  example : 1 = 2 := rfl
152-```
153--/
154-def expectFailureTk := leading_parser
155-  "sf_expect_failure"
156-
157-/-
158-  Like `sf_expect_failure` but reports the diagnostics.
159--/
160-def expectFailureInfoTk := leading_parser
161-  "sf_expect_failure?"
162-
163-@[command_parser] def expectFailureCmd := leading_parser
164-  expectFailureTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
165-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
166-
167-@[command_parser] def expectFailureInfoCmd := leading_parser
168-  expectFailureInfoTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
169-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
170-
171-@[command_elab experimentCmd]
172-def elabExperimentCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
173-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
174-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState true do
175-    runRawCmds body
176-
177-@[command_elab expectFailureCmd, command_elab expectFailureInfoCmd]
178-def elabExpectFailureCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
179-  let keepMsgs := stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureInfoCmd
180-  unless keepMsgs || stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureCmd do
181-    throwUnsupportedSyntax
182-  let tk := stx[0]
183-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
184-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState keepMsgs do
185-    withRef tk <| failIfSucceeds <| runRawCmds body
186-
187-end

HL/Slang.lean

1-import HL.SFLCompat
2-
3--- # Slang: Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
4-
5--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
6---     We need to figure out our approach to text width, especially for
7---     proofs. Quite a few proofs here don't render into the chosen page
8---     width, and for terse mode it will be worse.
9-
10--- In **Logical Foundations** (LF) we went through the basics of how to use
11--- Lean to prove theorems and write functional programs. Now, we begin to
12--- shift gears to using it to reason about properties of programs and
13--- programming languages. We begin by looking at a language we call **Slang**
14--- (for *simple language*). Despite its simplicity, Slang lets us introduce
15--- key concepts for specifying the *syntax* and *semantics* of programming
16--- languages and show how those concepts are realized in Lean.
17-
18--- (This chapter is shared, word for word, between two volumes: **Type
19--- Systems** (TS) and **Hoare Logic** (HL). If you have already worked through
20--- it in the other volume, you can safely skip ahead to the next chapter of
21--- this one.)
22-
23--- ## Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
24-
25--- Slang is a simple core language of *arithmetic and boolean expressions*
26--- sufficient to express simple computations and logical predicates.
27-
28--- ### Syntax
29-
30-namespace Slang
31-
32--- These two definitions specify the *abstract syntax* of arithmetic and
33--- boolean expressions.
34-
35-inductive Aexp where
36-  | num (n : Nat)
37-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
38-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
39-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
40-
41-inductive Bexp where
42-  | bool (b : Bool)
43-  | eq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
44-  | neq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
45-  | le (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
46-  | gt (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
47-  | not (b : Bexp)
48-  | and (b₁ b₂ : Bexp)
49-
50--- In this chapter, we'll ignore the translation from the *concrete syntax*
51--- that a programmer would actually write to these abstract syntax trees --
52--- the process that, for example, would translate the string `"1 + 2 * 3"` to
53--- the AST `.plus (.num 1) (.mult (.num 2) (.num 3))`.
54-
55--- For comparison, here's a conventional BNF (Backus-Naur Form) grammar
56--- defining the same abstract syntax:
57-
58--- a ::= nat
59---     | a + a
60---     | a − a
61---     | a * a
62--- b ::= bool
63---     | a = a
64---     | a ≠ a
65---     | a ≤ a
66---     | a > a
67---     | ¬ b
68---     | b ∧ b
69-
70--- Compared to the Lean version above...
71-
72--- - The BNF is more informal -- for example, it gives some suggestions about
73---   the surface syntax of expressions (like the fact that the addition
74---   operation is written with an infix `+`) while leaving other aspects of
75---   lexical analysis and parsing (like the relative precedence of `+`, `-`, and
76---   `*`, the use of parens to group subexpressions, etc.) unspecified. Some
77---   additional information -- and human intelligence -- would be required to
78---   turn this description into a formal definition, e.g., for implementing a
79---   compiler. The Lean version consistently omits all this information and
80---   concentrates on the abstract syntax only.
81-
82--- - Conversely, the BNF version is lighter and easier to read. Its informality
83---   makes it flexible, a big advantage in situations like discussions at the
84---   blackboard, where conveying general ideas is more important than nailing
85---   down every detail precisely.
86-
87---   Indeed, there are dozens of BNF-like notations and people switch freely
88---   among them -- usually without bothering to say which kind of BNF they're
89---   using, because there is no need to: a rough-and-ready informal
90---   understanding is all that's important.
91-
92--- It's good to be comfortable with both sorts of notations: informal ones for
93--- communicating between humans and formal ones for carrying out
94--- implementations and proofs.
95-
96--- ### Evaluation
97-
98--- *Evaluating* an arithmetic expression produces a number.
99-
100-namespace Aexp
101-def eval (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
102-  match a with
103-  | num   n     =>  n
104-  | plus  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval + a₂.eval
105-  | minus a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval - a₂.eval
106-  | mult  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval * a₂.eval
107-
108-@[simp] theorem eval_num (n : Nat) : (num n).eval = n := rfl
109-@[simp] theorem eval_plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (plus a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval + a₂.eval := rfl
110-@[simp] theorem eval_minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (minus a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval - a₂.eval := rfl
111-@[simp] theorem eval_mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (mult a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval * a₂.eval := rfl
112-
113-example : eval (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)) = 4 := by simp
114-end Aexp
115-
116--- Similarly, evaluating a boolean expression yields a boolean.
117-
118-namespace Bexp
119-def eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
120-  match b with
121-  | bool b     =>  b
122-  | eq   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval == a₂.eval
123-  | neq  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval != a₂.eval
124-  | le   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval
125-  | gt   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval > a₂.eval
126-  | not  b₁    =>  !eval b₁
127-  | and  b₁ b₂ =>  eval b₁ && eval b₂
128-
129-@[simp] theorem eval_bool (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval = b := rfl
130-@[simp] theorem eval_eq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (eq a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval == a₂.eval) := rfl
131-@[simp] theorem eval_neq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (neq a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval != a₂.eval) := rfl
132-@[simp] theorem eval_le (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (le a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval : Bool) := rfl
133-@[simp] theorem eval_gt (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (gt a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval > a₂.eval : Bool) := rfl
134-@[simp] theorem eval_not (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval = !b.eval := rfl
135-@[simp] theorem eval_and (b₁ b₂ : Bexp) : (and b₁ b₂).eval = (b₁.eval && b₂.eval) := rfl
136-end Bexp
137-
138--- It's worth noting that `≤` and `>` are `Prop`-valued, i.e.
139--- `a₁.eval st ≤ a₂.eval st` is a proposition, but `Bexp.eval` returns a
140--- `Bool`, so Lean implicitly inserts a `decide` coercion. You can observe the
141--- call to `decide` by hovering over `Bexp.eval_le` and `Bexp.eval_gt`.
142-
143--- _Quiz:_
144-
145--- What does the following expression evaluate to?
146-
147--- Aexp.eval (.plus (.num 3) (.minus (.num 4) (.num 1)))
148-
149--- (A) true (B) false (C) 0 (D) 3 (E) 6
150-
151--- ### Optimization
152-
153--- We can now start to get some mileage out of these definitions. Suppose we
154--- define a function that takes an arithmetic expression and slightly
155--- simplifies it, changing every occurrence of `0 + e` (i.e.,
156--- `.plus (.num 0) e`) into just `e`.
157-
158-def Aexp.optimize0plus (a : Aexp) : Aexp :=
159-  match a with
160-  | num   n          => num n
161-  | plus  (num 0) e₂ => optimize0plus e₂
162-  | plus  e₁      e₂ => plus  (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
163-  | minus e₁      e₂ => minus (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
164-  | mult  e₁      e₂ => mult  (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
165-
166--- To gain confidence that our optimization is doing the right thing, we can
167--- test it on some examples and see if the output looks OK.
168-
169-example :
170-    Aexp.optimize0plus (.plus (.num 2)
171-                               (.plus (.num 0)
172-                                      (.plus (.num 0) (.num 1))))
173-      = .plus (.num 2) (.num 1) := by rfl
174-
175--- But if we want to be certain the optimization is correct -- that evaluating
176--- an optimized expression *always* gives the same result as the original --
177--- we should prove it!
178-
179--- Here is a first, deliberately explicit, proof, by induction on `a`. The
180--- interesting case is `Aexp.plus`: because `Aexp.optimize0plus` treats
181--- `plus (num 0) e` specially, we case-split on the left operand `a₁` -- and,
182--- when it is a numeral, on whether that numeral is `0` -- to line the proof
183--- up with the function's own branches. Once the constructors are exposed,
184--- each case is discharged by essentially the same incantation: unfold
185--- `Aexp.optimize0plus`, rewrite `Aexp.eval` by its characterizing lemmas,
186--- then finish with the induction hypotheses. Notice how repetitive that makes
187--- the proof.
188-
189-theorem optimize0plus_sound (a : Aexp) :
190-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
191-  induction a with
192-  | num n => rfl
193-  | plus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
194-    cases a₁ with
195-    | num n =>
196-      cases n with
197-      | zero =>
198-        simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_num, Nat.zero_add]
199-        exact ih₂
200-      | succ n =>
201-        simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_num]
202-        rw [ih₂]
203-    | plus b₁ b₂ =>
204-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
205-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
206-    | minus b₁ b₂ =>
207-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
208-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
209-    | mult b₁ b₂ =>
210-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
211-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
212-  | minus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
213-    simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_minus]
214-    rw [ih₁, ih₂]
215-  | mult a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
216-    simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_mult]
217-    rw [ih₁, ih₂]
218-
219--- We can do much better. The case analysis we performed by hand -- peeling
220--- `plus` apart to reach the `plus (num 0) e` branch -- is exactly the case
221--- analysis that `Aexp.optimize0plus` itself performs.
222-
223--- The `fun_induction` tactic inducts along a function's **own** recursion
224--- structure: `fun_induction
225--- Aexp.optimize0plus a` hands us one goal per
226--- branch of `optimize0plus` -- the special `plus (num 0) e` branch included
227--- -- so the nested `cases` disappear.
228-
229--- Before applying `fun_induction` to a function as complex as
230--- `Aexp.optimize0plus`, let's see how it works on somthing simpler. Recall
231--- the definition of `Nat.even` and `Nat.odd`:
232-
233-def Nat.even (n : Nat) :=
234-  match n with
235-  | 0 => true
236-  | 1 => false
237-  | n' + 2 => even n'
238-
239-def Nat.odd (n : Nat) := Nat.even (n + 1)
240-
241--- Normally, if we perform induction on `n`, we get two cases - `0` and
242--- `n' + 1` - one for each of the cases in the inductive definition of natural
243--- numbers. Functional induction on `Nat.even`, however, gives us three cases
244--- - `0`, `1`, and `n' + 2` - corresponding to each of the cases of its
245--- definition.
246-
247-example (n : Nat) (h : Nat.even n = true) : Nat.odd n = false := by
248-  fun_induction Nat.even n
249-  . rfl
250-  . contradiction
251-  . simp [Nat.odd, Nat.even] at *
252-    lia
253-
254--- Now let's try using `fun_induction` on `Aexp.optimize0plus`. When we do
255--- this, every goal has the same shape, so we can attack them uniformly with
256--- the `<;>` combinator and a single tactic, `simp_all`, which rewrites
257--- `Aexp.eval` by the `@[simp]` characterizing lemmas and uses the induction
258--- hypotheses -- which it picks up from the local context automatically -- to
259--- close each goal. The whole proof collapses to two lines.
260-
261-theorem optimize0plus_sound' (a : Aexp) :
262-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
263-  fun_induction Aexp.optimize0plus a <;> simp_all
264-
265--- ### Exercise (3 stars): optimize0plusB_sound ⭐⭐⭐
266-
267--- Since the `Aexp.optimize0plus` transformation doesn't change the value of
268--- an `Aexp`, we should be able to apply it to all the `Aexp`s that appear in
269--- a `Bexp` without changing the `Bexp`'s value. Write a function that
270--- performs this transformation on `Bexp`s and prove it sound. Use the
271--- combinators we've just seen to make the proof as short and elegant as
272--- possible.
273-
274-def Bexp.optimize0plusB (b : Bexp) : Bexp := (
275-  match b with
276-  | bool b    =>  bool b
277-  | eq a₁ a₂  =>  eq a₁.optimize0plus a₂.optimize0plus
278-  | neq a₁ a₂ =>  neq a₁.optimize0plus a₂.optimize0plus
279-  | le a₁ a₂  =>  le a₁.optimize0plus a₂.optimize0plus
280-  | gt a₁ a₂  =>  gt a₁.optimize0plus a₂.optimize0plus
281-  | not b₁    =>  not (optimize0plusB b₁)
282-  | and b₁ b₂ =>  and (optimize0plusB b₁) (optimize0plusB b₂))
283-
284-theorem optimize0plusB_test1 :
285-    Bexp.optimize0plusB
286-        (.not (.gt (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 8)))
287-      = (.not (.gt (.num 4) (.num 8))) := (by rfl)
288-
289-theorem optimize0plusB_test2 :
290-    Bexp.optimize0plusB
291-        (.and (.le (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 5)) (.bool true))
292-      = (.and (.le (.num 4) (.num 5)) (.bool true)) := (by rfl)
293-
294-theorem optimize0plusB_sound (b : Bexp) :
295-    b.optimize0plusB.eval = b.eval := by
296-  induction b <;>
297-  simp_all [Bexp.optimize0plusB, optimize0plus_sound]
298-
299--- ### Exercise (4 stars): optimize (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
300-
301--- The optimization implemented by our `Aexp.optimize0plus` is only one of
302--- many possible optimizations on arithmetic and boolean expressions. Write a
303--- more sophisticated optimizer and prove it correct. (You will probably find
304--- it easiest to start small -- add just a single, simple optimization and its
305--- correctness proof -- and build up incrementally to something more
306--- interesting.)
307-
308--- ## Evaluation as a Relation
309-
310--- We have presented `Aexp.eval` and `Bexp.eval` as functions defined by
311--- recursion. Another way to think about evaluation -- one that is often more
312--- flexible -- is as a *relation* between expressions and their values. This
313--- perspective leads to inductive definitions like the following.
314-
315-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
316-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
317-  | plus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
318-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
319-  | minus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
320-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
321-  | mult {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
322-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
323-
324--- One comment on the style of this definition. We could instead have
325--- presented this relation with **positional** hypotheses -- no names for the
326--- premises.
327-
328-namespace ArithUnnamed
329-
330-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
331-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
332-  | plus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
333-  | minus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
334-  | mult {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
335-
336-end ArithUnnamed
337-
338--- The version above makes the rules somewhat easier to read, but gives less
339--- control over naming the hypotheses during proofs involving the relation.
340--- For this reason we adopt the named style.
341-
342--- It will be convenient to have an infix notation for `Aexp.EvalR`. We'll
343--- write `e ⇓ n` to mean that arithmetic expression `e` evaluates to value
344--- `n`. The `⇓` symbol is typed `\Downarrow`.
345-
346-scoped notation:55 e:56 " ⇓ " n:56 => Aexp.EvalR e n
347-
348--- The `notation` is declared right after the inductive. The `scoped` keyword
349--- allows us to scope the notation to the present namespace so it doesn't
350--- collide with other evaluation relations later.
351-
352--- ### Inference Rule Notation
353-
354--- In informal discussions, it is convenient to write the rules for
355--- `Aexp.EvalR` and similar relations in the more readable graphical form of
356--- *inference rules*, where the premises above the line justify the conclusion
357--- below the line. For example, the constructor `plus` can be written like
358--- this as an inference rule:
359-
360--- a₁ ⇓ n₁
361---                          a₂ ⇓ n₂
362---                     ------------------          (plus)
363---                     plus a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ + n₂
364-
365--- Notice the structural correspondence between this rule and our version of
366--- the inductive type with unnamed hypotheses:
367-
368--- | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) :
369---         EvalR a₁ n₁ →
370---         EvalR a₂ n₂ →
371---         EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
372-
373--- Formally, there is nothing deep about inference rules: they are just an
374--- informal notation for implications. You can read the rule name on the right
375--- as the name of the constructor and read each of the linebreaks between the
376--- premises above the line (as well as the line itself) as `→`. All the
377--- variables mentioned in the rule (`a₁`, `n₁`, etc.) are implicitly bound by
378--- universal quantifiers at the beginning. (Such variables are often called
379--- *metavariables* to distinguish them from the variables of whatever language
380--- we are defining. At the moment, our arithmetic expressions don't include
381--- variables, but we'll soon be adding them.) The whole collection of rules is
382--- understood as being wrapped, implicitly, in an inductive declaration. In
383--- informal prose, this is sometimes indicated by saying something like "Let
384--- `Aexp.EvalR` be the smallest relation closed under the following rules...".
385-
386--- To summarize: a group of inference rules corresponds to a single inductive
387--- definition; each rule's name corresponds to a constructor name; above the
388--- line are the premises, below the line the conclusion; metavariables like
389--- `a₁` and `n₁` are implicitly universally quantified. The whole collection
390--- of rules defines `⇓` as the smallest relation closed under them:
391-
392--- ---------                (num)
393---                         num n ⇓ n
394-
395---                          a₁ ⇓ n₁
396---                          a₂ ⇓ n₂
397---                     ------------------           (plus)
398---                     plus a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ + n₂
399-
400---                          a₁ ⇓ n₁
401---                          a₂ ⇓ n₂
402---                    -------------------           (minus)
403---                    minus a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ - n₂
404-
405---                          a₁ ⇓ n₁
406---                          a₂ ⇓ n₂
407---                     ------------------           (mult)
408---                     mult a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁*n₂
409-
410--- _Quiz:_
411-
412--- Which rules are needed to prove the following?
413-
414--- .mult (.plus (.num 3) (.num 1)) (.num 0) ⇓ 0
415-
416--- (A) `num` and `plus` (B) `num` only (C) `num` and `mult` (D) `mult` and
417--- `plus` (E) `num`, `mult`, and `plus`

429--- ### Exercise (1 star): beval_rules (Optional) ⭐

431--- Here, again, is the definition of the `Bexp.eval` function:
432-
433---   def Bexp.eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
434---     match b with
435---     | bool b     => b
436---     | eq   a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval == a₂.eval
437---     | neq  a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval != a₂.eval
438---     | le   a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval
439---     | gt   a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval > a₂.eval
440---     | not  b₁    => !eval b₁
441---     | and  b₁ b₂ => eval b₁ && eval b₂

448---                   -------------                (bool)
449---                    bool bv ⇓ bv
450-
451---                         a₁ ⇓ n₁
452---                         a₂ ⇓ n₂
453---                   ---------------------        (eq)
454---                   eq a₁ a₂ ⇓ (n₁ == n₂)
455-
456---                         a₁ ⇓ n₁
457---                         a₂ ⇓ n₂
458---                 ---------------------          (neq)
459---                  neq a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ != n₂
460-
461---                         a₁ ⇓ n₁

469---                   gt a₁ a₂ ⇓ !(Nat.ble n₁ n₂)
470-
471---                          b ⇓ bv
472---                      -----------               (not)
473---                      not b ⇓ !bv
474-
475---                         b₁ ⇓ bv₁

477---                  ----------------------        (and)

480--- ### Equivalence of the Definitions
481-
482--- It is straightforward to prove that the relational and functional
483--- definitions of evaluation agree.
484-
485-theorem Aexp.evalR_iff_eval (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
486-    a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
487-  constructor
488-  · intro h
489-    induction h with
490-    | num n => rfl
491-    | plus h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [Aexp.eval_plus]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
492-    | minus h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [Aexp.eval_minus]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
493-    | mult h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [Aexp.eval_mult]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
494-  · intro h
495-    subst h
496-    induction a with
497-    | num n => exact .num n
498-    | plus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .plus ih₁ ih₂
499-    | minus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .minus ih₁ ih₂
500-    | mult a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .mult ih₁ ih₂
501-
502--- We can make the proof quite a bit shorter using more automation like we did
503--- in the previous section.
504-
505-theorem Aexp.evalR_iff_eval' (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
506-    a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
507-  constructor <;> intro h
508-  · induction h <;> simp_all
509-  · subst h; induction a <;> constructor <;> assumption

511--- ### Exercise (3 stars): bevalR ⭐⭐⭐
512-
513--- Write a relation `Bexp.EvalR` in the same style as `Aexp.EvalR`, and prove
514--- that it is equivalent to `Bexp.eval`.
515-
516-inductive Bexp.EvalR : Bexp → Bool → Prop where
517-  | bool (b : Bool) : EvalR (.bool b) b
518-  | eq {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : a₁ ⇓ n₁) (h₂ : a₂ ⇓ n₂) : EvalR (.eq a₁ a₂) (n₁ == n₂)
519-  | neq {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : a₁ ⇓ n₁) (h₂ : a₂ ⇓ n₂) : EvalR (.neq a₁ a₂) (n₁ != n₂)
520-  | le {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : a₁ ⇓ n₁) (h₂ : a₂ ⇓ n₂) : EvalR (.le a₁ a₂) (n₁ ≤ n₂)
521-  | gt {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : a₁ ⇓ n₁) (h₂ : a₂ ⇓ n₂) : EvalR (.gt a₁ a₂) (n₁ > n₂)
522-  | not {b : Bexp} {bv : Bool} (h : EvalR b bv) : EvalR (.not b) (!bv)
523-  | and {b₁ b₂ : Bexp} {bv₁ bv₂ : Bool} (h₁ : EvalR b₁ bv₁) (h₂ : EvalR b₂ bv₂) :
524-      EvalR (.and b₁ b₂) (bv₁ && bv₂)
525-
526-scoped notation:55 e:56 " ⇓ " b:56 => Bexp.EvalR e b
527-
528-theorem Bexp.evalR_iff_eval (b : Bexp) (bv : Bool) :
529-    b ⇓ bv ↔ b.eval = bv := by
530-  constructor <;> intro h
531-  · induction h <;> simp_all [Aexp.evalR_iff_eval]
532-  · subst h
533-    induction b <;> constructor <;> simp_all [Aexp.evalR_iff_eval]
