535-end Slang
536-
537--- ### Computational vs. Relational Definitions
538-
539--- For the definitions of evaluation for arithmetic and boolean expressions,
540--- the choice of whether to use functional or relational definitions is mainly
541--- a matter of taste. However, there are situations where relational
542--- definitions work much better than functional ones.
543-
544-namespace Slang.AevalRDivision
545-
546--- For example, suppose that we wanted to extend the arithmetic operations
547--- with division:
548-
549-inductive Aexp where
550-  | num (n : Nat)
551-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
552-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
553-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
554-  | div (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)             -- NEW
555-
556--- Extending the definition of `Aexp.eval` to handle this new operation would
557--- not be straightforward due to division being a *partial* operation; i.e.,
558--- what should we return as the result of `.div (.num 5) (.num 0)`? One option
559--- would be to lift the definition of `Aexp.eval` to return an option:
560-
561-namespace Aexp
562-
563-def eval (a : Aexp) : Option Nat :=
564-  match a with
565-  | num   n     =>  some n
566-  | plus  a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
567-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ + n₂)
568-                    | _, _ => none
569-  | minus a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
570-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ - n₂)
571-                    | _, _ => none
572-  | mult  a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
573-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ * n₂)
574-                    | _, _ => none
575-  | div   a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
576-                    | _, some 0 => none
577-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ * n₂)
578-                    | _, _ => none
579-end Aexp
580-
581--- This definition is a lot wordier than the earlier version. There are tools
582--- to reduce this overhead, namely monads, but we will not discuss these in
583--- Software Foundations in Lean. Curious readers can learn more about them
584--- from [Functional Programming in
585--- Lean](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monads/).
586-
587--- By contrast, partiality is no problem for the relational version of the
588--- definition.
589-
590-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
591-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
592-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
593-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
594-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
595-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
596-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
597-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
598-  | div (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ n₃ : Nat)             -- NEW
599-      (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) (hpos : n₂ > 0) (hdiv : n₂ * n₃ = n₁) :
600-      EvalR (.div a₁ a₂) n₃
601-
602--- Notice that there are some inputs (those with a divisor of 0) for which
603--- this relation does not specify an output.
604-
605-end Slang.AevalRDivision
606-
607-namespace Slang.AevalRExtended
608-
609--- As another example, suppose that we want to extend the arithmetic
610--- operations by a nondeterministic number generator `any` that, when
611--- evaluated, may yield any number. (This is not the same as making a
612--- *probabilistic* choice among all numbers -- we only say which results are
613--- *possible*.)
614-
615-inductive Aexp where
616-  | any                            -- NEW
617-  | num (n : Nat)
618-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
619-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
620-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
621-
622--- Again, extending `Aexp.eval` would be tricky, since evaluation is now *not*
623--- a deterministic function from expressions to numbers; but extending the
624--- relation is no problem.
625-
626--- h₂
627-
628-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
629-  | any (n : Nat) : EvalR .any n                   -- NEW
630-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
631-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
632-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
633-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
634-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
635-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
636-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
637-
638-end Slang.AevalRExtended
639-
640--- At this point you may be wondering: which of these styles should I use by
641--- default?
642-
643--- Where the thing being defined is not easy to express as a function,
644--- definitions are often simpler. When both styles are workable, relational
645--- definitions can be more elegant and easier to understand, and Lean
646--- generates useful inversion and induction principles from them. On the other
647--- hand, functional definitions are automatically deterministic and total --
648--- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove* these if we need them -- and we
649--- can use Lean's computation mechanism to simplify them during proofs.
650-
651--- In large developments it is common to give a definition in *both* styles
652--- plus a lemma that the two coincide, allowing later proofs to switch between
653--- points of view at will -- exactly what we did above in
654--- `Slang.Aexp.evalR_iff_eval` and `Slang.Bexp.evalR_iff_eval`.
655-

13-/-- Internal syntactic representation of a single inversion alternative. -/

18-  expanding to multiple single [invAlt]s. -/

20-syntax (" | " caseArg)+ " => " tacticSeq : invAlts

22-/--
23-  `inversion t` generalizes nonvariable indices of the type of `t` before invoking `cases t`,
24-  then solves away contradictory generated goals.
25-  `t` itself will also be generalized with a heterogeneous equality `heq`
26-  if trying to generalize the indices produces an ill-typed result.
27-  * If `inversion +clear t` is set, then `heq` will be `clear`ed from the context if present,
28-    along with `t` if there are no dependencies on it.
29-  * The form `inversion t with (tac ...) | tag₁ x ... => tac ... | ... | tagₙ z ... => tac ...`
30-    is supported, similar to that of `cases` and `inversion`.
31--/
32-syntax (name := inversion)
33-  "inversion " optConfig ident (" with " (tacticSeq)? (colGe invAlts)*)? : tactic

39-/-- Get the user-facing name for the given metavariable. -/
40-def _root_.Lean.MVarId.getUserName (mvarId : MVarId) : MetaM Name := do
41-  let decl ← mvarId.getDecl
42-  return decl.userName
43-
44-/-- Get the string suffix of a name as a name -/
45-def _root_.Lean.Name.getSuffix : Name → Name
46-| .anonymous => .anonymous
47-| .str _ s => .str .anonymous s
48-| .num n _ => n.getSuffix
49-
50-/--
51-  This function is similar to `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`: Given `e` of the
52-  form `forall ..xs, A`, this combinator will create a new metavariable for
53-  each `x` in `xs` until it reaches an `x` whose type is defeq to `t`,
54-  and instantiate `A` with these, while also reducing `A` if needed.
55-  It uses `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`.
56-
57-  This function returns a triple `(mvs, bis, out)` where
58-  - `mvs` is an array containing the new metavariables.
59-  - `bis` is an array containing the binder infos for the `mvs`.
60-  - `out` is `e` but instantiated with the `mvs`.
61-
62-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Lean/Meta/Basic.lean#L41].
63--/
64-def forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq
65-    (e t : Expr) (kind : MetavarKind := MetavarKind.natural) :
66-    MetaM (Array Expr × Array BinderInfo × Expr) := do
67-  let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing e (some 1) kind
68-  unless ms.size == 1 do
69-    if ms.size == 0 then throwError m!"Failed: {← ppExpr e} is not the type of a function."
70-    else throwError m!"Failed"
71-  let mut mvs := ms
72-  let mut bis := bs
73-  let mut out : Expr := tp
74-  while !(← isDefEq (← inferType mvs.toList.getLast!) t) do
75-    let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing out (some 1) kind
76-    unless ms.size == 1 do
77-      throwError m!"Failed to find {← ppExpr t} as the type of a parameter of {← ppExpr e}."
78-    mvs := mvs ++ ms
79-    bis := bis ++ bs
80-    out := tp
81-  return (mvs, bis, out)
82-
83-/-- Given equations `eqs` in the local context of `mvarId`,
84-  unify them using [Lean.Meta.unifyEq?],
85-  but if unification fails, leave the equation in the context.
86-  This means we should never get a "Dependent elimination failed" error.
87-  While marked partial, this _should_ always terminate,
88-  decreasing on the sum of the sizes of the terms of each equation.
89-
90-  Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs]. -/
91-partial def unifyEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (mvarId : MVarId) (subst : FVarSubst) (caseName? : Option Name) : MetaM (MVarId × FVarSubst) := withIncRecDepth do
92-  match eqs with
93-  | [] => return (mvarId, subst)
94-  | eq :: eqs =>
95-    let some { mvarId, subst, numNewEqs } ← Option.join <$> (observing? $ unifyEq? mvarId eq subst MVarId.acyclic caseName?)
96-      | unifyEqs eqs mvarId subst caseName?
97-    let (newEqs, mvarId) ← mvarId.introN numNewEqs
98-    let eqs := eqs.map (Expr.fvarId! ∘ subst.get)
99-    unifyEqs (newEqs.toList ++ eqs) mvarId subst caseName?
100-
101-/-- Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyCasesEqs]. -/
102-def unifyCasesEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
103-  subgoals.filterMapM fun s => do
104-    let eqs := eqs.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
105-    let (mvarId, subst) ← unifyEqs eqs s.mvarId s.subst s.ctorName
106-    if (← mvarId.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned) then return none
107-    else return some { s with
108-      mvarId := mvarId,
109-      subst  := subst,
110-      fields := s.fields.map (subst.apply ·)
111-    }
112-
113-/-- Try to clear the given fvars from the local context of each subgoal,
114-  using the subgoals' substitution mappings to find the fvars.
115-
116-  As with [MVarId.tryClearMany], the fvars must be in the order they appear in the context.  -/
117-def casesClearMany (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) (fvarIds : Array FVarId) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
118-  subgoals.mapM fun s => do
119-    let fvarIds := fvarIds.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
120-    let mvarId ← s.mvarId.tryClearMany fvarIds
121-    return { s with mvarId }
122-
123-end Lean.Meta

133-/--
134-  `apply t at i` uses forward reasoning with `t` at the hypothesis `i`.
135-  Explicitly, if `t : α₁ → ⋯ → αᵢ → ⋯ → αₙ` and `i` has type `αᵢ`, then this tactic adds
136-  metavariables/goals for any terms of `αⱼ` for `j = 1, …, i-1`,
137-  then replaces the type of `i` with `αᵢ₊₁ → ⋯ → αₙ` by applying those metavariables and the
138-  original `i`.
139-
140-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/ApplyAt.lean].

142-elab "apply " t:term " at " i:ident : tactic => withSynthesize <| withMainContext do
143-  let f ← elabTermForApply t
144-  let some ldecl := (← getLCtx).findFromUserName? i.getId
145-    | throwErrorAt i m!"Identifier {i} not found"
146-  let (mvs, bis, _) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq (← inferType f) ldecl.type
147-  for (m, b) in mvs.zip bis do
148-    if b.isInstImplicit && !(← m.mvarId!.isAssigned) then
149-      try m.mvarId!.inferInstance
150-      catch _ => continue
151-  let (_, mainGoal) ← (← getMainGoal).note ldecl.userName
152-    (← mkAppOptM' f (mvs.pop.push ldecl.toExpr |>.map some))
153-  let mainGoal ← mainGoal.tryClear ldecl.fvarId
154-  replaceMainGoal <| [mainGoal] ++ mvs.pop.toList.map (·.mvarId!)

156-structure InversionConfig where
157-  clear : Bool := false

159-declare_config_elab elabInversionConfig InversionConfig

161-open Cases in
162-def inversionCore (h : FVarId) (config : InversionConfig) : TacticM (List MVarId) := withMainContext do
163-  let goal ← getMainGoal
164-  goal.withContext do
165-    let some ctx ← mkCasesContext? h
166-    | throwTacticEx `inversion goal "Target {Expr.fvar h} does not belong to an inductive type"
167-    -- If the target's type isn't a predicate with indices, behave like `cases`
168-    if ← hasIndepIndices ctx then
169-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn goal h default ctx
170-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
171-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h]
172-        else pure subgoals
173-      subgoals.toList.mapM setUserName
174-    -- Otherwise, use custom [unifyEqs] to not fail on unifying HEqs
175-    else
176-      let gis@⟨newGoal, _, newTarget, numEqs⟩ ← generalizeIndices goal h
177-      let (newEqs, newGoal) ← newGoal.introN numEqs
178-      let some targetEq := newEqs.back?
179-      | throwTacticEx `inversion newGoal "Failed to generalize target"
180-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn newGoal newTarget default ctx
181-      let subgoals ← elimAuxIndices gis subgoals
182-      let subgoals ← unifyCasesEqs newEqs.toList subgoals
183-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
184-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h, targetEq]
185-        else pure subgoals
186-      subgoals.toList.mapM setUserName
187-  where
188-    setUserName (subgoal : CasesSubgoal) : TacticM MVarId := do
189-      if let some name := subgoal.ctorName then
190-        subgoal.mvarId.setUserName name.getSuffix
191-      return subgoal.mvarId
192-
193-/-- Given an inversion alternative and a list of goals,
194-  solve the tagged goal with the provided tactics,
195-  throwing an error if the goal cannot be found or solved. -/
196-def evalInvAlt (goals : List MVarId) (alt : TSyntax `invAlt) : TacticM (List MVarId) :=
197-  match alt with
198-  | `(invAlt| | $tag:ident $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
199-    if let some goal ← goals.findM? (matchTag tag.getId <$> ·.getUserName) then
200-      return [← trySolveGoal vars tactics goal]
201-    else throwError m!"Invalid alternative name `{tag.getId}`: {← errorMsg}"
202-  | `(invAlt| | _ $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
203-    if !goals.isEmpty then
204-      goals.mapM (trySolveGoal vars tactics)
205-    else throwErrorAt alt m!"Invalid wildcard alternative: {← errorMsg}"
206-  | _ => throwErrorAt alt "Could not parse inversion alternative"
207-where
208-  matchTag tag name : Bool :=
209-    tag == name || tag.isPrefixOf name || tag.isSuffixOf name
210-  trySolveGoal vars tactics goal : TacticM MVarId := do
211-    let goals ← renameInaccessibles goal vars >>= evalTacticAt tactics
212-    unless goals.isEmpty do
213-      reportUnsolvedGoals goals
214-    return goal
215-  errorMsg : TacticM MessageData := do
216-    let goalMsgs ← goals.mapM (.ofName <$> ·.getUserName)
217-    return if goals.isEmpty
218-      then m!"There are no unhandled alternatives"
219-      else m!"Expected {.orList goalMsgs}"
220-
221-@[tactic Lean.Parser.inversion, inherit_doc Lean.Parser.inversion]
222-public meta def evalInversion : Tactic
223-  | `(tactic| inversion $config $h:ident $[with $[$tactics?:tacticSeq]? $[$alts?:invAlts]*]?) => do
224-    let config ← elabInversionConfig config
225-    let mut goals ← inversionCore (← getFVarId h) config
226-    if let some tactics := tactics?.join then
227-      let subgoals ← goals.mapM (evalTacticAt tactics)
228-      goals ← subgoals.flatten.filterM (not <$> ·.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned)
229-    if let some alts := alts? then
230-      let expandedAlts ← Array.flatten <$> alts.mapM expandInvAlts
231-      for alt in expandedAlts do
232-        let solvedGoals ← evalInvAlt goals alt
233-        goals := goals.filter (!solvedGoals.contains ·)
234-      unless goals.isEmpty do
235-        reportUnsolvedGoals goals
236-    replaceMainGoal goals
237-  | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion tactic"
238-where expandInvAlts
239-  | `(invAlts| $[| $args:caseArg]* => $tactics:tacticSeq) =>
240-    args.mapM (`(invAlt| | $(·) => $tactics))
241-  | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion alternatives"
242-
243-end Lean.Elab.Tactic
244-
245-end -- meta section

247-namespace Tests
248-open Nat
249-
250-set_option autoImplicit false
251-set_option pp.proofs true
252-set_option pp.fieldNotation false
253-
254-/-! # `inversion` tests -/
255-
256-/-- In Lean, "inversion" on `leq : f n ≤ 0`, where `f : Nat → Nat`,
257-  requires `generalizing e : f n = m`, since Lean does not perform
258-  the dependent case analysis automatically. `cases leq` will fail here.
259-  We want to keep the style of reasoning familiar to PL:
260-  "I know `h`; what must have been true for `h` to be true?"
261-  The technicality of needing to generalize hinders teaching and learning
262-  this style of reasoning for audiences new to proof assistants and logic.
263-  To solve this, we introduce and use the `inversion` tactic,
264-  which automatically generalizes varaibles, performs case analysis,
265-  and eliminates impossible subcases. -/
266-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
267-  -- cases leq /- Dependent elimination failed: Failed to solve equation 0 = f n -/
268-  inversion leq; assumption
269-
270-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
271-  inversion +clear leq; assumption
272-
273-/-- error: Unknown identifier `leq` -/
274-#guard_msgs(error) in
275-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
276-  inversion +clear leq
277-  guard_hyp leq
278-
279-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
280-  inversion leq with
281-  | refl heq eq =>
282-    guard_hyp heq : leq ≍ le.refl
283-    guard_hyp eq : 0 = f n
284-    assumption
285-
286-/-- warning: declaration uses `sorry` -/
287-#guard_msgs(warning) in
288-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
289-  inversion leq with
290-  | refl e _ | step k _ e _ =>
291-    try rw [← e]
292-    sorry
293-
294-/-- error: Invalid wildcard alternative: There are no unhandled alternatives -/
295-#guard_msgs(error) in
296-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
297-  inversion +clear leq with
298-  | refl e | step k _ e =>
299-    try rw [← e]
300-    sorry
301-  | _ => sorry
302-
303-/-- error: Invalid alternative name `step`: There are no unhandled alternatives -/
304-#guard_msgs(error) in
305-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
306-  inversion +clear leq with
307-  | _ e | step k _ e =>
308-    try rw [← e]
309-    sorry
310-
311-inductive The : ∀ {α}, α → Prop where
312-  | mk : The zero
313-
314-/-- sfl#40: Case names should be the constructors' names -/
315-example {x : Nat} (h : The x) : x = zero := by
316-  inversion h with
317-  | mk => rfl
318-
319-example {α} {n m k : α} : [n, m] = [k, k] → [n] = [m] := by
320-  intro h
321-  inversion h; rfl
322-
323-example {n : Nat} : n + 1 = 1 + n := by
324-  induction n with try rfl
325-  | succ => lia
326-
327-inductive NoStutter {α : Type} : List α → Prop where
328-  | nostutter0: NoStutter []
329-  | nostutter1 {n} : NoStutter (n :: [])
330-  | nostutter2 {x y l} (hneq : x ≠ y) (h : NoStutter (y :: l)) : NoStutter (x :: y :: l)
331-
332-/-- The last (only) case name need not be provided -/
333-example : ¬ (NoStutter [3, 1, 1, 4]) := by
334-  intro contra
335-  inversion contra with | _ contra =>
336-  inversion contra with | _ h _ =>
337-  apply h
338-  rfl
339-
340-/-- Inversion may optionally take a sequence of tactics on all goals -/
341-example {α x y} {l : List α} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
342-  inversion h with
343-    injections
344-    try subst_vars
345-  | nostutter2 => assumption
346-
347-/-- `with` acts similarly to `<;>` on the optional sequence of tactics -/
348-example {α x y} {l : List α} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
349-  inversion h with
350-    injections
351-    try (subst_vars; assumption)
352-
353-example {x y} {l : List Nat} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
354-  inversion h with
355-    injections
356-    try cases x
357-  | nostutter2.zero => subst_vars; assumption
358-  | nostutter2.succ => subst_vars; assumption
359-
360-inductive Vec α : Nat → Type where
361-  | nil : Vec α 0
362-  | cons {n} : α → Vec α n → Vec α (n + 1)
363-
364-/-- Inversion should work on indexed `Type`s as well -/
365-example {α} (n : Nat) (v : Vec α (n + 1)) : ∃ hd tl, v = Vec.cons hd tl := by
366-  inversion v with
367-  | cons hd tl => exists hd, tl
368-
369-inductive Wec α : Nat → Type where
370-  | nil : Wec α 0
371-  | cons {n} (f : Nat → Nat) : α → Wec α n → Wec α (f n)
372-
373-/-- warning: declaration uses `sorry` -/
374-#guard_msgs(warning) in
375-example {α} (n : Nat) (v : Wec α (succ n)) :
376-    ∃ hd tl, v = Wec.cons succ hd tl := by
377-  inversion v with
378-  | cons m f hd tl eq heq =>
379-    guard_hyp eq : succ n = f m
380-    guard_hyp heq : v ≍ Wec.cons f hd tl
381-    sorry
382-
383-inductive EmptyRelation : Nat → Nat → Prop where
384-
385-/-- sfl#52: Inversion should still work on nonindexed `Prop`s -/
386-example n m : ¬ EmptyRelation n m := by
387-  intro contra; inversion contra
388-
389-/-- With `inductive.autoPromoteIndices` true (the default),
390-  this is also a nonindexed `Prop`... -/
391-inductive silly : Nat → Prop where
392-| silly1 n (h : n > 1) : silly n
393-| silly2 n (h : exists m, m * 2 = n) : silly n
394-| silly3 n (h : exists m, n = m + 2) : silly n
395-
396-/-- ...and inversion should continue to work -/
397-example {n} (h : silly n) : n ≠ 1 := by
398-  inversion h <;> omega
399-
400-/-- Inversion should also work on nonindexed `Type`s -/
401-example (n : Nat) : Nat := by
402-  inversion n with
403-  | zero => exact zero
404-  | succ n' => exact n'
405-
406-/-! # `lemma` tests -/
407-
408-lemma doubleNegation : ∀ P, P → ¬ ¬ P := by
409-  intro P p np; exact (np p)
410-
411-/-! # `apply` tests -/
412-
413-example (H : Bool → Nat → False) (n : Nat) : False := by
414-  apply H at n; apply n; exact true
415-
416-end Tests

LF/Typeclasses.lean

1-import HL.SFLCompat
2-
3--- # Typeclasses
4-
5--- Chapter Poly introduced **parametric polymorphism**, declaring a type
6--- variable with no constraint on it.
7-
8--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
9---     Students will run across universes, though. When looking at List
10---     lemmas, for example, they will see things like:
11---
12---     `List.reverse.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : List α`
13---
14---     Are we explaining these things somewhere, maybe in Poly ?
15-
16--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
17---     Yes, in Poly!
18-
19--- This lets us work with a type like `List α`, writing functions like
20--- `List.reverse` and `List.length` and proofs like `List.length_reverse`,
21--- which use only the list's structure and never inspect any particular
22--- `a : α`.
23-
24--- Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than leaving `α` completely
25--- generic, we want to partially specify its behavior. In Lean, this is done
26--- through a form of "ad hoc polymorphism" called **typeclasses**. The concept
27--- originated in Haskell and is analogous to features you may know from other
28--- languages, such as traits in Rust.
29-
30--- ## Why We Need Typeclasses
31-
32--- Consider the following function, which checks whether a natural number
33--- occurs in a list:
34-
35-def List.elem_nat (a : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Bool :=
36-  match xs with
37-  | [] => false
38-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_nat a tl
39-
40-theorem List.elem_nat_nil (a : Nat) : [].elem_nat a = false := rfl
41-
42-theorem List.elem_nat_cons (a b : Nat) (xs : List Nat) :
43-    (b :: xs).elem_nat a = bif a == b then true else elem_nat a xs := rfl
44-
45-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 0
46-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 1
47-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 2
48-
49--- What if we want this to work for lists of *any* element type, not just
50--- `Nat`? Parametric polymorphism suggests simply replacing `Nat` with a type
51--- variable `α`, but that produces a puzzling error:
52-
53-sf_expect_failure
54-  def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
55-    match xs with
56-    | [] => false
57-    | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
58-
59--- failed to synthesize instance of type class
60---   BEq α
61-
62--- Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
63-
64--- Lean is trying to use typeclasses to work out how `==` should behave on a
65--- value of type `α`. We'll see exactly why shortly; for now, here's one way
66--- to sidestep the problem: have the caller supply the equality test to use.
67-
68-def List.elem_poly_eq {α : Type} (eq : α → α → Bool) (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
69-  match xs with
70-  | [] => false
71-  | b :: tl => bif eq a b then true else elem_poly_eq eq a tl
72-
73-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0
74-
75--- This works, but it's tedious: every caller has to know, and remember to
76--- supply, the right equality function.
77-
78--- Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer passing the function
79--- explicitly, Lean searches for one and provides it on its own. We specify
80--- something we want Lean to search for by declaring a `class` with the needed
81--- function as a field; a `class` is like an interface in Java or a trait in
82--- Rust. Particular implementations of that class are called *instance*; each
83--- type can have its own instance of a class. For functions that would use
84--- such instances, we specify the name of the class in a *instance implicit*
85--- on the polymorphic variable that the instance's function applies to. This
86--- directs Lean to rely on the class inside the function, and to find and fill
87--- in the appropriate instance when the function is called.
88-
89--- Here is what this looks like for `List.elem_poly`:
90-
91-def List.elem_poly {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
92-  match xs with
93-  | [] => false
94-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
95-
96-theorem List.elem_poly_nil {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) : [].elem_poly a = false := rfl
97-
98-theorem List.elem_poly_cons {α : Type} [BEq α] (a b : α) (xs : List α) :
99-    (b :: xs).elem_poly a = bif a == b then true else elem_poly a xs := rfl
100-
101-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly 0
102-
103--- Comparing `List.elem_poly_eq` with `List.elem_poly`, we see three
104--- differences. First, `List.elem_poly_eq` takes an *explicit* parameter `eq`,
105--- whereas `List.elem_poly` specifies an instance implicit `[BEq α]`. The
106--- instance implicit indicates that an instance of `BEq` must be provided at
107--- call sites for the particular type `α` that is used. Second, whereas
108--- `List.elem_poly_eq` invokes parameter `eq` to test equality,
109--- `List.elem_poly` uses `==` instead. As Lists noted when we first used it,
110--- `==` on `Nat` comes from the `BEq` typeclass. Finally, whereas
111--- `[0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0` passes the equality function `Nat.beq`
112--- explicitly, in `[0, 1].elem_poly 0` Lean fills it in automatically based on
113--- the type `Nat` of the `List`.
114-
115--- Note to developers (xhalo32):
116---     This is technically incorrect, the instance `BEq Nat`, which comes from
117---     `DecidableEq`, does not contain `Nat.beq`. You can see in proofs of
118---     `List.elem_nat` versus `List.elem_poly_eq` versus `List.elem_poly` and
119---     how `Nat.beq` and `==` play different roles.
120-
121--- Going back to the earlier version of `List.elem_poly`, without the instance
122--- implicit, we can now understand the error message: `α` was fully generic —
123--- so the `==` in its body would have needed to work for *every* type `α`, and
124--- no single `BEq` instance can do that. So Lean's search failed.
125-
126--- Now it is time to dig into the details of what we have seen so far. We'll
127--- see exactly how `[BEq α]` gets filled in below, starting with how to define
128--- a typeclass in the first place.
129-
130--- ## Defining Your Own Typeclasses
131-
132--- `BEq` comes from Lean's standard library. Let's define a typeclass of our
133--- own, to see the mechanism — classes, instances, and synthesis — that made
134--- `==` resolve automatically above.
135-
136--- Suppose we want a function that returns the first element of a list,
137--- defaulting to a given value if the list is empty. As with
138--- `List.elem_poly_eq` above, here is a version that makes the default value
139--- an explicit parameter:
140-
141-def List.headOr_ex {α : Type} (defaultValue : α) (xs : List α) : α :=
142-  match xs with
143-  | [] => defaultValue
144-  | hd :: _ => hd
145-
146-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr_ex 0
147-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr_ex 0
148-
149--- This works, but again it's tedious: every caller has to supply an element
150--- of `α` to default to, even when there's an obvious choice based on the type
151--- of the things in the list, like `0` for `Nat`.
152-
153--- Getting Lean to fill in `defaultValue` automatically takes two things. One
154--- is marking the parameter as "searchable," rather than something the caller
155--- always supplies explicitly. The other is giving Lean some information about
156--- what it should search *for*.
157-
158--- Considering the second problem first: the way to provide this information
159--- is to *name* the data we're after — the **default value** of a type. In
160--- particular, a `structure` (chapter Lists) is a good way to give this
161--- information a name; structures can also bundle together more than one piece
162--- of data, which will come in handy later, though we only need a single field
163--- here.
164-
165--- To address the first problem, we need to mark this particular structure as
166--- one Lean should search for automatically — not every `structure`-typed
167--- argument should be.
168-
169--- Let's build up to what we want in two steps: first the naming, as a plain
170--- `structure`; then the marking, by upgrading it to a `class`. Here's the
171--- structure — we'll put it in its own namespace so we can reuse the name
172--- `DefaultValue` for the class version below:
173-
174-namespace DefaultValueScratch
175-
176-structure DefaultValue (α : Type) where
177-  value : α
178-
179--- A value of type `DefaultValue Nat` picks out a particular `Nat` to serve as
180--- the type's default: it's built the same way any structure is, by supplying
181--- a `Nat` for the `value` field:
182-
183-def natDefault : DefaultValue Nat where
184-  value := 0
185-
186-end DefaultValueScratch
187-
188--- Now for the marking: we need to tell Lean that `DefaultValue` is the sort
189--- of structure it should search for automatically, the way it needs to for
190--- `List.headOr_ex`'s `defaultValue` argument. We do this by writing `class`
191--- in place of `structure`:
192-
193-class DefaultValue (α : Type) where
194-  value : α
195-
196--- We then provide values of this type a bit differently. Instead of `def`, we
197--- use `instance`:
198-
199-instance instDefaultValueNat : DefaultValue Nat where
200-  value := 0
201-
202--- Lean can now find this instance on its own, via *typeclass synthesis* (or
203--- *typeclass inference*) — the same process that found `BEq Nat` earlier.
204--- That means we can rewrite `List.headOr_ex` the same way we rewrote
205--- `List.elem_poly_eq` into `List.elem_poly` above, replacing the explicit
206--- `defaultValue` parameter with an instance implicit:
207-
208-def List.headOr {α : Type} [DefaultValue α] (xs : List α) : α :=
209-  match xs with
210-  | [] => DefaultValue.value
211-  | hd :: _ => hd
212-
213-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr
214-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr
215-
216-example : DefaultValue.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
217-
218--- Notice that we refer to `DefaultValue.value` alone, with no instance named.
219--- Because the expression equates `DefaultValue.value` with the `Nat` `0`,
220--- Lean selects `instDefaultValueNat`, the instance for `DefaultValue Nat`. We
221--- know this because we are able to prove that `DefaultValue.value` is equal
222--- to `0`.
223-
224--- Let's declare a second instance, for `Int`, the type of integers
225--- `... -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...`:
226-
227-instance instDefaultValueInt : DefaultValue Int where
228-  value := -1
229-
230--- We can also create instances for polymorphic types, like `Option α`, whose
231--- default is `none`, by giving the instance declaration a parameter:
232-
233-instance instDefaultValueOption {α : Type} : DefaultValue (Option α) where
234-  value := none
235-
236--- Now, Lean can infer instances for all these types, including inside
237--- `List.headOr`:
238-
239-example : DefaultValue.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
240-example : DefaultValue.value = (-1 : Int) := by rfl
241-example : DefaultValue.value = (none : Option Bool) := by rfl
242-example : DefaultValue.value = (none : Option (List Nat)) := by rfl
243-example : ([] : List Nat).headOr = 0 := by rfl
244-example : ([] : List Int).headOr = -1 := by rfl
245-example : ([] : List (Option Bool)).headOr = none := by rfl
246-example : ([] : List (Option Bool)).headOr = none := by rfl
247-
248--- Synthesis infers instances we could have specified explicitly:
249-
250-example : instDefaultValueNat.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
251-example : instDefaultValueInt.value = (-1 : Int) := by rfl
252-example : instDefaultValueOption.value = (none : Option Nat) := by rfl
253-
254--- The option `pp.all` shows which instance Lean picked:
255-
256-set_option pp.all true in
257-#check (DefaultValue.value : Nat)
258-
259--- @DefaultValue.value Nat instDefaultValueNat : Nat
260-
261-set_option pp.all true in
262-#check (DefaultValue.value : Int)
263-
264--- @DefaultValue.value Int instDefaultValueInt : Int
265-
266--- This reveals `instDefaultValueNat` and `instDefaultValueInt` as the
267--- instances Lean picked. The `#synth` command runs the same search directly:
268-
269-#synth DefaultValue Nat
270-
271--- instDefaultValueNat
272-
273--- For a typeclass like `DefaultValue` that carries data — a term, such as the
274--- `1` above, rather than only proofs (which we will see below) — we expect at
275--- most one instance per type, so this search has a unique answer.
276-
277--- We'll put `DefaultValue`'s standard-library equivalent, `Inhabited`, to
278--- work later in this chapter, when we define maps that need a default value
279--- for a generic type. First, though, let's go back to `List.elem_poly` and
280--- see how its `[BEq α]` argument actually gets resolved.
281-
282--- ## Using Typeclasses
283-
284--- Let's check what `==` meant for `List.elem_nat`, with notation display
285--- turned off:
286-
287-set_option pp.notation false in
288-#check 1 == 2
289-
290--- BEq.beq 1 2 : Bool
291-
292--- Rather than `Nat.beq`, `==` turns out to be notation for `BEq.beq`, a field
293--- of exactly the kind of typeclass we just learned to define:
294-
295--- /--
296---   `BEq α` is a typeclass for supplying a boolean-valued equality relation on
297---   `α`, notated as `a == b`. Unlike `DecidableEq α` (which uses `a = b`), this
298---   is `Bool` valued instead of `Prop` valued, and it also does not have any
299---   axioms like being reflexive or agreeing with `=`. It is mainly intended for
300---   programming applications. See `LawfulBEq` for a version that requires that
301---   `==` and `=` coincide.
302-
303---   Typically we prefer to put the "more variable" term on the left,
304---   and the "more constant" term on the right.
305---   -/
306---   class BEq (α : Type u) where
307---     /-- Boolean equality, notated as `a == b`. -/
308---     beq : α → α → Bool
309-
310--- Writing `a == b` makes Lean search for an **instance** of `BEq` for the
311--- type of `a` and `b`, the same way it searched for a `DefaultValue` instance
312--- above. For `Nat`, that instance is:
313-
314-instance (priority := low) : BEq Nat where
315-  beq := Nat.beq
316-
317--- This is the instance Lean supplies for `[BEq α]` when `List.elem_poly` is
318--- called on a `List Nat` — no different from Lean choosing
319--- `instDefaultValueNat` for `DefaultValue.value` earlier when it was equated
320--- with `(1 : Nat)`.
321-
322--- ### Exercise (1 star): List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat ⭐
323-
324--- Prove that `List.elem_poly` agrees with `List.elem_nat` when specialized to
325--- natural numbers.
326-
327-theorem List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat (xs : List Nat) (n : Nat) : xs.elem_poly n = xs.elem_nat n := by
328-  (
329-  induction xs with
330-  | nil =>
331-    rewrite [List.elem_poly_nil, List.elem_nat_nil]
332-    rfl
333-  | cons hd tl ih =>
334-    rewrite [List.elem_poly_cons, List.elem_nat_cons, ih]
335-    rfl)
336-
337--- ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
338-
339--- The above examples enforce no conditions on the data an instance may carry
340--- — any value of the right type will do. But sometimes enforcing constraints
341--- on data is useful. For example, suppose we want to specify that a type has
342--- not just a single element, but two. Here is a first attempt:
343-
344-sf_experiment
345-  class HasTwoIncomplete (α : Type) where
346-    one : α
347-    two : α
348-
349--- Unfortunately, this specification isn't precise because it allows `one` and
350--- `two` to refer to the same term. Fortunately, Lean's typeclasses can carry
351--- proofs along with data, so we can write the following to enforce that `one`
352--- and `two` are distinct.
353-
354-class HasTwo (α : Type) where
355-  one : α
356-  two : α
357-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
358-
359--- Declaring instances works in much the same way as before, except that now
360--- the `HasTwo.one_neq_two` field requires a proof:
361-
362-instance : HasTwo Nat where
363-  one := 1
364-  two := 2
365-  one_neq_two := by intro contra; contradiction
366-
367--- In most languages that support typeclasses (or traits) it is not possible
368--- to formally enforce laws such as `one_neq_two`. Thus it falls to the author
369--- to check, informally, that any required invariants are satisfied, which can
370--- lead to bugs.
371-
372--- ### Exercise (1 star): HasThree ⭐
373-
374--- Following the pattern of `DefaultValue` and `HasTwo`, define a class
375--- `HasThree` that specifies a type with at least three distinct elements, and
376--- give an instance of it for `Nat`.
377-
378-class HasThree (α : Type) where
379-  one : α
380-  two : α
381-  three : α
382-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
383-  one_neq_three : one ≠ three
384-  two_neq_three : two ≠ three
385-
386-instance : HasThree Nat where
387-  one := 1
388-  two := 2
389-  three := 3
390-  one_neq_two := (by intro contra; contradiction)
391-  one_neq_three := (by intro contra; contradiction)
392-  two_neq_three := (by intro contra; contradiction)
393-
394-namespace Algebra
395-
396--- This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively in Lean to define
397--- mathematical structures that carry both operators and laws about how those
398--- operators interact. As a simple example, let's use a typeclass to define a
399--- *monoid*, a simple algebraic structure that includes four things:
400-
401--- - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
402-
403--- - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that combines two
404---   elements of type `α` into one,
405-
406--- - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call the "identity
407---   element", and
408-
409--- - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`, namely that:
410-
411---   - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
412---   - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗` is associative)
413-
414--- We can express these requirements in the form of a typeclass:
415-
416--- first we define a notation typeclass for our operator ⊗
417-class OpSet (α : Type) where
418-  op : α → α → α
419-
420-infixr:70 " ⊗ " => OpSet.op
421-
422-class Monoid (α : Type) extends (OpSet α) where
423-  id : α
424-  left_id : ∀ (x : α), id ⊗ x = x
425-  right_id : ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ id = x
426-  assoc : ∀ (x y z : α), x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
427-
428--- The `extends` keyword indicates that the `Monoid` typeclass extends the
429--- `OpSet` typeclass, which just defines a set with an operator and some
430--- notation for it. The `Monoid` typeclass "inherits" the fields of `OpSet`,
431--- similar to how a class would in an object-oriented language.
432-
433--- As one might expect, the `+` operator over `Nat`s forms a monoid, where `0`
434--- is the identity element. Note that we don't have to define `Nat`'s `OpSet`
435--- instance separately, we can define a single instance that implements both
436--- classes.
437-
438-instance : Monoid Nat where
439-  op := Nat.add
440-  id := 0
441-  left_id := by lia
442-  right_id := by lia
443-  assoc := by lia
444-
445--- ### Exercise (1 star): NatMonoidMul ⭐
446-
447--- However, multiplication on `Nat`s *also* forms a monoid. What is its
448--- identity element?
449-
450-instance : Monoid Nat where
451-  op := Nat.mul
452-  id := (1)
453-  left_id := (by lia)
454-  right_id := (by lia)
455-  assoc := (by lia)
456-
457--- ### Exercise (1 star): ListMonoidAppend ⭐
458-
459--- There are also many monoids over other types. Most usefully in computer
460--- science, lists of any type also form a monoid, with `List.append` as the
461--- operator in question:
462-
463-instance {α : Type} : Monoid (List α) where
464-  op := List.append
465-  id := ([])
466-  left_id := (by simp)
467-  right_id := (by simp)
468-  assoc := (by simp)
469-
470--- In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can also prove some
471--- properties about monoids in general, just based on the laws defined on the
472--- typeclass. One simple theorem about monoids is that the identity element of
473--- a monoid is unique. That is, if we have two monoids over the same set with
474--- the same operator, their identity elements must also be the same:
475-
476-theorem id_unique {α : Type} {m₁ m₂ : Monoid α} (h : m₁.op = m₂.op) : m₁.id = m₂.id := by
477-  obtain @⟨op₁, id₁, left_id₁, right_id₁, assoc₁⟩ := m₁
478-  obtain @⟨op₂, id₂, left_id₂, right_id₂, assoc₂⟩ := m₂
479-  have h' : id₁ = id₂ := by
480-    -- this introduces a use of m₁'s operator
481-    rw [← left_id₁ id₂]
482-    -- we use our hypothesis to rewrite m₁'s operator into m₂'s
483-    rw [h]
484-    -- then, we can use m₂'s right id
485-    rw [right_id₂]
486-  -- the goal `m₁.id = m₂.id` is equivalent with `id₁ = id₂` even though it displays `Monoid.id = Monoid.id`
487-  exact h'
488-
489--- In the above proof, we can destructure the monoid instances `m₁` and `m₂`
490--- with the `obtain` tactic we saw in the Logic chapter. When we do so
491--- however, because these are class instances instead of normal structures, we
492--- preface our tuple with the `@` symbol. When stepping through the above
493--- proof, if the notation is confusing to you, remember that you can set
494--- `set_option pp.all true` or `set_option pp.explicit true` to make Lean show
495--- you more clearly what is going on. For example, the goal is displayed as
496--- `Monoid.id = Monoid.id` since the instances `m₁` and `m₂` are implicit
497--- arguments to `Monoid.id`. Setting `pp.explicit true` displays the goal as
498--- `@Eq α (@Monoid.id α m₁) (@Monoid.id α m₂)`.
499-
500--- A *group* is a special kind of monoid with an *inverse* operation `inv`,
501--- which has the property that `∀ x, inv x ⊗ x = id = x ⊗ inv x`. We can
502--- extend the definition of a `Monoid` to capture this new feature:
503-
504-class Group (α : Type) extends (Monoid α) where
505-  inv : α → α
506-  left_inv : ∀ (x : α), inv x ⊗ x = id
507-  right_inv: ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ inv x = id
508-
509--- Now, the monoids we described earlier are not groups: there is no inverse
510--- operation on the natural numbers such that
511--- `∀ x, x + inv x = 0 = inv x + x`, for example. However, addition does form
512--- a group over the integers:
513-
514--- ### Exercise (1 star): IntGroupAdd ⭐
515-
516-instance : Group Int where
517-  op := Int.add
518-  id := (0)
519-  inv := (Int.neg)
520-  left_id := (by lia)
521-  right_id := (by lia)
522-  assoc := (by lia)
523-  left_inv := (by lia)
524-  right_inv := (by lia)
525-
526--- The study of groups is called *group theory* and is a rich area of
527--- mathematics. Here, we will only prove a handful of its simplest results:
528-
529--- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
530---     This also prints weird.
531-
532--- ### Exercise (1 star): InverseUnique ⭐
533-
534--- Two groups defined with the same operation over the same set must have the
535--- same inverse as well.
536-
537-theorem inv_unique {α : Type} {g₁ g₂ : Group α} (h : g₁.op = g₂.op) : g₁.inv = g₂.inv := by
538-  ext a
539-  rw [←g₁.right_id (Group.inv a), ←g₁.right_inv a]
540-  rw [g₁.assoc, h, g₂.left_inv a, g₂.left_id]
541-
542--- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
543---     Taking suggestions for additional simple group theory theorems to prove
544---     here.
545-
546-end Algebra
547-
548--- ## Maps
549-
550--- *Maps* (or "dictionaries") are ubiquitous data structures both in ordinary
551--- programming and in the theory of programming languages; we're going to need
552--- them in many places in later volumes.
553-
554--- We'll define two flavors of maps: *total maps*, which include a "default"
555--- element to be returned when a key being looked up doesn't exist, and
556--- *partial maps*, which instead return an option to indicate success or
557--- failure. Partial maps are defined in terms of total maps, using `none` as
558--- the default element.
559-
560--- ### Key and Value Types
561-
562--- To define maps, we first need a type for the keys that we will use to index
563--- into our maps and a type for the values the maps return. In this section,
564--- we'll use the type variable `α` for the type of keys and `β` for values. In
565--- addition to `BEq`, which we have already seen, our key type `α` requires
566--- instances of the `ReflBEq` and `LawfulBEq` typeclasses:
567-
568--- /-- `ReflBEq α` says that the `BEq` implementation is reflexive. -/
569---   class ReflBEq (α) [BEq α] : Prop where
570---     /-- `==` is reflexive, that is, `(a == a) = true`. -/
571---     protected rfl {a : α} : a == a
572-
573--- /--
574---   A Boolean equality test coincides with propositional equality.
575-
576---   In other words:
577---    * `a == b` implies `a = b`.
578---    * `a == a` is true.
579---   -/
580---   class LawfulBEq (α : Type u) [BEq α] : Prop extends ReflBEq α where
581---     /-- If `a == b` evaluates to `true`, then `a` and `b` are equal in the logic. -/
582---     eq_of_beq : {a b : α} → a == b → a = b
583-
584--- These classes refine `BEq`, specifying that (`==`) is reflexive and
585--- coincides with proposition equality `=`.
586-
587--- In general, we place no constraints on the value type `β`.
588-
589--- ### Total Maps
590-
591--- The Lists chapter introduced a partial map abstraction, `PartialMap`, with
592--- a `find` function for lookup, based on lists of key-value pairs. Here, we
593--- are going to build a map abstraction using functions instead. The advantage
594--- of this representation is that it offers a more *extensional* view of maps,
595--- as we saw with functions in the Logic chapter: two maps that respond to
596--- every query in the same way will be represented as exactly the same
597--- function, rather than just as "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies
598--- proofs that use maps.
599-
600--- Instead of using functions directly, we encapsulate them inside a
601--- `structure` which we call `TotalMap`. Intuitively, a total map just
602--- contains a function `inner` from a key of type `α` to a value of type `β`.
603-
604-structure TotalMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
605-  inner : α → β
606-
607-namespace TotalMap
608-
609--- In order to declare a default value of `β` we will use the `Inhabited`
610--- typeclass, which is the standard library's implementation of our
611--- `DefaultValue` example from above:
612-
613--- The function `TotalMap.empty` yields an empty total map, given a default
614--- element; this map always returns the default element when applied to any
615--- key.
616-
617-def empty {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : TotalMap α β where
618-  inner := fun _ ↦ default
619-
620--- These types and implicit instances are now available automatically to all
621--- the definitions in this section.
622-
623--- Just as declaring `BEq`/`DefaultValue` instances above hooked `==` and
624--- `DefaultValue.value` up to our types, we can declare an instance of the
625--- standard library's `EmptyCollection` typeclass to associate `∅` with this
626--- empty map.
627-
628-instance {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : EmptyCollection (TotalMap α β) where
629-  emptyCollection := TotalMap.empty
630-
631-theorem empty_def {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : (∅ : TotalMap α β) = { inner := fun _ ↦ default } := by rfl
632-
633--- Here, for example, is an empty map that takes `Nat` keys to `Nat` values:
634-
635-def emptyNatMap : TotalMap Nat Nat := ∅
636-
637--- #### Getting Elements
638-
639--- While `TotalMap`s happen to be implemented as functions under the hood, we
640--- would prefer not to expose this fact in its public interface. Accordingly,
641--- we define new operations for querying and updating mappings. We define a
642--- function `get` for getting the value associated with a key playing the role
643--- that `find` played for the Lists chapter's list-based maps,
644-
645-def get {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) := m.inner a
646-
647-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `TotalMap`.
648-Avoid using this outside the `TotalMap` namespace. -/
649-theorem get_def {α β : Type} {m : TotalMap α β} {a : α} : m.get a = m.inner a := by rfl
650-
651-example : emptyNatMap.get 2 = 0 := by rfl
652-
653--- Here is an example that uses the API lemmas `empty_def` and `get_def`:
654-
655-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap.get n = 0 := by
656-  rewrite [get_def, emptyNatMap, empty_def, Nat.default_eq_zero]
657-  rfl
658-
659--- In the above example, we use `rewrite` and `rfl` instead of the usual `rw`
660--- to highlight something interesting. After the rewrites in this proof, we
661--- end up with a goal that looks like `{ inner := fun x => 0 }.inner n = 0`,
662--- which we can solve with `rfl`. This is because the projection `.inner` on a
663--- structure of the form `{ inner := x }` is definitionally equal to `x`.
664-
665--- `get` is the public API counterpart to `inner` which is an
666--- implementation-specific detail of `TotalMap`. Because `get_def` "peeks"
667--- through the abstraction, it should be used sparingly, and only inside the
668--- `TotalMap` namespace.
669-
670--- To make element-getting more convenient, let's define notation so we can
671--- write `emptyNatMap[2]` rather than `emptyNatMap.get`. We could notate `get`
672--- directly — we'll do exactly that for `update` below — but here we'll
673--- instead make "getting an element" its own typeclass, `MyGetElem`, and
674--- notate it. Doing so means `m[a]` resolves to `MyGetElem.getElem m a` for
675--- any type with a `MyGetElem` instance, not just `TotalMap`.
676-
677--- Using typeclasses to define notation is typical in Lean when the same
678--- notation is useful for many different types. We have seen the approach
679--- already with `==`: writing `a == b` is notation for `BEq.beq`, resolved by
680--- instance search for whatever type `a` and `b` have. We also just saw
681--- overloaded notation for `EmptyCollection` above, where `∅` is notation for
682--- `EmptyCollection.emptyCollection`. Our typeclass `MyGetElem` is a simpler
683--- version of the standard library's `GetElem` typeclass, which has many
684--- instances such as `Array`, `List`, and `Vector`. We develop it to
685--- illustrate the notation-as-typeclass approach.
686-
687--- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
688---     A reason I can come up with why we use a notation typeclass (in library
689---     code) over a plain notation is that it makes it possible (for a
690---     downstream consumer) to write `open scoped MyGetElem` instead of
691---     writing `open scoped TotalMap` and `open scoped PartialMap`
692---     individually. This wouldn't be a good sell if `→ₜ` and `→ₚ` are scoped
693---     notations, but they're currently global.
694-
695-end TotalMap
696-
697--- The `MyGetElem` typeclass takes three type parameters: the map
698--- implementation, its keys, and its values.
699-
700-class MyGetElem (coll : Type) (idx : Type) (elem : outParam Type) where
701-  getElem (xs : coll) (i : idx) : elem
702-
703--- (Don't worry about the `outParam` qualifier; it is a hint to Lean that
704--- helps typeclass inference.)
705-
706--- The appropriate instance of `MyGetElem` for our `TotalMap` is:
707-
708-instance {α β : Type} : MyGetElem (TotalMap α β) α β where
709-  getElem m a := m.get a
710-
711--- Now we can associate the bracket syntax with `MyGetElem.getElem`. We've
712--- defined custom notation before — `::` and `[...]` for lists (chapter Lists,
713--- including an `app_unexpander` for printing `[...]`-notation lists back
714--- out), or `+`/`*`/`==` for arithmetic — but always with `infixl`/`infixr` or
715--- `scoped macro`; this is the first time we reach for the more general
716--- `notation`/`macro_rules` forms for getting the `m[a]` syntax to work.
717-
718--- Don't worry about following the mechanism in detail — the `macro_rules` and
719--- the `app_unexpander` below are minor technicalities. However, if you do
720--- wish to learn more, Chapter 5 and 6 of [Metaprogramming in Lean
721--- 4](https://leanprover-community.github.io/lean4-metaprogramming-book/)
722--- contain more detail.
723-
724-namespace MyGetElem
725-
726-scoped macro_rules | `($xs[$i]) => ``(getElem $xs $i)
727-
728-@[app_unexpander getElem]
729-def unexpandGetElem : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
730-  | `($_ $xs $i) => `($xs[$i])
731-  | _ => throw ()
732-end MyGetElem
733-
734-open scoped MyGetElem
735-
736--- Since the standard library already declares the `x[i]` syntax for
737--- `GetElem`, we only need to define the `macro_rules`, not the `notation` as
738--- we have done previously. It's scoped since we don't want to override the
739--- default `GetElem` everywhere, but only when `open scoped MyGetElem` is in
740--- force.
741-
742--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
743---     Make sure we've really explained `open scoped` somewhere...
744-
745--- Since we provided a `MyGetElem` instance for `TotalMap`, we can now use the
746--- notation `m[a]` to access elements of a map `m`.
747-
748-namespace TotalMap
749-
750-theorem getElem_def {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m.get a := by rfl
751-
752-example : emptyNatMap[1] = default := by rfl
753-
754-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap[n] = 0 := by
755-  rw [getElem_def, get_def, emptyNatMap, empty_def, Nat.default_eq_zero]
756-
757--- We want the public API of `TotalMap` to use the `m[a]` notation instead of
758--- `m.get a` so we provide the reverse direction of `getElem_def` as a `simp`
759--- lemma; the `m[a]` notation is the `TotalMap` API's `simp` normal form.
760-
761-@[simp]
762-theorem get_eq_getElem {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m.get a = m[a] := rfl
763-
764-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap.get n = emptyNatMap[n] := by
765-  simp
766-
767--- This design minimizes the need to use `getElem_def` outside concrete
768--- examples (which are typically solvable with `rfl` anyways).
769-
770--- #### Updating Elements
771-
772--- Now we turn to the `update` function, which takes a map `m`, a key `a`, and
773--- a value `b` and returns a new map that takes `a` to `b` and takes every
774--- other key to whatever `m` does. We do this by wrapping a new map function
775--- around the old one.
776-
777-def update {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) [BEq α] (a : α) (b : β) : TotalMap α β where
778-  inner := fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a']
779-
780--- For example, we can build a map taking `String` to `Bool`, where `"foo"`
781--- and `"bar"` are mapped to `true` and every other key is mapped to `false`,
782--- like this:
783-
784-def exampleMap :=
785-  (∅ : TotalMap String Bool)
786-    |>.update "foo" true
787-    |>.update "bar" true
788-
789--- Here `|>` is Lean's **pipe** notation: `x |>.f y` means `x.f y`, letting us
790--- chain a sequence of function or method calls left to right without nested
791--- parentheses.
792-
793--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
794---     Should we introduce this notation earlier? (Are there good places to
795---     use it earlier?)
796-
797--- We also introduce a notation for updating maps — this time, rather than
798--- going through a typeclass and its own `notation`/`macro_rules` machinery as
799--- we did for `MyGetElem`, we write a `notation` that references
800--- `TotalMap.update` directly. Unlike indexing, `update` doesn't need to work
801--- generically across container types (there's no standard-library operation
802--- like `GetElem` that we're mirroring here), so the simpler, direct route
803--- suffices.
804-
805-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => TotalMap.update m a b
806-
807-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `TotalMap`.
808-Avoid using this outside the `TotalMap` namespace. Prefer `update_apply` if possible. -/
809-theorem update_def {α β : Type} [BEq α] (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) :
810-  a →ₜ b ; m = { inner := fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a'] } := by rfl
811-
812-theorem update_apply {α β : Type} [BEq α] (m : TotalMap α β) (a a' : α) (b : β) :
813-  (a →ₜ b ; m)[a'] = bif a == a' then b else m[a'] := by rfl
814-
815--- We can omit the map from the notation when we want it to be empty:
816-
817-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 => TotalMap.update ∅ a b
818-
819--- The `examplemap` above can now be defined as follows:
820-
821-def exampleMap' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅
822-def exampleMap'' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true
823-
824-example : exampleMap = exampleMap' := by rfl
825-example : exampleMap' = exampleMap'' := by rfl
826-
827-example : exampleMap'["bar"] = true := by rfl
828-example : exampleMap'["foo"] = true := by rfl
829-example : exampleMap'["quux"] = false := by rfl
830-
831--- Let's also see a couple of examples of working with updated maps using
832--- rewrites:
833-
834-example : exampleMap'["bar"] = true := by
835-  rw [exampleMap', update_apply, BEq.rfl, cond_true]
836-
837-example : exampleMap'["foo"] = true := by
838-  rw [exampleMap', update_apply, show ("bar" == "foo") = false by simp, cond_false]
839-  rw [update_apply, BEq.rfl, cond_true]
840-
841-example : exampleMap'["quux"] = false := by

887--- say when two maps are equal. Since a total map is implemented as a
888--- function, this is effectively the functional extensionality principle
889--- (`funext`) from the Logic chapter: two maps are equal when they agree at
890--- every key. Recording it once, for maps, and tagging it `@[ext]` lets the
891--- `ext` tactic reduce a goal `m₁ = m₂` to the pointwise one in the proofs
892--- below.

897--- `m₁.inner = m₂.inner` or vice versa.

1035--- ### Notation for Concrete Maps
1036-
1037--- Wouldn't it be nice if we could use a more natural notation for concrete
1038--- maps like `{ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }`? To accomplish this we define a
1039--- simple structure that consists of a key and a value along with `↦` notation
1040--- for it.
1041-
1042-/--
1043-A key-value pair with `↦` syntax.
1044--/
1045-@[ext]
1046-structure KVPair (K : Type) (V : Type) where
1047-  key : K
1048-  value : V
1049-
1050-namespace KVPair
1051-scoped notation k " ↦ " v => KVPair.mk k v
1052-end KVPair
1053-
1054-open scoped KVPair
1055-
1056--- Next, we declare `Insert` and `Singleton` instances — the standard-library
1057--- typeclasses behind the `{x, y, ...}` and `{x}` collection-literal notation
1058--- that `List`, `Finset`, and other stdlib containers already support — so
1059--- that `TotalMap` can use it too.
1060-
1061-namespace TotalMap
1062-
1063-instance {α β : Type} [BEq α] : Insert (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
1064-  insert kv m := kv.key →ₜ kv.value ; m
1065-
1066-instance {α β : Type} [BEq α] [Inhabited β] : Singleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
1067-  singleton kv := insert kv ∅
1068-
1069-instance {α β : Type} [BEq α] [Inhabited β] : LawfulSingleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
1070-  insert_empty_eq _ := rfl
1071-
1072-end TotalMap

1076-example : ({ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }) = "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅ := rfl

1083--- doesn't know what type of collection `{ "foo" ↦ true }` is without type

1097--- ### Partial Maps
1098-
1099--- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
1100---     We should spend some time discussing differences between the inductive
1101---     approach in Lists.lean and the approach here. The inductive approach
1102---     could be made polymorphic and proven to be equivalent with partial maps
1103---     (I believe), so the point is not that the maps are extensionally
1104---     different. A question (that I don't have an answer to) is then: what
1105---     makes the new partial map better?
1106-
1107--- Lastly, we define *partial maps* on top of total maps. A partial map with
1108--- elements of type `β` is simply a total map with elements of type
1109--- `Option β`, whose default element is `none`.
1110-
1111-structure PartialMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
1112-  /-- The underlying total map. Lean always generates a public projection for a structure
1113-  field, so `inner` is technically accessible, but it isn't part of the intended interface:
1114-  use `PartialMap.toTotal` instead, so there's exactly one sanctioned way to get at it. -/
1115-  inner : TotalMap α (Option β)
1116-
1117-/- Note that this definition of `EmptyCollection` doesn't need `β` to have an `Inhabited` instance
1118-   like `TotalMap` did. This is because `Option β` has its own `Inhabited` instance: `none` is a value
1119-   of every `Option` type. -/
1120-instance {α β : Type} : EmptyCollection (PartialMap α β) where
1121-  emptyCollection := { inner := ∅ }
1122-
1123-namespace PartialMap
1124-
1125-def toTotal {α β : Type} (m : PartialMap α β) : TotalMap α (Option β) := m.inner
1126-
1127-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `PartialMap`.
1128-Avoid using this outside the `PartialMap` namespace. -/
1129-theorem toTotal_def {α β : Type} (m : PartialMap α β) : m.toTotal = m.inner := by rfl
1130-
1131-instance {α β : Type} : MyGetElem (PartialMap α β) α (Option β) where
1132-  getElem m a := m.toTotal[a]
1133-
1134-theorem getElem_def {α β : Type} (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m.toTotal[a] := rfl
1135-
1136-def emptyNatMap : PartialMap Nat Nat where

1147-theorem toTotal_eq_getElem {α β : Type} (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) :
1148-    m.toTotal[a] = m[a] := rfl

1150--- We previously defined `TotalMap.get` so that users can retrieve elements
1151--- from a `TotalMap` in a manner independent of its actual implementation,
1152--- which is a function stored in `TotalMap.inner`. We follow a similar
1153--- principle with `PartialMap`s, and define `PartialMap.toTotal` to be the
1154--- public API counterpart to `PartialMap.inner`.
1155-

1160--- Updating a partial map at a key means storing a `some` value there. To
1161--- update, we create a new partial map from `a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal` by
1162--- wrapping it in angle brackets, i.e. using the anonymous constructor syntax.
1163--- This is equivalent to writing `{ inner := a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal }`. We
1164--- also introduce a similar notation for it as for total maps.
1165-
1166-def update {α β : Type} [BEq α] (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : PartialMap α β :=
1167-  ⟨a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal⟩

1169-notation a:55 " →ₚ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => PartialMap.update m a b

1171-notation a:55 " →ₚ " b:55 => PartialMap.update ∅ a b

1266--- One last thing: for partial maps, it's convenient to introduce a notion of
1267--- map inclusion, stating that all the entries in one map are also present in
1268--- another. Lean already has notation for this — `m₁ ⊆ m₂` — which we get by
1269--- supplying a `HasSubset` instance.
1270-
1271-def Subset {α β : Type} (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) : Prop :=
1272-  ∀ {a : α} {b : β}, m₁[a] = some b → m₂[a] = some b
1273-
1274-instance {α β : Type} : HasSubset (PartialMap α β) where
1275-  Subset := PartialMap.Subset
1276-
1277-theorem subset_def {α β : Type} (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) :
1278-    m₁ ⊆ m₂ ↔ (∀ {a : α} {b : β}, m₁[a] = some b → m₂[a] = some b) := .rfl
1279-
1280--- We can then show that map update preserves map inclusion, that is:
1281-
1282-theorem update_subset {α β : Type} [BEq α] [LawfulBEq α] (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β)
1283-    (h : m₁ ⊆ m₂) : (a →ₚ b ; m₁) ⊆ (a →ₚ b ; m₂) := by
1284-  rw [subset_def] at h ⊢
1285-  intro a' b' hb
1286-  by_cases ha : a = a'
1287-  · subst ha
1288-    rw [update_eq] at hb ⊢
1289-    exact hb
1290-  · rw [update_neq ha] at hb ⊢
1291-    exact h hb
1292-
1293-end PartialMap

1296--- binding — e.g., the Simply Typed Lambda Calculus, which we will see in
1297--- *Type Systems*, where maps are used to keep track of which program
1298--- variables are defined in a given scope.

1300--- ## Reflection

1302-namespace Reflection
1303-
1304--- In this section, we will make use of some definitions and theorems about
1305--- natural numbers that we discussed and proved in previous chapters; copy
1306--- your solutions to those problems here:
1307-
1308-namespace Nat
1309-
1310-def even (n : Nat) :=

1339--- We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims in Lean: with
1340--- booleans (of type `Bool`), and with propositions (of type `Prop`).
1341-
1342--- Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1343-
1344--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
1345---     Check formatting:
1346-
1347--- - ⠀
1348--- - `Bool`
1349--- - `Prop`
1350--- - decidable?
1351--- - yes
1352--- - no
1353--- - useable with `match`?
1354--- - yes
1355--- - no
1356--- - works with `rewrite` tactic?
1357--- - no
1358--- - yes

1360--- The crucial difference between the two worlds is decidability. Every
1361--- (closed) Lean expression of type `Bool` can be simplified in a finite
1362--- number of steps to either `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a terminating
1363--- mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is true.
1364-
1365--- This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is inhabited only by
1366--- functions that, given a `Nat`, always yield either `true` or `false` in
1367--- finite time; and this, in turn, means (by a standard computability
1368--- argument) that there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether a
1369--- given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1370-
1371--- By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1372--- mathematical propositions; in particular, the type `Nat → Prop` does
1373--- contain functions representing properties like "the nth Turing machine
1374--- halts." The second row in the table follows directly from this essential
1375--- difference. To evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on a boolean, we
1376--- need to know whether the scrutinee evaluates to `true` or `false`; this
1377--- only works for `Bool`, not `Prop`.
1378-
1379--- The third row highlights an important practical difference: equality
1380--- functions like `Nat.beq` that return a boolean cannot be used directly to
1381--- justify rewriting with the rewrite tactic; propositional equality is
1382--- required for this. Since `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1383--- properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a property that
1384--- happens to be decidable: we can express it either as a boolean computation
1385--- or as a function into Prop.
1386-
1387--- As an example, we can write
1388-
1389-example : Nat.even 42 := rfl
1390-
1391--- or that there exists some `k` such that `42 = double k`.
1392-
1393-example : Nat.Even 42 := by exists 21
1394-
1395--- Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two characterizations of
1396--- evenness did not describe the same set of natural numbers!
1397-
1398--- Fortunately, they do! To prove this, we first need two helper lemmas.
1399-
1400-theorem even_double (k : Nat) : Nat.even (Nat.double k) = true := by
1401-  induction k with
1402-  | zero =>
1403-    rewrite [Nat.double_zero, Nat.even_zero]
1404-    rfl
1405-  | succ n ih =>
1406-    rewrite [Nat.double_succ, Nat.even_succ, Nat.even_succ, Bool.not_not]
1407-    exact ih

1411-theorem even_double_exists (n : Nat) :
1412-    ∃ (k : Nat), n = bif Nat.even n then Nat.double k else Nat.double k + 1 := by (
1413-  induction n with
1414-  | zero =>
1415-    exists 0
1416-  | succ n ih =>
1417-    obtain ⟨k, ih⟩ := ih
1418-    rewrite [Nat.even_succ]
1419-    by_cases h : Nat.even n
1420-    · exists k
1421-      rewrite [h] at ih ⊢
1422-      subst ih
1423-      rfl
1424-    · exists k + 1
1425-      rewrite [Bool.not_eq_true] at h
1426-      rewrite [h] at ih ⊢
1427-      subst ih
1428-      rewrite [cond_false, Bool.not_false, cond_true]
1429-      rfl)

1431--- Now the main theorem:
1432-
1433-theorem even_iff_Even {n : Nat} : Nat.even n = true ↔ Nat.Even n where
1434-  mp h := by
1435-    have ⟨k, hk⟩ := even_double_exists n
1436-    rewrite [h, cond_true] at hk
1437-    subst hk
1438-    exists k
1439-  mpr h := by
1440-    obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := h
1441-    subst hk
1442-    exact even_double k

1445--- is reflected in the truth of the proposition `∃ (k : Nat), n = k.double`.

1460--- So what should we do in situations where some claim could be formalized as
1461--- either a proposition or a boolean computation? Which should we choose?
1462-
1463--- In general, both can be useful. Which we choose has to do with the
1464--- *computational* nature of Lean's core language, which is designed so that
1465--- every function it expresses is total, and by default computable unless we
1466--- explicit indicate otherwise. As an example, consider trying to write a
1467--- function `α → α → Bool` checking for equality on an arbitrary type:

1527--- In general, Lean will try to use typeclass synthesis with `Decidable` in
1528--- order to determine when it is appropriate to use `Prop` and `Bool`
1529--- interchangeably. For instance, while our example `eq` failed above while
1530--- trying to use propositional equality `=` in the condition of an `if`
1531--- statement, we are allowed to write
1532-
1533-def nat_eq (m n : Nat) : Bool := if m = n then true else false
1534-
1535--- Why is this allowed? It is precisely because equality of natural numbers is
1536--- decidable, and Lean makes use of this fact. If we print this definition
1537--- with notation unset, we would find that it is using `instDecidableEqNat`
1538-
1539-set_option pp.all true in
1540-#print nat_eq
1541-
1542--- which proves that this equality is decidable.
1543-
1544--- This is only half the story however: while Lean's core theory enables this
1545--- computation, Lean is also often used in applications where we don't care
1546--- about computability, such as pure mathematics. In particular, it is
1547--- possible to write a function for arbitrary equality:
1548-
1549-sf_experiment
1550-  open scoped Classical in
1551-  noncomputable def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false
1552-  
1553-  set_option pp.all true in
1554-  #print eq
1555-
1556--- But we have indicated to Lean, using the `noncomputable` keyword and
1557--- `Classical` namespace, that we are *not* interested in computation. What is
1558--- happening in the background is that this allows typeclass synthesis to find
1559--- the scoped instance `Classical.propDecidable`, which makes use of the axiom
1560--- of choice to provide a proof that all propositions are *classically*
1561--- decidable. This sort of definition is suitable for use with proofs, but is
1562--- not allowed to be used in conjunction with computational features of Lean
1563--- such as the `decide` tactic or the `#eval` command.
